events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description: Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the VIDRINE present four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light's BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels.Featured Artworks: Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner — AnointedMichael Light — BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023Michael Pinsky — MammothDavid Buckland �� Bikini TextsAbout Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley (http://ourlifeishere.org)In 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with Marshallese youth and elders. This expedition—organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, with support from Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell—was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. Throughout 2026–27, the project runs across campus in exhibitions at Doe Library, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, Worth Ryder, and BAMPFA, along with courses and public programs. It culminates in an exhibition of original works at the David Brower Center, September 2027 – February 2028. ourlifeishere.org (https://art.berkeley.edu/ourlifeishere.org)About Worth Ryder Art Gallery / VIDRINE (https://art.berkeley.edu/gallery)The Worth Ryder Art Gallery (WRAG) is an educational art space that has served as a cultural and artistic resource and community center for undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, alumni, and the Bay Area community since 1960, and is a central social and artistic hub of the UC Berkeley Department of Art Practice. The gallery supports students in exhibiting their artwork in a professional gallery context, serves as an exhibition platform for emerging contemporary artistic strategies, and brings challenging and thought-provoking artwork to the UC Berkeley campus. It is named after painter and founding chair of the department, Worth Ryder. VIDRINE is Worth Ryder Art Gallery's ancillary space showcasing video, digital art, and installation. It is located around the corner from the Worth Ryder Art Gallery in the lobby of the Anthropology and Art Building.

events.title: Film Screening: Vivre sa vie
events.description: Vivre sa vie depicts Nana (Anna Karina), a naive shopgirl, at the brief, flickering moment when she takes responsibility for her life. Nana takes to the streets, becoming a prostitute and a student of human emotions. Brechtian in its use of twelve dispassionately announced tableaux, Vivre sa vie is also intensely personal. Nana's crucible is Jean-Luc Godard's existential epiphany: Nana struggles to see, and say, things as they are, bravely concluding, "All is good." In the famous scene in a movie theater, Nana's rapt attention to Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc is a tribute to another who sacrificed control to take control.

events.title: Film Screening: Kwaidan
events.description: Breathtakingly photographed on hand-painted sets, Kwaidan is at once a Japanese woodcut writ large, and an abstract wash of luminescent colors that seem to come from another world. An electronic soundtrack by avant-garde composer Toru Takemitsu plays hauntingly with natural sounds—crickets, rain, the cracking of wood, the loud silence of snow. Yet the stories—four of Lafcadio Hearn's ghostly tales—strangely contradict this plastic splendor in their simple, aching humanity. All are tales of mortals caught by forces beyond their comprehension when the supernatural world intervenes in their lives. This version of Kwaidan is the original three-hour Director's Cut.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ——————���—- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: Film Screening: GoodFellas
events.description: Working with trusted accomplices, including editor Thelma Schoonmaker, cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, actors Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci, and brilliant first-time collaborators Ray Liotta and Lorraine Bracco, Martin Scorsese combines varied cinematic styles, camera techniques, and a precisely executed collage of popular music, adapting Nicholas Pileggi's chronicle of real-life Mafia associate Henry Hill. Hurtling through some twenty-five years of "family" life, the riveting Liotta gives voice to Hill's chilling and funny first-person account. As focused on quotidian details as on dramatic moments, Scorsese wanted the movie to have a documentary feel, "as if you had 16mm cameras with these guys for 20, 25 years."

events.title: Galan Trio Concert
events.location: Wu Performance Hall (Morrison Hall Room 125), UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: In fall 2026, Galan Trio celebrates the 10th edition of Kinesis, marking five years since the project was launched in 2021. With this tour, Kinesis will reach the milestone of 50 U.S. universities, reflecting a network of collaborations that has continued to grow since the project's beginnings. For Kinesis, vol. 10, Galan Trio returns to the San Francisco Bay Area for the second time before continuing north to Oregon and Washington, expanding the project into the Pacific Northwest for the first time. The program features music by Bonnie Miksch, Ryan M. Howard, Bruce Hamilton, Ryan Francis, Michael Johanson, Cindy Cox, and Inés Thiebaut, including five new works commissioned by Galan Trio. The anniversary comes in the same year as the release of Kinesis Vol. 3 on Neuma Records, the third album dedicated to the project, marking another chapter in a series that continues to grow through new commissions, collaborations, performances and recordings.The first edition of the project featured the work of five composers who contributed one original work for piano trio reflecting on the period of the pandemic. Galan Trio counts four editions by now in East Coast, Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and South Central regions and works by Yiorgos Vassilandonakis, Martin Gendelman, Matthew Greenbaum, David Martynuik, Ken Steen, Alex Lubet, Navid Bargrizan, Larry Alan Smith and Richard Lavenda among others. The April 2024 edition in California features the work of Robert Denham, David Carter, Christopher Dobrian, Kevin Zhang, Pamela Madsen, Joao Pedro Oliveira, Deborah Kavasch, Ines Thibaut, Cindy Cox and Patricia Allessandrini.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z_2$ graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting , Wassersrein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans of tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondencebetween fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: NORTH STAR: A Movement Workshop
events.description: "you begin underneath all that concrete, down inside corridors, labyrinthine" —Quincy Troupe, "moving toward the open, toward the light" About the workshop: Where are you; where am I? How do we orient ourselves in relation to one another? In dialogue with the children's game "Marco Polo"—in which players with closed eyes orient themselves in response to sound and voice—artist Steffani Jemison will lead participants through a series of playful prompts connecting perspective, movement, language, and relation through guided improvisation. Gameplay will be preceded by a somatic warm-up and will integrate theory, fiction, and poetry; references may include Dionne Brand and Tyrone S. Palmer alongside Quincy Troupe. The workshop is suitable for anyone interested in testing contact, entanglement, and antagonism through lived experience; it might resonate particularly with creative writers, theorists, and performing artists. Physical movement in this workshop is adaptable to all bodies and physical capacities; no movement experience required. Come as you are.About the Artist: Steffani Jemison is an interdisciplinary artist and writer. In dialogue with interlocutors (living and ancestral), her work connects mark-making, gesture, projection, movement, and document. In 2026, her work is included in solo and group exhibitions at Lafayette Anticipations, Paris, FR; the New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York, NY; the Westfälischer Kunstverein, Münster, DE; the Moody Center, Houston, TX; the Studio Museum in Harlem, New York, NY; Buffalo AKG, Buffalo, NY; and the Carpenter Center, Cambridge, MA; among other venues. Jemison's work is part of many public collections, including the Museum of Modern Art, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Guggenheim Museum, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Studio Museum in Harlem. Jemison's novella A Rock, A River, A Street was published by Primary Information in 2022. She is an Associate Professor in the Department of Art & Design at Rutgers University-New Brunswick.

events.title: TAC Seminar - Konstantinos Kritos (Johns Hopkins)
events.description: Title: Two in one: gravitational-wave and electromagnetic signals from dense stellar environmentsAbstract: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaborations have observed a plethora of stellar-mass binary black holes merging in the local Universe through the detection of gravitational waves. Simultaneously, the JWST has revealed a diverse population of supermassive black holes and bound star clusters within the first billion years after the Big Bang. Moreover, an abundant number of Little Red Dots, which are hypothesized to be a new class of actively accreting massive black holes, have also been discovered by the JWST at high redshifts. In this seminar, I will introduce RAPSTER, a population synthesis code that simulates the evolution of the million-body problem within seconds, and is used to generate catalogs of compact object coalescences and stellar disruption events by compact objects in star clusters. I will argue that dense star clusters are ideal environments for the assembly of intermediate-mass black holes that bridge the gap between the stellar and supermassive species. Moreover, high-energy few-body dynamical interactions involving a massive black hole lead to rich multimessenger signals including extreme-mass ratio inspirals and tidal disruption events, that can be observed by current and future telescopes, such as the Rubin Observatory, the Roman Space Telescope, and LISA.Host: TBD

events.title: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing
events.description: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing Monday, November 2, 12:30 - 2:00 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1Rd-bqIFW9uq2WJK95uHg8WOYJHOAI14DXYfJCj-d0fk/edit) The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing (Cambridge University Press, 2026) examines the politics of Tunisia after the Arab Spring. Tunisia emerged as the one success story to transition to democracy, winning a Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its focus on inclusion and power-sharing. How, then, did its democracy collapse in 2021? Drawing on unique interviews with senior Tunisian officials, alongside three nationally representative surveys of the population, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy points to an overemphasis on compromise, consensus, and power-sharing. Although power-sharing institutions can be useful at the start of a transition, the book finds that extending them beyond that point can lead democracy to unravel by frustrating voters and spurring the rise of populists and extremists. The book takes an in-depth look at Tunisia's transition and then explores how far the theory travels through a quantitative analysis of all democratic transitions between 1942–2020. Overall, the book reveals the dark side of power-sharing, broadening our understanding of the causes of populism, polarization, and democratic breakdown. Sharan Grewal is an Associate Professor of Government at American University (https://www.american.edu/spa/faculty/sgrewal.cfm) and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution (https://www.brookings.edu/experts/sharan-grewal/). He was previously assistant professor at William & Mary and a research fellow at the Middle East Initiative (https://www.belfercenter.org/person/sharan-grewal) at Harvard. He received a PhD in Politics from Princeton University in 2018. Sharan's research examines revolutions and democratic transitions, particularly in the Arab world. His first book, Soldiers of Democracy? Military Legacies and the Arab Spring (Oxford University Press, 2023), explores the conditions under which militaries support or thwart democratic transitions, drawing on interviews and surveys of military personnel in Egypt and Tunisia. It received APSA's Best Book in MENA Politics (https://apsamena.org/2024/10/19/2023-mena-politics-section-award-winners/) Award and the Robert Jervis Best International Security Book (https://apsanet.org/membership/organized-sections/organized-section-awards/past-awards/section-19/) Award. His second book, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing, is forthcoming with Cambridge University Press in October 2026. Sharan's work has also been published in the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, and British Journal of Political Science, among other journals. These papers have explored when Islamists become democrats, how discrimination shapes Muslim migrants, and why US training politicizes foreign militaries. These pieces have won Best Paper and Article Awards from APSA MENA and APSA's Democracy & Autocracy section, as well as the Perry World House-Foreign Affairs Emerging Scholars Prize. Sharan's research has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the Henry Luce Foundation, the John Templeton Foundation, the Smith Richardson Foundation, and the Defense Security Cooperation University. He writes regularly about Middle East politics for Brookings andthe Washington Post, and has been interviewed by the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Reuters, among others. He serves on the editorial board of the journal Comparative Politics.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Chenhao Jin: Emergent Excitations in Semiconducting Moiré Superlattices
events.description: Emergent Excitations in Semiconducting Moiré Superlattices Excitations in quantum systems govern their responses to intrinsic and extrinsic perturbations. Emergent excitations from the interplay between topology and correlation can drive new phase instabilities and enable novel device concepts. While a plethora of intriguing ground states are reported in two-dimensional flatband systems, it has been challenging to directly probe excitations, particularly those decoupled from the charge sector. In this talk, I will discuss our recent efforts to investigate excitations in semiconducting moiré superlattices. We developed an ultrafast imaging technique to record their complete space-time evolution, such as space-and-time-resolved transport. This allows us to simultaneously capture and separate multiple collective excitations, identify their nature, and distinguish them from conventional ones. These emergent excitations govern dynamic responses of the system and play a central role in phase stability and transition. Our results highlight new insights encoded in collective excitations and open avenues for studying and engineering correlated quantum systems through nonequilibrium approaches.Speaker Bio: Dr. Chenhao Jin is an assistant professor of Physics at UC Santa Barbara. He received a B.S. in Physics from Peking University and PhD in Physics from UC Berkeley. He was a Kavli fellow at Cornell University before moving to UC Santa Barbara in 2021. Dr. Jin's research focuses on developing new optical spectroscopy and imaging techniques to "watch" quantum phenomena in space and time; and has made seminal contributions to optical studies of van der Waals materials and moiré superlattices. Dr. Jin has received multiple awards, including AFOSR YIP award, NSF CAREER award, ARO ECP award, Blavatnik Regional Awards for Young Scientists, and Sloan Research Fellowship.

events.title: RTG Arithmetic Geometry, Number Theory and Representation Theory Seminar: Algebraic theory of indefinite theta functions
events.description: Speaker: Kenz Kallal, Princeton UniversityJacobi's theta function $\Theta (q) := 1 + 2q + 2q^4 + 2q^9 + \cdots $, and more generally the theta functions associated to positive-definite quadratic forms, have the property that they are modular forms of half-integral weight. The usual proof of this fact is completely analytic in nature, using the Poisson summation formula. However, Θ is also related to diffusion of heat on a uniform circle-shaped material: it is a restriction of the fundamental solution to the heat equation on a circle. By algebraically characterizing the heat equation as a specific flat connection on a certain bundle on a modular curve, we produce a completely algebraic technique for proving modularity of theta functions. More specifically, we produce a refinement of the algebraic theory of theta functions due to Moret-Bailly, Faltings–Chai, and Candelori. As a consequence of the algebraic nature of our theory and the fact that it applies to indefinite quadratic forms / non-ample line bundles (which the prior algebraic theory does not), we also generalize the Kudla–Millson analytic theory of theta functions for indefinite quadratic forms to the case of torsion coefficients. This is joint work with Akshay Venkatesh.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Gabriel Granato - "Can Religion Bridge Ethnic Divides? Pastors, Chiefs, and a Field Experiment on Collective Action"
events.description: Abstract: Ethnic fragmentation is often associated with worse economic development. In one prominent mechanism, free-riding in heterogeneous societies undermines public good provision. This paper examines whether religious and ethnic leaders can sustain cooperation in a voluntary public-works program in an ethnically diverse city in the D.R. Congo. Residents are randomly assigned to ethnically homogeneous or mixed work teams that either include an ethnic chief, a pastor, or no leader at all. Chiefs increase work by 6.0 percentage points in homogeneous teams but not in mixed ones, while pastors increase work by 5.8 points in mixed teams but not in homogeneous ones. Heterogeneity by the strength of ethnic attachment explains this reversal. Chiefs still mobilize their coethnics on mixed teams, and on homogeneous teams their effect is concentrated among teams of residents who report a strong ethnic identity. Pastors do increase work on homogeneous teams whose members have weak ethnic attachments, and their effect is largest on mixed teams whose members hold strong but competing ethnic identities. A cross-randomized public disclosure intervention provides further evidence that the chief mobilizes labor contributions through social enforcement while the pastor uses internal incentives. The paper provides the first experimental evidence on how religious leaders can sustain voluntary public-goods provision in fragmented societies.

events.title: R. Aída Hernández Castillo | Digging for Hope: A Feminist Ethnography in the Land of Mass Graves
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event description In the shadow of Mexico's ongoing human rights crisis, Digging for Hope: A Feminist Ethnography in the Land of Mass Graves (University of Arizona Press, 2026) offers a powerful feminist ethnography of resistance, care, and collective memory. Drawing on nearly a decade of fieldwork, R. Aída Hernández Castillo documents the courageous work of women-led search collectives who, in the face of extreme violence, search for their disappeared loved ones. Through physical and spiritual practices such as exhumation, mourning, and poetic remembrance, these women reclaim dignity for the dead and challenge a society that has normalized disappearance. At the heart of this book is a profound exploration of what Hernández Castillo calls a "pedagogy of love" — a political and ethical framework rooted in care, solidarity, and the refusal to forget. These women are not only searching for bodies; they are building emotional communities, crafting new languages of justice, and offering a reimagining of what it means to resist violence. Their practices, often overlooked by traditional scholarship, restore humanity and dignify the disappeared. Digging for Hope is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand the gendered dimensions of violence and the grassroots movements that rise in response. With clarity and compassion, Hernández Castillo brings readers into the intimate spaces of grief and resistance, offering a model for feminist ethnography that is both rigorous and deeply humane. Hernández Castillo will discuss her book in conversation with Diana Negrin and Omar Gómez Trejo. Hybrid event: in person and on Zoom. Zoom meeting link: https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/99595708560SpeakersRosalva Aída Hernández Castillo is a professor and senior researcher at the Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (Center for Research and Higher Studies in Social Anthropology) in Mexico City. Her academic work has promoted Indigenous and women's rights in Latin America with a focus on Mexico's incarcerated and disappeared populations. She is the author of 22 books.Diana Negrin (Geography) is a geographer and curator with a focus on identity, space, and social movements in Latin America and the United States. She conducts ethnographic and archival research in the Mexican states of Jalisco and Nayarit with a primary focus on urban Indigenous university students and young professionals. Her scholarship engages human and cultural geography, critical race theory, cultural studies, political ecology and urban studies. Her current research examines the politics of solidarity within interracial and cross-geographic alliances that mobilize around Indigenous culture and territory.Omar Gómez Trejo received his law degree from the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (National Autonomous University of Mexico) and holds a master's from the Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (Latin American Faculty of Social Sciences). He worked for the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights for 12 years in Mexico and Central America. He was the Executive Secretary of the Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts for the Ayotzinapa case (2015-2016) and was the lead Prosecutor of the Special Unit for the Investigation and Litigation of the Ayotzinapa case at Mexico's Attorney General Office from June 2019 to September 2022. Most recently, he was a visiting scholar at the Berkeley Law Human Rights Center through the Practitioners at Risk program.

events.title: Seminar 208, Microeconomic Theory: "Asymmetric Rationality: Protocol Design and Behavioral Anomalies."
events.description: Abstract: We study how asymmetric rationality in strategic interactions can generate seemingly anomalous patterns of belief updating and behavior. A boundedly rational receiver designs a finite-state decision protocol to learn from a fully rational, privately informed, and biased sender who controls the flow of information. The receiver must allocate scarce memory between learning and incentive provision. We identify a simple class of protocols sufficient for optimal design and show how their structure generates information disengagement, indecision, and polarization. The receiver hesitates before deciding but becomes unresponsive to further evidence afterward. Identical receivers following the same protocol can reach opposing decisions despite receiving the same sequence of signals, with the probability of disagreement remaining bounded away from zero as their payoffs approach the optimum. These behaviors, which might otherwise appear erratic or psychologically driven, arise from the strategic use of limited memory.

events.title: Shu-ou Shan: "Accurate Decision Making during Protein Biogenesis"
events.description: Proper protein biogenesis is a pre-requisite for the generation and maintenance of a functional proteome. Accumulating data show that this process begins early, when nascent proteins emerge from the ribosome. Within seconds, the nascent polypeptide must engage the correct set of biogenesis factors and commit to the proper biogenesis pathway. These early decisions profoundly influence the folding, assembly, localization, maturation, and quality control of nascent proteins. How are nascent proteins selected and triaged into the appropriate biogenesis pathways? How does the cellular chaperone network handle aggregation-prone membrane/organellar proteins during their biogenesis? Our work aims to address these fundamental questions at biochemical and biophysical resolution, by integrating quantitative approaches in biochemistry, biophysics and mechanistic enzymology with structural and molecular cell biology. In this talk, I will describe recent work that begin to elucidate how diverse protein biogenesis machinery coordinate in space and time at the ribosome to ensure the efficiency and fidelity of cotranslational protein biogenesis, and how the biophysical properties of nascent proteins shaped the emergence of multi-layered biogenesis pathways.

events.title: Analysis and PDE Seminar: Multi-channel distorted Fourier analysis and stability of one-dimensional multi-solitons.
events.description: Speaker: Gong Chen, Georgia TechDistorted Fourier transforms diagonalize perturbed Schrödinger operators and play a central role in the analysis of asymptotic stability for a single soliton. In the multi-soliton problem, however, linearization around a train of moving coherent structures leads instead to an equation with several localized potentials moving at distinct velocities, commonly known as a charge-transfer model. Thus, to prove asymptotic stability of multi-solitons, one needs robust dispersive and localized decay estimates for such multi-potential linear flows. In this talk, I will focus on the one-dimensional setting, where the main linear difficulty is no longer the construction of a single distorted Fourier transform, but rather the need to use several moving distorted Fourier charts and glue them consistently across the regions between solitons. I will describe a multi-channel scattering construction for one-dimensional charge-transfer models.As an application, I will discuss the asymptotic stability problem for multi-solitons of the one-dimensional $L^2$-supercritical nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The linear charge-transfer theory provides dispersive and localized decay estimates for radiation in moving multi-potential backgrounds. Combined with modulation equations and a finite-dimensional center-stable condition that removes the unstable modes of the supercritical solitons, this yields asymptotic stability of multi-solitons.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Chung-Pei Ma: Gravity's Fatal Attraction: Black Holes at the Centers of Galaxies
events.description: Gravity's Fatal Attraction: Black Holes at the Centers of Galaxies Black holes are spectacular end products of the fatal attraction of gravity. Residing at the centers of galaxies, supermassive black holes have masses up to 20 billion suns and directly impact the evolution of their host galaxies. I will highlight recent progress in studying black holes in the giant elliptical galaxy M87 and other massive galaxies enabled by integral-field spectroscopy on the James Webb Space Telescope and the Keck Telescopes. I will also discuss the implications of these results for the low-frequency gravitational waves from merging supermassive black hole binaries probed by the ongoing Pulsar Timing Array experiments. Speaker Bio: Chung-Pei Ma is the Judy Chandler Webb Professor in Physical Sciences and Distinguished Professor in Astronomy and Physics at UC Berkeley. She uses luminous matter to study dark components in the universe: dark matter, dark energy, and black holes. Her research group develops both theoretical and observational tools to investigate the cosmic assembly of black holes and galaxies. She is an avid violin player and was a student at the New England Conservatory of Music in Boston while pursuing her undergraduate and PhD studies in physics at MIT.

events.title: Julia Budka (LMU Munich), "Cultural Diversity in the Nile Valley during the New Kingdom: Challenging Monolithic Understandings of Egypt and Nubia"
events.description: In recent years, Egyptian and Sudanese archaeology has made significant progress in exploring cultural variability and diversity. Moving beyond oversimplified notions of identity, the concept of cultural diversity enables us to develop more nuanced narratives by integrating a wide range of archaeological evidence and analytical approaches. This lecture offers a fresh perspective on cultural diversity in the Nile Valley during the New Kingdom, drawing on recent excavations and new scientific analyses of material culture. It highlights the complexity of ancient social dynamics and challenges modern perceptions of fixed cultural and political boundaries between Pharaonic Egypt and Nubia (present-day northern Sudan). Furthermore, it questions the long-standing assumption that Egyptian and Nubian societies can be understood as culturally homogeneous or monolithic entities.

events.title: Tendon thread feat. Tanya Lukin Linklater
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture, presented as part of BCNM's Indigenous Technologies program, curated by Indigenous Technologies Coordinator Talia Dixon, co-sponsored by the Arts Practice Department, the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies, and the Graduate Students of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies with Tanya Lukin Linklater Artist-Choreographer and Faculty Mentor, Institute of American Indian Arts - Monday, November 2, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScK01nSupvyyNJV1xSGzG8Gol7h0iXJEiqUM9ucuwBhNkMCuA/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=N3FoYm1uYWs0b25vb2FnazZyaDcybWhxNzYgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Compelled by lineages of Sugpiaq cultural work and our continuance despite imperial and colonial disruptions of our lifeways, Tanya Lukin Linklater will discuss her ongoing practice of visiting ancestral belongings, Sugpiaq technologies, in museum collections. The talk will then bring into focus her speculative responses to photographic documentation of Sugpiaq belongings in the Kunstkamera in St. Petersburg, Russia. Coupled with her meditations on estuaries, grasses, and customary practices of the Kodiak archipelago, these threads organize Crested, her solo exhibition at Portikus, Frankfurt, and Tendon thread, a performance commission for the Center for Human Rights and the Arts and Fisher Center at Bard College, premiering in winter 2026. Workshop Opportunity Tanya Lukin Linklater will also host a hands-on workshop for UC Berkeley students and community members, expanding on the content of her talk, the following afternoon, Tuesday, November 3, from 4:30 to 6:30 pm, at Bancroft Dance Studio (https://tdps.berkeley.edu/about/directions/bancroft). Participation is limited to 25 people, and requires completion of this brief application (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf2zl8_3bpc7HPinRsBotpgW9yoCmahdgrUtbY6FTxiMKFRMg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Selected participants will be notified approximately one week prior to the workshop. About Tanya Lukin Linklater Tanya Lukin Linklater makes dances in museums, videos, sculptures, and works on paper. She thinks with weather, embodiment, beingness, and ancestral belongings in her practice. She is compelled by scores, orality, poetics, embodied inquiry, Indigenous knowledge transmission, and ephemerality. Her recent and forthcoming exhibitions and performances include Camden Art Centre, London, UK; Dia Art Foundation, New York; National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa; Portikus, Frankfurt; Rudolfinum, Prague; SITE SANTA FE; and Fisher Center at Bard, Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. Her artworks have entered the collections of Agnes Etherington Art Centre, Art Gallery of Ontario, Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Remai Modern, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Tate Americas Foundation, Vancouver Art Gallery, Walker Art Center, and elsewhere. Her book, Slow Scrape (2nd edition, Talonbooks, Vancouver 2022), draws on documentary poetics, concrete-based installations, event scores, and can be read alongside her choreographic practice. Her recent publications include contributions to The Routledge Companion to Indigenous Art Histories in the United States and Canada, Jeffrey Gibson: the space in which to place me, Mark: Sonya Kelliher-Combs, and Native Visual Sovereignty: A Reader on Art and Performance. In 2024 she was awarded a post-doctoral fellowship in Decolonial and Transformational Indigenous Art Practices with Dr. Heather Igloliorte, Canada Excellence Research Chair, at University of Victoria. A dedicated educator, Tanya was a faculty mentor in the Institute of American Indian Arts' MFA in Studio Arts 2021-2026. About Indigenous Technologies Indigenous Technologies is a program of BCNM that engages questions of technology and new media in relation to global structures of indigeneity, settler colonialism, and genocide in the 21st century. Our Indigenous Tech events and ongoing conversations with Indigenous scholars and communities aim to critically envision and reimagine what a more just and sustainable technological future can look like. We highlight Indigenous engagements with robotics, computer science, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, social media, online activism, video games, and more.

events.title: 3-Manifold Seminar: 1-pronged pseudo-Anosov flows, contact structures, and entropy
events.description: Speaker: Audrey Rosevear, UC BerkeleyRecent work by a variety of people has uncovered deep connections between certain pseudo-Anosov flows and associated contact structures via open book decompositions. In this talk, I'll discuss how to extend those results to the 1-pronged case. I'll show that there are infinitely many Reeb-like 1-pronged pseudo-Anosov flows on every 3-manifold, and that the associated 1-pronged singular set shares many properties of the binding of an open book decomposition: in its complement, the contact structure is tight, has 0 Giroux torsion, and the cylindrical contact homology has exponential homotopical growth. This final property gives the first non-fibered knots in the standard $S^3 $ which force positive topological entropy for Reeb flows.

events.title: Merck Symposium
events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeMerck Symposium Flyer (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/72-merck-symposium-flyer)Catalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Kapil Ramachandran: Neuroproteasomes and the spatial control of neuronal proteostasis
events.description: Neurons must synthesize proteins at precise times, in response to external cues, and in compartments far from the cell body. Nascent proteins are particularly susceptible to misfolding, yet the mechanisms that rapidly monitor proteins made in dendrites remain poorly understood. We discovered a distinct population of proteasomes that appears to span the neuronal plasma membrane, where these "neuroproteasomes" degrade a subset of proteins during or immediately after translation. Despite evidence for neuroproteasomes across multiple systems, how they associate with the membrane, which proteins they select, and their functions in neurons remain largely unknown. I will argue that neuroproteasomes offer a new cell biological framework for the initiation of protein aggregation, while their constitutive activity converts intracellular proteolysis into extracellular neuromodulation.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: Joshua Schwartzstein "Channeled Attention and Stable Errors"
events.description: Abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant fail, in the long run, to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn't matter or that a distinction doesn't exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the model. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its stakes; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves. Paper Link: https://gagnon-bartsch.com/files/ChanneledAttention2026.pdf

events.title: Topology Seminar: Exotic R4's with Compactly Supported Diffeomorphisms
events.description: Speaker: Abhishek Shivkumar, UT AustinA diffeomorphism is exotic if it is topologically but not smoothly isotopic to the identity. We show that for diffeomorphisms of closed simply-connected $4$-manifolds dissolving under a single stabilization, there is a natural induced diffeomorphism on an exotic copy of $R^4$. We thereby construct exotic copies of $R^4$ with nontrivial compactly supported mapping class groups of arbitrarily large rank. This follows from a modified construction of corks for exotic diffeomorphisms due to Krushkal-Mukherjee-Powell-Warren. Time permitting, we will show how these examples can be extended to uncountable families thereof by end-summing with a particular exotic R4.

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Fueling Patriarchy: Coal and Gender in the Upper Silesian Cultural Imagination
events.description: As the material foundation of industrialization, coal shaped not only economic processes but also social orders and cultural imaginaries in Central Europe – nowhere more visibly than in Upper Silesia, where coal's materiality helped generate a gendered division of labor: men worked below ground as active providers, women remained above ground in domestic, passive roles. Coal did not merely accompany this patriarchal gender order; it materially produced and sustained it. Drawing on energy humanities and feminist resource theory – most notably Cara Daggett's concept of petromasculinity – this talk traces how this coal-based gender matrix was consolidated, reproduced, and eventually destabilized in Upper Silesian literature, film, and performance from the early twentieth to the twenty-first century. Beginning with early twentieth-century literary representations, I show how cultural production consolidated a patriarchal, heteronormative matrix marked by hypermasculinity and the marginalization of women – a matrix that persisted through socialist realism and postsocialist transformation despite shifting political contexts. Only with the gradual closure of Upper Silesia's coal mines amid Poland's and the Czech Republic's energy transitions in the twenty-first century does a break emerge with this symbolic order: as coal's material grip loosens, so too does the heteronormative order it once underwrote. At the same time, cultural representation takes on a new discursive role, shifting from an instrument consolidating heteronormative codes into a space for renegotiating them. This becomes visible, for instance, in the Netflix series Królowa (2022) and in the drag and burlesque performances of the artistic-research collective Śląsk Przegięty, both of which recast coal and queerness not as opposites but as entangled parts of the region's identity. The talk aims to uncover the entanglements of coal and gender in Upper Silesia, showing how, as coal itself recedes, cultural representation becomes the space where its gender legacies are contested, undone, and reimagined.

events.title: Stefanie Hutka // What Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Stefanie Hutka, design leader and author ofWhat Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation. Stefanie has spent her career asking a question that sounds simple until you try to answer it: what should automation actually do, and for whom? ​Her talk centers on what she calls the "Automation Strategy Gap," the yawning distance between an organization's AI ambitions and its actual readiness to do something useful with them. It is, she argues, alarmingly wide. Drawing on human factors, cognitive science, and management theory, her book makes the case that AI is the latest chapter in a long history of automation, and that the durable lessons were always there, we just got distracted by the hype. One particularly useful provocation: automation accelerates the system you already have. Which means the first thing worth mapping is the beliefs driving your organization before you automate anything at all. ​This is a book launch talk. It will be an essential conversation for anyone who has sat through a roadmap presentation where "AI-powered" was doing a lot of heavy lifting where a strategy should have been. This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Joy Nakato (CTML GSR)
events.description: Don't miss the next session of the CTML Seminar Series on Wednesday, November 4th, where CTML GSR Joy Nakato (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/joy-zora-nakato) will discuss "Leveraging Historical Data to Improve Efficiency in Longitudinal Clinical Trials." This talk will take place from 12:00PM-1:00PM at Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401. Abstract: Covariate adjustment is a well-established way to increase the precision of treatment effect estimates in randomized trials and has been endorsed by regulators. Recent methods extend this idea by using historical data to build prognostic scores that summarize a patient's expected outcome. In this talk, I will give an overview of how these approaches extend to longitudinal continuous outcomes, discuss the statistical challenges that arise in these settings, and share practical considerations and recommendations. Bio: Joy Zora Nakato is a PhD student in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley mentored by Laura Balzer and Mark van Der Laan. Her research interests include using targeted machine learning and causal inference to address challenges that arise during design and analysis of clinical trials and observational studies. She is currently working on efficient estimation of causal effects in Cluster Randomized trials addressing differential measurement and mediation with an application to uptake of HIV biomedical prevention among high risk populations in rural Uganda and Kenya.

events.title: Italian Lives, Belgian Coal An Environmental History of Labor and Migration
events.description: On June 23, 1946, Italy and Belgium signed the "men in exchange for coal" agreement, in which Italy committed to sending fifty thousand workers each year to the Belgian coal mines, and Belgium pledged to supply a few thousand tons of coal to Italy each month. The first treaty of its kind, the agreement paved the way for the European Coal and Steel Community, a precursor of the European Union. In Italian Lives, Belgian Coal, Daniele Valisena explores the relationship between labor migration, coal extraction, and environmental transformation in the Belgian coalfields of Wallonia. Drawing from French, Italian, and Belgian archival documents; printed primary sources; and oral history interviews conducted by the author, this book breaks new methodological and empirical ground, blending environmental history and the history of migration, historical literature and anthropological work, and history and the contemporary. Each chapter captures and interrogates the agency of different actors, including the Italian and Belgian states, the coal industry, medical experts, miners, and the ecologies that develop in polluted areas left by the coal industry. Italian Lives, Belgian Coal tells a sobering story of the environmental and corporeal injustice wielded by capitalist institutions and its impact on health and medical science, society, and nature.Daniele Valisena, Visiting Fellow, German Historical Institute, UC Berkeley

events.title: Joel Lehman: Open-endedness, Intelligence, and Flourishing
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, November 28, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill Hall Speaker: Joel Lehman (https://joellehman.com/) Affiliation: Author of Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned

events.title: REI Colloquium: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability
events.location: Social Sciences Building 402 Barrows Hall Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability Imigration policy and enforcement practices in the United States now extend beyond the border to the country's interior, impacting the private lives of millions of undocumented and mixed-status families in new ways. Sanctuary Making traces this shift, showing how as enforcement has expanded and deepened, new "hot spots" have appeared across nontraditional sites such as neighborhoods, roads, worksites, hospitals, grocery stores, and homes. Undercurrents of fear, anxiety, and loss permeate the everyday lives of the families navigating these terrains of enforcement. Carolina Valdivia reveals the emotional and material labor of young adults that often underpins families' sanctuary making efforts—strategies to shield against the worst outcomes of enforcement. Many young adults are compelled to take on parental responsibilities and serve as a primary source of emotional support for family members while also brokering legal processes tied to their family's immigration cases. How might policymakers, organizers, educators, and the wider community better support these young people in their efforts to create sanctuary for their families in an increasingly hostile landscape? More about the book: https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper)This event is co-organized by the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative and the Institute of Governmental Studies' Race, Ethnicity, and Immigration Colloquia Series. The event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Center for Race and Gender.About the Speaker:Carolina Valdivia is an Associate Professor of Criminology, Law and Society at the University of California, Irvine. Carolina's research interests include immigration, law and society, the sociology of education, race and ethnicity, youth and families, and the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Her work explores how various forms of legal and social exclusion impact the lives of immigrant youth and their families, including their educational trajectories, mental health, and political participation. You can find the rest of her biography here: https://carolinavaldivia.org/ (https://carolinavaldivia.org/)This is an accessible event. events.title: What Can Israeli Theatre Do? From Screen to Stage with Ronnie Brodetzky
events.description: Helen Diller Institute Literary Series, Session I*Co-sponsored by the Center for Jewish Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature, UC BerkeleyPublic Event What can Israeli theatre say at a moment when the boundaries of permissible speech are being fiercely contested? Ronnie Brodetzky, one of Israel's most successful contemporary theatre directors, belongs to a new generation of women reshaping a field long dominated by men. From bold stagings of canonical works such as Tartuffe and Twelfth Night to experimental productions like Typing…, created from real WhatsApp conversations, and How to Get Up from a Chair, inspired by YouTube tutorials, Brodetzky transforms both dramatic literature and the media of everyday life into surprising theatrical forms. In conversation with Yael Segalovitz, she will discuss making art amid Israel's political pressures, turning private speech into public performance, and what live theatre can reveal about contemporary Israeli society. Expect a lively conversation about art, politics, digital life, and the pleasures and perils of putting Israel onstage.Ronnie Brodetzky, Israeli theatre director, creator, and writer; winner of the 2020 Rosenblum Performing Arts Award and 2023 Directing Award by The Cameri Theatre; author of An Almost Olympic-Sized Pool (2016)Yael Segalovitz, Joan Bieder Visiting Professor of Jewish and Hebrew Literature, Helen Diller Institute, UC Berkeley; Comparative Literature Department, UC Berkeley; Assistant Professor, Ben-Gurion University of the NegevRegister: https://HDILiterarySeries2.rsvpify.com (https://HDILiterarySeries2.rsvpify.com)

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: If it looks like a duck…
events.description: Speaker: Izak Oltman, Northwestern University…and quacks like a duck, it might be a Berezin–Toeplitz operator. In this talk, I will present a version of Beals's theorem for Berezin–Toeplitz operators, specifically for the quantization of the complex projective line. Beals's theorem gives a criterion for recognizing pseudodifferential operators. Roughly speaking, if an operator satisfies certain bounds on its repeated commutators, then it is the quantization of a function with uniform derivative estimates. I will first go over Beals's theorem, then briefly discuss Berezin–Toeplitz operators. Finally, I will present a Beals-type theorem for the complex projective line and go over the proof. The talk will include many animations and examples. This is joint work with Simon Becker and Akshat Kumar.
