events.title: Hanna Martens: Aging: A Glitch in the Matrix?
events.description: Aging is accompanied by profound changes in tissue architecture, extracellular matrix (ECM) composition, and mechanical properties. Yet how cells sense and respond to these changes, and how the progressive loss of mechanical homeostasis contributes to age-associated tissue dysfunction, remains poorly understood.Our work explores how mechanotransduction pathways integrate physical cues from the extracellular environment to maintain cellular identity, tissue organization, and organ function throughout life. In particular, we focus on the transcriptional co-regulators YAP and TAZ, key effectors of mechanotransduction that couple ECM-derived signals to gene expression programs governing tissue homeostasis.We investigate how age-associated alterations in YAP/TAZ signaling disrupt the reciprocal relationship between cells and their extracellular environment, promoting cellular senescence, aberrant tissue remodeling, and deterioration of specialized cellular niches. Together, our findings highlight mechanical homeostasis as a fundamental determinant of tissue integrity and suggest that its disruption is an important driver of organ aging and age-associated tissue dysfunction.Division(s): Divisions of Biochemistry, Biophysics & Structural Biology, Division of Cell Biology, Development & Physiology, and Genetics, Genomics, Evolution & Development

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Quantum Interconnects and Modularity via Waveguide QED
events.description: In this talk, we present a demonstration of entanglement distribution via directional photon emission and absorption along a microwave waveguide [1,2]. Superconducting qubits couple to the waveguide at multiple, well-separated locations through modules that deterministically emit and absorb single microwave photons. Using this architecture, we demonstrate directional single-photon emission with 96% fidelity and single-photon absorption exceeding 60% efficiency. We then use partial emission and absorption to generate remote entanglement – a four-qubit W-state ��� between qubits in the emitter and absorber modules with 62% fidelity. Time permitting, we also present an example of driven dissipative entanglement reaching 89% fidelity [3]. These works along with 3D integration target modular and extensible quantum information processing mediated by quantum interconnects. [1] B. Kannan, et al., Nature Physics 19, 394 (2023) | arXiv:2203.01430 (2022) [2] A. Almanakly, et al., Nature Physics 21, 825 (2025) | arXiv:2408.05164 (2024) [3] A. Almanakly, et al., arXiv:2606.13375 (2026) William D. Oliver is jointly appointed the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Professor of Physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he leads the Engineering Quantum Systems Group. He is presently on partial leave as Chief Engineer withGoogle Quantum AI. Will's research interests include the materials growth, fabrication, design, control, and measurement of superconducting qubit processors. From 2003-2023, Will also worked at MIT Lincoln Laboratory – most recently as Laboratory Fellow (2017-2023) – where he was instrumental in growing the quantum computing group to its present levels. Will stepped down from this position to co-found Atlantic Quantum, a quantum computing start-up. Atlantic Quantum was acquired by Google in October 2025. Will is elected Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Fellow of the American Physical Society, and Fellow of the IEEE. He also serves on the U.S. National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee. Will earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University, his M.S. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from MIT, and a B.S. in Electrical Engineering and B.A. in Japanese from the University of Rochester (NY).

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Marshall Burke
events.description: Description: Wildfires and the smoke they produce are the fastest growing environmental threat in the US and many other parts of the world. I review recent advances in the measurement of smoke and its constituents, and recent advances in the quantification of both short- and long-term health impacts from smoke exposure and from exposure to the fires themselves. We estimate that short-run smoke exposure causes tens of thousands of deaths annually, a number that will likely grow due to climate change absent substantial intervention. We study the impacts of a leading proposed intervention – prescribed burning – and estimate meaningful net reductions in smoke exposure if the state were to meet its stated prescribed burning targets. Bio: Marshall Burke is professor of Global Environmental Policy in the Doerr School of Sustainability at Stanford, and a senior fellow at the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, and Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, all at Stanford. He is also a research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. He holds a PhD in Agricultural and Resource Economics from UC Berkeley, and a BA in International Relations from Stanford. He directs the Environmental Change and Human Outcomes Lab at Stanford, is co-founder of AtlasAI, and co-creator of the Environmental Hazards Adaptation Atlas.

events.title: Ergodic operators Seminar: Sturmian discrete and metric graphs - appearance and absence of gaps.
events.description: Speaker: Ram Band, TechnionWe study the spectra of Sturmian Schrödinger operators on graphs (either metric or discrete). A Sturmian sequence is an aperiodic sequence which is determined by an irrational frequency. These sequences are used to form aperiodic graph structures.We consider the integrated density of states (IDS) for Schroedinger operators on such graphs. The gap labelling theory predicts all the possible gaps in the spectra of these operators. We explicitly compute the gap labels; we show which gaps appear in the spectrum and which are absent, and why.The talk is based on joint works with Siegfried Beckus, Raphael Loewy and Gilad Sofer.

events.title: Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans
events.description: Racism in maternal healthcare is not reserved for the poor. Wealthier black people are much more likely to die during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period than their white counterparts. Expecting Inequityfocuses on a San Francisco obstetrics clinic that caters to the affluent, examining the choices around prenatal care and childbirth that class-privileged, pregnant black people are making in order to survive what has been called the "black maternal health crisis."Khiara M. Bridges is the Earl Warren Professor of Public Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. She is a nationally-recognized expert on the intersection of race, class, and reproductive rights. Her scholarship has appeared in the most influential law reviews in the country, including the flagship law journals at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and UC Berkeley, among many others. She is also the author of several books: Reproducing Race: An Ethnography of Pregnancy as a Site of Racialization (2011), The Poverty of Privacy Rights (2017), and Critical Race Theory: A Primer (2019, 2026). Her fourth book, Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans, was released in March 2026. Bridges graduated as valedictorian from Spelman College, receiving her degree in three years. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School and her Ph.D., with distinction, from Columbia University's Department of Anthropology. She speaks fluent Spanish and basic Arabic, and she is a classically-trained ballet dancer who danced professionally in New York City for twenty years before moving to the Bay Area.

events.title: From Evening Fog to Light and Dark: What Sōseki took from "The Tale of Genji"
events.description: Natsume Sōseki is usually read as the Japanese novelist who learned his craft from the West. But what did he take from Murasaki Shikibu, his greatest Japanese predecessor? Although he claimed not to care much for the Tale of Genji, I present evidence in the talk that Sōseki did read the Genji closely. Tracing echoes of the Genji in Sanshiro,The Gate, Kokoro, and Light and Dark, I argue that Sōseki learned more from Lady Muraski than he acknowledged about how the art of the novel can shed light on the darkest corners of the emotional lives of men and women. [BIO] Keith Vincent teaches in the Department of World Languages & Literatures at Boston University, where he directs the MFA Program in Literary Translation. Recent publications include "Genji's Ghosts" in The Literary Imagination (Spring 2026) and "Proust in Japan and Japan in Proust: Notes on Yoshida Jō and the École japonaise of Proust Studies" in Global Japanese History and Culture(Routledge, 2026). Forthcoming this year is an essay on Proust and TheThousand and One Nights.

events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: Cacti, toggles, and reverse plane partitions
events.description: Speaker: Iva Halacheva, Northeastern UniversityWe consider crystals B(nx) for a simply-laced Lie algebra, where n is a positive integer, and x is a minuscule highest weight. In this setting, the crystals are captured by a combinatorial model of reverse plane partitions on heaps, visualized as an abacus sitting on top of the Dynkin diagram. There are two group actions in this setting that capture some of the symmetries of the crystals – by the cactus group and the so-called toggle group which in type A corresponds to the Berenstein-Kirillov group of Bender-Knuth involutions. It is expected that the cactus group action will factor through the action of the toggle group – a property known in type A. I will discuss work in progress that establishes this property in type D, as well as some consequences for the cactus group. This is joint work with Devin Brown and Balazs Elek.

events.title: [BCLB] Smaller Scope, High Stakes: The EU Due Diligence Directive and Business
events.description: The EU's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) was once billed as the most ambitious corporate accountability law in the world. It creates a direct obligation on corporations to conduct sustainability and human rights due diligence. Then came the Omnibus. The scope has narrowed and the timeline has shifted, but the directive has not gone away, and it still reaches large non-EU companies with significant business in the EU. What does the CSDDD now require, which U.S. companies remain in scope, and what cannot be negotiated away? Looking ahead, how might further changes to EU rules and diverging U.S. approaches reshape companies' obligations and strategies, and what should businesses be doing now? This BCLB webinar brings together academic, advisory, and law firm perspectives on what the directive means in practice: why it matters for business, how companies are approaching implementation, and whether it makes a real difference for the workers and communities it is meant to protect. Confirmed Speakers: Gustavo Becker, Executive Research Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and Business Faris Natour, Principal and Co-Founder, Article One Ashley Walter, Partner and Chief Sustainability Officer, Orrick Moderator: Sanchita Banerjee Saxena, Professional faculty member, Haas School of Business and Senior Academic Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and BusinessRegister here (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_39n2nRyVRN-2KxaKYQ97TQ#/registration)

events.title: Alessandro Ori: From Translation Stalling to Organellar Maps: Molecular Drivers and Therapeutic Targets in Brain Aging and Neurodegeneration
events.description: Aging is the primary risk factor for major neurodegenerative disorders, driven by a progressive breakdown of cellular proteostasis. Yet, uncovering the precise causal mechanisms—and translating them into viable therapeutic strategies—remains a fundamental challenge. In this seminar, I will discuss multi-omics and proteomic advances that illuminate disease drivers across scales, from protein synthesis defects to organellar dysfunction. First, using the turquoise killifish brain aging model, we reveal that protein-transcript decoupling is fueled by ribosome pausing and disome accumulation at basic amino acid stretches (Arg, Lys). This stalling stems from altered tRNA charging, declining building block availability, and molecular ribosome aging, leading to the selective loss of critical RNA-binding proteins like TDP-43. Second, applying cell-type-specific LysoTag proteomics across intact mouse brain lineages, we established a brain lysosome atlas that uncovered cell-tailored organellar functions and novel disease-relevant proteins, notably the neuron-specific glucose transporter SLC45A1 whose loss compromises lysosomal pH and mitochondrial integrity. Furthermore, comparative profiling across neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis models identified a shared lysosomal disease signature centering on sphingolipid catabolism and organelle contact sites. Finally, I will highlight how high-throughput perturb-proteomics in human iPSC-derived neurons couples arrayed CRISPR screening with global proteomic readouts to map TDP-43 loss-of-function phenotypes and accelerate therapeutic target discovery.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: The maintenance of diversity in plant communities: insights from Amazonian forest dynamics and California serptentine annual plants
events.description: Despite centuries of research, many fundamental features of the structure and dynamics of plant communities defy simple explanation. My research group pursues general answers to these questions through integrative approaches that combine community ecology perspectives with insights from functional ecology, floristics and macroecology. Our lab uses a variety of observational, theoretical and experimental approaches, many of them rooted in plant collections and functional trait databases. First, I will share recent projects exploring the dynamics of a large forest plot in the hyperdiverse Ecuadorian Amazon, where we use functional-trait based approaches and novel computational tools to explore the ways in which edaphic specialization, spatial aggregation, and competition dynamics shape one of the most species-rich forests on the planet. Next, I will highlight our recent work in annual plant communities associated with serpentine soils in coastal California, a species-rich system that is ideal for detailed, theoretically-grounded experiments to disentangle mechanisms of species coexistence. Our recent experimental work demonstrates how species trait differences, contrasting responses to spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity, and complex higher-order interactions combine to shape the diversity of these systems at both local and landscape scales. Finally, I will share insights from my lab's work on continental and global scale patterns of plant diversity, work that is intimately connected to the development of plant trait and occurrence databases. Taken together, these efforts inform our understanding of the mechanisms that drive the fundamental distribution of plant diversity and function across the planet, as well as our predictions of how species and communities will respond to ongoing global change.

events.title: Amogh Dhar Sharma | The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them
events.description: A talk by Amogh Dhar Sharma (https://www.qeh.ox.ac.uk/people/amogh-sharma), a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow at the University of Oxford, on his new book, The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/backstage-of-democracy/C063953713758327233B0ACBFF9F37FC), that examines the growing influence of political consultants and data-driven campaigning in Indian elections, revealing how these shifts reflect broader transformations in political expertise, power within parties, and citizen participation. Event moderated by Anahitha Sagar (https://www.linkedin.com/in/anahitha-sagar/) (MPP Candidate' 27) and Arushi Choudhary (https://www.linkedin.com/in/arushi-choudhary-b008ab88/) (MDP Candidate' 27), UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, November 5, 2026 TIME: 3:30-5 pm PST VENUE: 240 Mulford Hall RSVP: HERE (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdhOD-LHyw2Ctn17BCTs4uLyhuq2JkD_gkFCwrq4gu66amKzw/viewform) —————- ABOUT THE BOOKOver the last decade, election campaigns in India have undergone a dramatic shift. Political parties increasingly rely on political consultants, spin-doctors, pollsters, and data-driven insights to mobilize voters. But what is driving these changes? Drawing upon my recently published monograph, this talk explores the hidden arena of strategizing and deliberations that takes place between politicians and a new cabal of political professionals as they organize election campaigns in India. I argue that the changes in electioneering are not reducible to a story of technological innovations alone. Rather, they are indicative of a new landscape where ideas of political expertise, the distribution of power within parties, and citizens' attitudes towards political participation have undergone a profound change. ABOUT THE SPEAKERAmogh Dhar Sharma (https://www.qeh.ox.ac.uk/people/amogh-sharma) is a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow in the Oxford Department of International Development, University of Oxford. He holds a PhD from the University of Oxford, where he has previously taught South Asian politics. His first book, The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2024. Currently, he is working on a project on the history of opinion polls and psephology in post-independence India. EVENT POSTER —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - David Charbonneau (Harvard)
events.description: Title: Do Rocky Exoplanets Retain Their Atmospheres?Abstract: The presence or absence of a planetary atmosphere is the outcome of a multi-billion-year-long struggle between the planet's surface gravity, its outgassing rate, its magnetic field, and the stellar XUV and particle flux incident upon the world. The orbs found to transit nearby M-stars are more observationally accessible owing to the diminutive sizes and low luminosities of the central stars. However, recent work has demonstrated that these stars sustain high XUV fluxes for billions of years, much longer than the epoch of atmospheric production. With powerful infrared observatories in orbit and on the ground, we are now mapping the cosmic shoreline that separates airlines worlds from those with atmospheres, possibly even ones containing biosignature gases. Unlike their smaller cousins, Sun-like stars will reveal their planets and any life upon them only through imaging, and this demanding task will fall squarely on the shoulders of the Habitable Worlds Observatory.Host: Courtney Dressing

events.title: Hitchcock Grant Lecture with Kelly Lytle Hernández | Racist by Design - Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control
events.location: Banatao Auditorium, Sutardja Dai Hall - UC Berkeley Campus
events.description: In this lecture, award winning historian Kelly Lytle Hernández will be presenting her work, Racist by Design. She reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcers built the American immigration system to encourage white immigrants while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, punishment, and removal. The goal, often explicitly stated by the system's architects, was to create a permanent caste of undocumented and criminalized workers to provide cheap labor for the American economy.About Kelly Lytle Hernández Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), and Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). Her forthcoming book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control, will be published by W. W. Norton in 2026. In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based but community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative's principal advisor. Professor Lytle Hernández is currently a principal investigator for two additional research collaborations: Mapping Deportations, which maps the history of mass deportation from the United States, and Archiving the Age of Mass Incarceration, which preserves a historic cache of LAPD files and documents the impact of policing on LA residents since the 1970s. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández's scholarship has been awarded numerous prizes and honors, including a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, and she is currently an elected member of the Society of American Historians, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board.

events.title: Matrix on Point: Propaganda Machines
events.description: REGISTER In the age of AI, what is the future of "public truths"? AI-driven tech platforms and companies, influencers, and deepfakes are issuing ever-new challenges for journalism, media integrity, and related mechanisms through which democratic societies hold power to account. At the same time, universities – erstwhile guardians of critical inquiry and independent knowledge production – are increasingly entering into partnerships with AI companies, in a new kind of knowledge compact. This panel brings together scholars of AI and influence in journalism, media, and California's universities to address this technology's increasingly powerful role in the current U.S. landscape of information and knowledge politics. The panel will feature Maty Bohacek, Researcher at Stanford University; Martha Kenney, Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University; Martha Lincoln, Associate Professor of Anthropology at SF State; and Edward Wasserman, Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley. Cori Hayden, Director of Social Science Matrix and Robert H. Lowie Professor of Anthropology, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS), the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), the UC Berkeley School of Information, and the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (EECS).PanelistsMaty Bohacek (https://matybohacek.com/) is a researcher at Stanford University, working at the intersection of AI and media integrity. In a world that is becoming increasingly AI-mediated, his goal is to build AI systems and networks that are inherently trustworthy and interpretable, resulting in productive, democratic discourse. Maty built a deepfake detector for President Zelenskyy of Ukraine and created a deepfake CNN news anchor, which opened a primetime news segment to raise awareness of AI threats. Beyond media integrity, he demonstrated that AI models trained on their own data collapse, developed a method to determine whether specific data were used to train a model, and developed an AI-powered sign language translator. His work has been featured in Forbes, CNN, Science, Nature, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and others.Martha Kenney (https://transforms.sfsu.edu/martha-kenney) is a Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University. She earned a Ph.D. from the History of Consciousness at UC Santa Cruz, where she was a founding member of the Science & Justice Research Center. Located in the tradition of feminist science studies, her research examines how narratives from new fields of biomedical research — such as environmental epigenetics and precision medicine—support, contest, and reconfigure collective visions of social justice, environmental justice, and health equity. She has a track record of collaborative, interdisciplinary inquiry, often publishing with colleagues across institutions and national contexts. She was recently a TUM Global Visiting Professor at the Department of Science, Technology, and Society at the Technical University of Munich. She is currently a Health Equity Institute Faculty Scholar at SFSU.Martha Lincoln (https://anthropology.sfsu.edu/people/martha-lincoln) is a medical and cultural anthropologist. Prior to joining the Anthropology Department at SF State in 2017, she received her Ph.D. from the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Prevention Research Center, affiliated with UC Berkeley's School of Public Health. Broadly, her research addresses the cultural politics of public health, biopolitics, and the effects of political economic change on health systems and health outcomes. Since 2008, she has conducted field research in Vietnam, leading to published research on Hanoi's informal sector, stratification and deregulation in health care provision, the ghosts of war, alcohol use and drinking cultures, the redefinition of poverty under late socialism, and urban cholera outbreaks. Her book, Epidemic Politics in Contemporary Vietnam: Public Health and the State, was published in 2021 by Bloomsbury Academic. She serves as co-editor-in-chief of the Journal of Vietnamese Studies. Her current project is based in the United States, and focuses on affective economies in medical crowdfunding for cancer.Edward Wasserman (https://journalism.berkeley.edu/person/ed_wasserman/), Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley, served as Dean of the Graduate School of Journalism from 2013 to 2020. Before coming to Berkeley, he spent a decade as the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation Professor of Journalism Ethics at Washington and Lee University, home of the nation's first college-level journalism program. Wasserman's journalism career spanned 30 years. He was CEO and editor in chief of American Lawyer Media's Miami-based Daily Business Review newspaper chain, executive business editor of The Miami Herald, city editor of The Casper (Wyo.) Star-Tribune, and editorial director of Primedia's 140-publication Media Central division in New York. Wasserman received a B.A. cum laude in politics and economics from Yale, a licence in philosophy from the University of Paris I, and a Ph.D. from the London School of Economics, where his thesis was on the politics of innovation in communications technology.Cori Hayden (https://anthropology.berkeley.edu/cori-hayden)'s research and teaching focus on the anthropology of science, technology, and medicine. She received her PhD in Anthropology from UC Santa Cruz in 2000 and has held fellowships at the Center for US-Mexican Studies in San Diego, the University of Cambridge, and the Center for Advanced Studies in the Social and Behavioral Sciences (CASBS) in Palo Alto. At Berkeley, she has served as the Chair of the Department of Anthropology and was the Director of the Center for Science, Technology, Medicine, and Society from 2010-2013. Hayden is the author of When Nature Goes Public: The Making and Unmaking of Bioprospecting in Mexico (Princeton University Press, 2003), and The Spectacular Generic: Pharmaceuticals and the Simipolitical in Mexico (2023, Duke University Press). Her more recent research and writing projects explore, respectively, the reanimation of crowd theory as an avenue for exploring contemporary market formations, political atmospheres, and modes of inquiry; and the sciences of Long Covid in a moment of resurgent authoritarianisms.

events.title: Racist by Design - Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control
events.description: About the lecture Award winning historian Kelly Lytle Hernández will be presenting her work, Racist by Design. In it she reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcers built the American immigration system to encourage white immigrants while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, punishment, and removal. The goal, often explicitly stated by the system's architects, was to create a permanent caste of undocumented and criminalized workers to provide cheap labor for the American economy. Lytle Hernández calls Racist by Design "an act of sabotage", a book that will expose the blueprints of the system, so it can be dismantled. About Kelly Lytle Hernández Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), and Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). Her forthcoming book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control, will be published by W. W. Norton in 2026. In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based but community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative's principal advisor. Professor Lytle Hernández is currently a principal investigator for two additional research collaborations: Mapping Deportations, which maps the history of mass deportation from the United States, and Archiving the Age of Mass Incarceration, which preserves a historic cache of LAPD files and documents the impact of policing on LA residents since the 1970s. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández's scholarship has been awarded numerous prizes and honors, including a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, and she is currently an elected member of the Society of American Historians, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board. Meet and mingle before the lecture on November 5 from 3:00 – 4:00 pm at Kvamme Atrium (outside of Banatao Auditorium). Please join us!

events.title: Fascism After Work: Post-Fordism, Abandonment, and Care
events.description: This work-in-progress seminar asks what fascism looks like after the eclipse of the factory as capitalism's organizing stage of exploitation. Delivered in the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections and near the first anniversary of Paolo Virno's death, the seminar returns to Virno's account of post-Fordism to track how immaterial labor—the shared linguistic, cognitive, and affective capacity Virno saw as a site of potential liberation—has become the privileged site of extraction and, for many, of organized abandonment. Bringing Virno into dialogue with Black studies (Ruth Wilson Gilmore especially), the seminar argues that today's political ambivalence—the same capacities that promise exodus also expose populations to premature death—demands a new diagnosis of fascism, one grounded not in discipline but in freedom, deregulation, and a disfigured abolitionism. As the midterms reopen the question of what kind of political order the United States is choosing, the seminar closes by asking what infrastructures of care and sociality might sustain good lives amidst labor's ruins.Lorenzo Fabbri is a McKnight Land-Grant Associate Professor of French and Italian at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities. Author of Cinema is the Strongest Weapon. Race-Making and Resistance in Fascist Italy (University of Minnesota Press, 2023).

events.title: Lia, Mira, Maria: Performance/Reading with Marília Garcia (2026 Brazilian Writer-in-Residence)
events.location: Spanish & Portuguese Library, 5125 Dwinelle, Level E
events.description: What are the stages of mourning? Which path should one follow: that of memory? That of the archive (papers, traces)? After the loss of her mother, Lia, and of a friend, Maria, the author is eventually led to the monotypes of the Swiss-born artist Mira Schendel, who lived in Brazil. In the 1960s, Mira would sit in her kitchen and "engrave," in the presence of friends, drawings on the backs of Japanese paper, making lines and writing letters on the reverse side of the paper with a pointed object. Through this and other material and manual processes (handling papers, sorting through photographs, taking up swimming), the book Lia, Mira, Maria seeks to move through the stages of mourning. It includes images from archives, artworks, and family photographs, composing a kind of personal album of mourning. The performance combines the reading of a text with the live projection of images. The performance will be in English and will be followed by a conversation between Marília Garcia and Nathaniel Wolfson. Marília Garcia is a poet, translator, and researcher at the Rui Barbosa Foundation. She is the author of, among other books, Câmera lenta (Companhia das Letras, 2017; Oceanos Prize), Expedição: nebulosa (Companhia das Letras, 2023), and Pensar com as mãos (WMF Martins Fontes, 2025). In English, her chapbook The territory is not the map, translated by Hilary Kaplan, was published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2017.

events.title: Seeing Through a Mirror: The 1948 War in the Eyes of the World
events.location: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life, 2121 Allston Way, Berkeley, CA
events.description: Annual Diller Lecture Reception and Light Refreshments: 5:00-5:30pm Presentation and Conversation 5:30-7:00pm The 1948 Arab-Israeli War attracted attention from the highest levels of international society, state governments, transnational NGOs, journalism, and public opinion. Palestine and the emerging state of Israel functioned as both a mirror and a magnifier. Israel's establishment and the Palestinian Nakba were interpreted through countries' specific interests, histories, and cultures. These events also elicited tremendous passion. Palestine's mirroring and magnifying effects did not originate in 1948, but the events of that year drastically augmented them, and the patterns of global reaction remain with us to this day. To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/e1v2ubg7fkEif56n8)Derek Penslar is the William Lee Frost Professor of Jewish History and the Director of the Center for Jewish Studies (https://cjs.fas.harvard.edu/) at Harvard University. Derek previously taught at Indiana University, the University of Toronto, and the University of Oxford, where he was the inaugural holder of the Stanley Lewis Chair in Modern Israel Studies. Derek has published a dozen books, including Theodor Herzl: The Charismatic Leader (2020) and Zionism: An EmotionalState (2023). He is currently writing a book titled The War for Palestine, 1947-1949: A Global History. Derek is a past president of the American Academy for Jewish Research, a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, and an Honorary Fellow of St. Anne's College, Oxford. – If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible. events.title: Film Screening: The Secret
events.description: Loosely based on a real-life double-homicide case, Ann Hui's grisly debut feature is a key film of the early Hong Kong New Wave. A young couple has been murdered—strung up in the woods—and Lin (Sylvia Chang), a friend of one of the victims, takes it upon herself to investigate. Interviews provide scarce clues, but every tree, alleyway, and red coat suggest something spectral. "The airy musical leitmotifs of Violet Lam Man-yee's ghostly score send shivers down the spine" (Faith Everard, Senses of Cinema). Through a series of labyrinthine flashbacks, a refracted truth is revealed.

events.description: The Grammar of the Mandala: The Five Families in Buddhist Thought and Practice By the seventh century, Mahāyāna Buddhists had begun to classify their buddhas by type. events.description: This event is part of ALBA (https://alba-valb.org/)'s events series, "Making Memory Visible: Anti-Fascism, UC Berkeley, and The Spanish Civil War (https://alba-valb.org/making-memory-visible-anti-fascism-uc-berkeley-and-the-spanish-civil-war/)" History and photography are practices concerned with time. Both transform the fleeting into a foothold for memory, thought, and action. Queralt Solé (https://dlcl.stanford.edu/people/queralt-sole-barjau) (historian at the University of Barcelona) and Espe Pons (https://espepons.com/) (photographer) discuss their work on the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) and its ongoing echoes. Underlying their conversation is the question of the gaze: who sees what, and what it means to have seen it. Landscapes, mass graves, monuments, archives, documents, people, and objects become materials through which to consider how the visible and the invisible are articulated, and how we might move beyond the immediate. Anchored in their most recent work on mass graves (Solé) and international women volunteers in the Spanish Civil War (Pons), the conversation explores the intersections between art and the social sciences and their shared efforts to make memory visible. Moderated by Dr. Luis Madrigal (Department of Film & Media) *This event is in Spanish*

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Vivian Feig, Stanford University | Engineering Piezoelectric Biomaterials Across Length Scales for Transient Bioelectronics
events.description: Abstract: Bioelectronic technologies hold immense potential for monitoring, stimulating, and interfacing with living systems, but realizing their full impact requires materials that are less invasive, more adaptive, and accessible for widespread use. Achieving this vision demands new approaches that address the entire device lifecycle: from sustainable sourcing of raw materials; to integration with soft and dynamic tissues; to maintaining stable function over operational lifetimes; and ultimately to safe degradation or removal. Biomolecules are attractive building blocks for this task. Certain amino acids and peptides can assemble into crystalline structures that combine piezoelectricity with abundant, biodegradable, and chemically tunable components. But several challenges must be addressed before these molecules can be used to build practically useful materials. In this talk, I will discuss how my group engineers biomolecule-based piezoelectric materials across length scales to tune key performance attributes like stability and sensitivity to specific deformation modes. This work lays the foundation for new transient bioelectronic sensors and energy harvesters built from simple, naturally occurring molecules. Bio: Dr. Vivian Feig (pronounced "F-eye-g") is the Reid and Polly Anderson Faculty Fellow, Gabilan Fellow, and Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering and, by courtesy, Materials Science and Engineering at Stanford University. She has a multi-disciplinary background with academic and industrial training in chemical, materials, mechanical, and biomedical engineering. She obtained her B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Columbia University in 2012 and then spent 3 years working in the petrochemicals industry in both scale-up and manufacturing. In 2020, she obtained her PhD. in Materials Science and Engineering from Stanford University as a National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) fellow under the guidance of Prof. Zhenan Bao. Subsequently, she received the Schmidt Science Fellows postdoctoral fellowship, which allowed her to pivot into translational medical research and mechanical engineering by joining the labs of Prof. Giovanni Traverso and Prof. Robert Langer at MIT and the Brigham and Women's Hospital.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Efficient Power Modeling of Processors Across Design Abstractions
events.description: As technology scaling slows, power has become the primary constraint on processor design. From embedded devices with tight energy budgets to datacenters facing thermal and operational limits, power efficiency now drives all architectural and design decisions. Designers need accurate power estimates early in the design process, but that accuracy is only guaranteed by gate-level analysis that are is slow for long and realistic workloads. In this talk I present my work on reducing the time required to produce a power estimate at each level of design abstraction. First I describe a gate-level power methodology and study how power estimates change as a design moves from RTL to final layout. Next I present ProxyLM, which uses large language models to select on-chip power proxy signals directly from RTL without simulation traces. I then discuss ProfilePoint, which samples fast architectural simulation to find the few intervals that need detailed power analysis. Finally, I combine these methods and compare them against the gate-level baseline to show which approach best fits each design question.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Julius Dobos
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: TITLE:Spatial Composition: The New Frontier Composers have been using rhythm and melody for thousands of years; harmony for centuries. Musique concrète expanded the use of timbre some 75 years ago. Are we on the verge of another musical disruption? What if, using spatial location and movement as compositional tools, songwriters, composers, and producers not only mixed but composed in and for immersive systems? Can SPACE be considered a new element of music? Do spatial decisions made during the composition phase have an effect on the musical content itself? Do listeners respond differently to spatially composed music than to immersive mixes of non-spatial concepts? How should one approach writing in an immersive environment to yield conceptually novel musical content? Based on his latest research in spatial composition and reflecting the global interest among music professionals in its findings, this presentation and immersive demonstration by composer Julius Dobos explores the use of spatial location and movement in music composition and production.

events.title: "The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, & Movement Building with Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio
events.description: Register here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSck0HiXajzxnYA-1toomi9Q11AQkUjSVXio5GojYDxBJDbh-g/viewform?usp=dialog). Please note that space is limited. Confirmation information will be shared upon registration and as capacity allows."The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, and Movement Building This two-part workshop explores how we build movements rooted in deep relationships, collective responsibility, and intentional strategy. Grounded in the premise articulated by @eroticsofliberation that "relationships are the smallest unit of liberation," we begin by strengthening our understanding of kuleana—our responsibilities to one another, our communities, and the lands that sustain us. We then turn to the practical work of developing campaigns, sharpening our organizing strategies, and building the collective power necessary to win. Because liberation is not something we achieve alone, we must learn not only how to fight together, but how to build the relationships and movements that can sustain that fight.Part One: How Does Your Kuleana Move You? In this hands-on writing workshop, we will use poetry and storytelling to explore the many layers of kuleana, including our responsibilities to ourselves, our families, our lands, and our communities, as well as the privileges and obligations that shape how we show up in movement work. Through guided writing exercises, we will map our relationships, reflect on how we care for what we hold dear, and practice bringing those commitments to life through storytelling. No prior writing experience is necessary—just a willingness to reflect, imagine, and create. Participants will leave with a deeper understanding of the kuleana that shapes who we are, how we relate to one another, and how we move in the world.Part Two: Kiaʻi Basics—Campaigns, Strategy, and the Work of Getting Free Made possible through the movement training and organizing experience of SOUL, RUKUS Society, and the Huli Movement, this truncated facilitated learning workshop gets into the nitty-gritty of building effective campaigns and movements. We will explore the relationships between strategy, tactics, targets, messaging, and security culture, asking how these elements work together to build power and advance our collective struggles. Through discussion and practical exercises, we will examine not only what it takes to organize a campaign, but how to make strategic decisions, respond to challenges, and build movements capable of sustaining themselves over time.Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio is a Kanaka Maoli organizer, artist, scholar, and public intellectual whose work is rooted in aloha ʻāina and the struggle for collective liberation. Born and raised in Hawaiʻi, Jamaica is a longtime participant in movements for Kanaka ʻŌiwi sovereignty, land and water protection, demilitarization, decolonization, and is the Vice President the Hawaiian National organization of Hui Aloha ʻĀina o Honolulu. Her organizing, teaching, and creative work are grounded in a belief that movements are sites of knowledge-making and that another world is not only possible, but already being built through collective action. Jamaica is also an Associate Professor of Indigenous and Native Hawaiian Politics at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where she teaches and writes at the intersections of Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, militarism, and collective liberation. Her work moves across the boundaries of scholarship, poetry, film, and movement organizing. She is the author of the award-winning Remembering Our Intimacies: Moʻolelo, Aloha ʻĀina, and Ea (https://www.nativebookshawaii.org/products/remembering-our-intimacies) (University of Minnesota Press, 2021) and her poetry and activism are the subject of the award-winning film This Is the Way We Rise (Sundance 2021). She was also a lead artist and co-writer of the award winning VR documentary On the Morning You Wake (To the End of the World) (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KyTb_56XzN8) (Premier:Sundance 2022 and XR Experience Jury Award at SXSW). Across these forms, Jamaica's work asks what it means to build liberatory futures from the places, relationships, and movements that have survived colonial violence. She writes and organizes toward a world grounded in aloha ʻāina, collective responsibility, Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, and abundance—and toward movements powerful enough to make that world real.

events.title: Fizzah Sajjad | Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan
events.description: The S. S. Pirzada Lecture on Pakistan by Fizzah Sajjad (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784), the winner of the S. S. Pirzada Dissertation Prize for 2025 for her dissertation titled, Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan (London School of Economics and Political Science, 2025).Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Fri, Nov 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABSTRACT: This dissertation studies the dynamics of Lahore's rapidly expanding residential real estate market as a means to contextualize and understand growing housing pressures in the city. Specifically, it examines developer motivations and mechanisms of profitmaking to uncover why and how expansion has taken place in recent years, and in whose interests. By studying and centring the actions of supply side actors such as real estate developers, whose activities and modes of profitmaking remain understudied and undertheorized within existing scholarship, it investigates why the city's real estate market remains inaccessible for a majority of the city's residents. Drawing on sixteen months of fieldwork, this dissertation shows that actors in the business of land development in Lahore have devised a mechanism that overcomes constraints in accessing institutional finance and allows them to profit off land conversions without using their own resources. This mechanism – what I characterize as accumulation by speculative circulation – relies on market-making techniques and the circulation of a market-based instrument of land acquisition and sales known as 'the file' to finance land conversions. The file, as I show, is an object but also a future. It is a fictional commodity that turns 'land' into 'liquid' form, helping create a real estate market that is structured, first and foremost, to accommodate the interests of investors and state actors, rather than those looking to meet their housing needs. This thesis argues that the valorisation and repurposing of land for investment purposes serves as both site and mechanism of housing exclusion, contributing to spatial inequality in the city and heightening the odds against more equitable interventions. It also shows how state entities themselves are implicated in this accumulation model, and remain invested in furthering sprawl, gentrification and dispossession. By illustrating how speculative practices operate in real estate markets, especially in contexts where theory expects otherwise, the thesis contributes empirically and theoretically to questions of land commodification and peri-urban transformations, particularly in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. It also extends and complicates theories of speculative urbanisms, financialization and dispossession. SPEAKER BIOFizzah Sajjad i (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784)s an Assistant Professor at the Lahore University of Management Sciences. Her research focuses on questions of land, housing, transport and the politics of infrastructure development in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. Fizzah holds a PhD in Human Geography and Urban Studies from the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) where her dissertation looked at speculative practices in residential real estate and the market for land in Lahore, Pakistan. She also has a Masters in City Planning from MIT.Her work has been published in leading journals including Antipode and Environment & Planning D, and she has co-edited the volume "Lahore in Motion: Infrastructure, History and Belonging in Urban Pakistan" (UCL Press, 2025). Fizzah also contributes to public scholarship through media outlets such as Dawn, Himal South Asia, and Jamhoor. Most recently, she was Co-Investigator on the project 'Navigating the grid in the 'world-class city: poverty, gender and access to services in India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka,' under the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) GCRF '(Re)Thinking the Off-Grid City' programme. This work examined how the urban poor access basic services in South Asian cities. The Pakistan sub-project more specifically explored peri-urban expansion in the city of Lahore, focusing on transformations and service provision challenges in formerly rural 'urban villages' that are now surrounded and encircled by suburban residential real estate projects. Pirzada Dissertation Prize). Rafat Pirzada is a Silicon Valley based entrepreneur and venture capitalist. _________________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Film Screening: Harakiri
events.description: Masaki Kobayashi harnesses the breathtaking beauty of black-and-white, widescreen cinematography to create an abstract epic. Starring Tatsuya Nakadai, the film depicts one man's desperate attempt to crack the blind, absolute authority that characterizes the feudal age and, Kobayashi suggests, our own. In an Edo-period mansion, the camera inches down hallways and finds rooms within rooms to explicate a complex flashback narration. In the bloody climax, the black-robed figures who were caught and dissected by a stationary camera throughout the film come into their own as an inexorable prophecy, like Toru Takemitsu's haunting music and the words that emerge almost rhythmically from the dialogue: harakiri . . . (seppuku).

events.description: Berkeley World Language Project - 2026-2027 LEARN | CONNECT | INSPIREJoin us for a year of learning in community! Practical Strategies & Real Classroom Impact Engaging Workshops: Practical ideas you can use right away Supportive Community: Collaborate with educators who inspire Student Success: Build world language skills that last Office Hours: Collaborate between workshop sessions! Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! This strand is for all language teachers who want to take their instruction to the next level, whether beginning or experienced. You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. You will build a complete Lesson over time while learning and practicing strategies to implement immediately. Prerequisite: an open mind, curiosity, and a desire to grow. Strand B: Creating Authentic Themed Units for Today's Learners Develop meaningful, real-life themed Units for modern language learners. Build a thematic unit grounded in authentic materials that reflect real language and culture. You will learn how to design a unit that aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), AP themes and CA World Languages Standards while integrating global competence, social justice, and social-emotional learning. Using backward design, you'll craft essential questions, Can-Do statements, and assessments that support meaningful communication across all modes—creating immersive, relevant learning experiences that connect students to the real world and help them grow as confident, culturally aware language users. Prerequisite: Strand A or equivalent recommended. events.title: Film Screening: Kwaidan
events.description: Breathtakingly photographed on hand-painted sets, Kwaidan is at once a Japanese woodcut writ large, and an abstract wash of luminescent colors that seem to come from another world. An electronic soundtrack by avant-garde composer Toru Takemitsu plays hauntingly with natural sounds—crickets, rain, the cracking of wood, the loud silence of snow. Yet the stories—four of Lafcadio Hearn's ghostly tales—strangely contradict this plastic splendor in their simple, aching humanity. All are tales of mortals caught by forces beyond their comprehension when the supernatural world intervenes in their lives. This version of Kwaidan is the original three-hour Director's Cut.

events.title: Film Screening: The Sword
events.description: An ambitious swordsman looking to bolster his reputation hunts for an older master to defeat in a duel. On his quest, he gets embroiled with a young woman chased by bandits (no slouch with a sword herself), his childhood sweetheart (unhappily married into wealth), and a cursed, evil sword. Patrick Tam's iconoclastic convictions are already apparent in this feature debut: "Martial arts films give an impression of being conventional; I wanted to push the envelope in visual experiment." The fight choreography is fluid and fast, and the film's expressive use of color would become one of Tam's signatures.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ——————���—- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: Film Screening: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love
events.description: It is rare when an episode of national history can be interpreted without the burden of illusions, both obsolete and nostalgic. This is one of the great strengths of Masaki Kobayashi's The Human Condition, a nine-hour epic about Japan's occupation of China during World War II. The trilogy begins with an attack on inhuman practices in the Japanese army and ends with a bitter denunciation of Stalinism by the would-be-socialist hero, Kaji (the great Tatsuya Nakadai), a Japanese soldier who has confronted the reality of war and found it unyielding. In grand Dostoyevskian flourishes, Kobayashi suggests the impossibility of an individual altering the ethical standards of a social system. Standing in for the director, Kaji says, "Minor facts ignored by history can be fatal to the individual." It is Kobayashi's recognition of "minor facts" that joins the poetic to the journalistic in a scathing epic about the cruelties of war. This first part of the trilogy finds Kaji working as a supervisor in a forced labor camp in southern Manchuria, where he and his wife attempt to better the lot of the enslaved Chinese workers. Kaji is accused of dissent, tortured, and then inducted into the army.

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: A computable wandering and tracelike vector for modular orbits in the Bergman space
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote online talk
events.description: Speaker: Luis Daniel Abreu, University of ViennaWe construct a function Φ such that the orbit under the representation of $\Gamma = PSL(2,Z)$ is an orthonormal basis for the Bergman space with weight $q=12$. Moreover, we show that Φ is effectively computable as a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane (in the precise sense of computable analysis), by providing an effective procedure. This constructs a wandering and tracelike vector for $PSL(2,Z)$, whose abstract existence was proved by Sir Vaughan Jones in his last paper, where the corresponding construction was left as a problem. The construction of the function, which can also be represented as an orthonormal wavelet in the half-line, reproduces the method used in the signal approximation practice: the off-diagonal decay of the Gramian operator allows to control its restriction to nested finite subsets of $PSL(2,Z)$, where it becomes a finite matrix and can be inverted, leading to a convergent sum where all objects and bounds are computable in the cyclotomic field generated by the 12th-root of unity over the rationals. Since modular actions on the Bergman kernel enter the construction, Φ displays Bergman and modular reminescences, despite appearing to be modular itself. As suggested by Jones, it provides a computable implementing vector for th abstract anti-isomorphism between the von Neumann algebra $M_{12} (\Gamma )$and its commutant. With minor adaptations, the construction works for any cocompact Fuchsian group, but the more involved proof of computability is only executed for $PSL(2,Z)$.
