events.title: IES Rapid Response | Student Protests in France
events.description: Hundreds of thousands of people have engaged in protest across France since mid September. The movement started with high school students dissatisfied with overcrowded, decrepit classrooms, missing teachers, and an opaque university placement system that seemed to work against the disadvantaged. Parents, teachers, labor unions, and members of local government have joined the high school students. The backdrop for these protests is a program of economic liberalization pursued by French president Emmanuel Macron since 2017 that combined tax cuts with reduced spending on public services including education. Join us for a rapid response lecture by expert in French politics and economic liberalization, Professor Jonah Levy, for a deep dive into the issues animating the student protests in France and the implications of these protests for the French economy and society as well as for far-right and far-left parties in the upcoming 2027 elections. Professor Jonah D. Levy teaches courses in the areas of comparative political economy, welfare policy, French and West European politics, and the politics of dystopian novels. In 2023, Levy published Contested Liberalization: Historical Legacies and Contemporary Conflict in France (Cambridge University Press, 2023), which describes and analyzes the contentious politics surrounding economic liberalization in France. In 2025, Levy published Rethinking Economic Liberalization (Edward Elgar), which traces progressive opportunities within liberalizing reforms. Levy has received a Phi Beta Kappa award for excellence in teaching and been selected as the UC Berkeley, Undergraduate Political Science Association Professor of the Year.Photo Credit: The Wallstreet Journal, https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758 (https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (Nizar Touzi, NYU)
events.description: Title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations Abstract: We investigate a new class of infinite-horizon backward stochastic differential equations for ergodic optimal control where the cost and state dynamics are time and path-dependent. The state process is defined on an unbounded underlying domain and satisfies an extended dissipativity condition. In contrast with the time-homogeneous Markovian setting, the optimal ergodic cost in our framework is characterized by the asymptotic behavior of a deterministic function, rather than by a single real constant. We obtain well-posedness, verification and stability properties, which extend the previous results in the literature on the Markov case. Bio: Nizar Touzi is a Professor at New York University, Chair of the Department of Finance and Risk Engineering at the Tandon School of Engineering. He has been an invited session speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians (Hyderabad 2010). He received the Louis Bachelier Natixis prize of the French Academy of Sciences in 2012, the Paris Europlace prize of Best Young Researcher in Finance in 2007, and he was awarded an Advanced ERC grant 2012-2017. He is co-editor and associate editor in various international journals in the fields of financial mathematics, applied probability, and control theory.

events.title: Robert Saxton (Chemistry/MCB Seminar): "Decoding the Molecular Logic of Tissue-Intrinsic Inflammatory Signaling"
events.description: Inflammation is regulated not only by immune cells, but also by receptor signaling circuits within tissues themselves. Epithelial and stromal cells produce cytokines that act locally on neighboring cells or feed back on the producing cells to regulate tissue responses to injury and inflammation. However, the molecular mechanisms governing these tissue-intrinsic signaling pathways, and their role in chronic inflammatory disease, remain poorly understood. In this talk, I will discuss our work on two epithelial cytokines, IL-24 and IL-17C. Combining structural biology, protein engineering, and mouse models, we are investigating how these cytokines engage their receptors to regulate tissue inflammation, as well as how this knowledge can guide the development of new therapeutics for chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics (Joint with Theory): David Dillenberger "Pure Risk"
events.description: Abstract: We introduce a behavioral notion of domain-specific risk aversion that separates attitudes toward risk from deterministic utility: an agent is more pure risk averse in one domain than in another if, for prizes that are indifferent under certainty, he is more averse to risk in the former domain than in the latter. We develop a model that goes beyond expected utility by allowing risk attitudes to vary across domains, while preserving expected utility within each domain. The domains are subjective and need not be specified in advance; they are identified from choice behavior. We establish uniqueness of the model's parameters and provide an axiomatic characterization. events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: Sunrise Lecture by Leif Weatherby: "Has Reason Finally Actually Lost Its Mind?"
events.description: As the Cold War ended, a prominent group of scholars told the story of how reason had "almost lost its mind" in the excesses of Game Theory and optimization. According to that story, the episode was bizarre and dangerous, but had more or less dissipated along with the Soviet Republics. The idea of a quantitative rationality, an automatic basis for executing social judgments, had splintered into various disciplines and quieted down. We know today that this is not what happened. Out-of-control Bayesians and other so-called "rationalists" are in control of technology, markets, and even policymaking, writing what amounts to science fiction about a reason far more literally automated - superceding the human mind - than any rational choice or decision theorist could have dreamed. The ideology of perfectly automated reasoning now also has "evidence" in the form of AI models that scour the written record for solutions to mathematical conjectures and clever ways to commit random cybercrimes. This talk argues that reason was never in possession of the type of mind implied by the earlier, triumphalist stories of the historians of science, and turns to the philosophy of culture that traces from German Idealism to the present to recast the problem of reason in the age of AI. Leif Weatherby is the director of the Digital Theory Lab and Professor of German at New York University. He writes about systems of representation, especially computation and language, especially in their cultural aspects. His book, Language Machines, about AI and literary theory, appeared in 2025. He is currently a fellow of the Ideas Workshop of the Open Society Foundations working on a new book titled The Mismeasure of Mind: Against the Prediction of Everything. There is a workshop that goes with this lecture on November 10th, 10 am. Sign up here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScrZwzVwX9zV5RIxmih3fINUcClvefUOyZdND9gvs3vjz07oQ/viewform).

events.title: The Bomb in/and/out of the Archive. feat. Zoé Samudzi
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture with Zoé Samudzi Postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at Ohio State University - Monday, November 9, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeykJAzTsXRPcjwOetCQvBjTYgUR_hNZbyFZzKTNKnwucsB-Q/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MHRhNmwwNmJwZGxrMGFvZjlkZ3M5MG1xc2IgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Begun during her 2026 residency at La Becque in Switzerland, Zoé Samudzi presents the inaugural project of the research constellation "Can the African Steal?" Through archival photographs of the Belgian Congo (c. 1929-30) at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Samudzi stitches together a variegated visual forensic through image absence through the deployment of the black planetary (after Canham and Seedat) as an onto-epistemic and transnational geographic frame. The negative spaces in the Swiss archive enable a positively articulated materiality of the atomic bomb. Her tracing of uranium extraction and/as warcraft conjoins King Leopold's free state and the Katangese mines in the Belgian Congo, the Trinity test in Los Alamos and Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and nuclear afterlives in Japan. About Zoé Samudzi Zoé Samudzi is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at The Ohio State University. She holds a PhD in Medical Sociology from the University of California, San Francisco. Her research contends with genocide memory and the multiplicity of denialisms, political mythologies of the postcolonial African state, visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing and witnessing, and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. An art critic and writer, Samudzi is an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine, a popular magazine dedicated to psychoanalytic thinking. She is a 2026 Public Parking editorial resident, a 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom," a 2026 resident at La Becque's Principal Residency Program, and an awardee of the 2026 Fire Station Studios' International Curator Residency.

events.title: POSTPONED, New Date TBD: One In A Million: film screening and Q&A
events.description: Join us for a screening of Frontline's new award-winning documentary One in a Million. Filmed over 10 years, it follows Israa's epic journey from Syria to Germany and back again. She and her family navigate war, exile, and heartbreak in a foreign land, revealing the complexities of the refugee experience. After the film, producer and Frontline Editor-In-Chief Raney Aronson-Rath will discuss the film and take questions. Snacks will be available before the screening in the lobby. RSVP HERE (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeWjaO2EXvnExACSuCMOGInO8-TQ4f1rSaYPWarYbBSZu61cg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). In September 2015, filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa, an 11-year-old Syrian girl selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, alongside her father, Tarek. The family had fled Aleppo to join the largest movement of people since the Second World War. Together they trekked through Eastern Europe before finding refuge in Germany, where more than one million asylum seekers were registered by the end of that year. For ten years, the filmmakers continued to document Israa's life as the challenges of integration and cultural adjustment led to family breakdown as Western culture clashed with Syrian traditions. Following the fall of the Assad regime in 2025, the film culminates when the filmmakers follow Israa, now a mother herself, back to the ruins of Aleppo as she confronts her own questions of identity and belonging. The film is a Sundance Winner for both the 'Audience Award: World Cinema Documentary' and the 'World Cinema Documentary Directing Award'.

events.title: Yes Duffy: Who Gave You Permission? | Arcus Social Justice Corps Lecture
events.description: An Activist Architect on Designing Good TroubleWho Gave You Permission? traces a journey from graffiti artist to architect and civic changemaker. From designing treehouses to transit-oriented housing to farmworker land trusts, it explores how designing for social impact can challenge exclusion and shift power through creative collaboration, unexpected common ground, and a willingness to redesign the rules, not just the buildings. The talk also reflects on the uncertainty, setbacks, and compromises involved in sustaining a social-justice practice. It invites emerging designers to trust their lived experience and see how their unique passion, perseverance, and creativity can design more inclusive cities, and the systems that shape them.Yes Duffy is an architect, activist, graffiti writer, skateboarder, and founder of YES Community Architects (YCA) (https://www.yescommunityarchitects.com/), a Bay Area–based architectural practice dedicated to designing systems of inclusion that focus on housing, community, and social justice. Moving fluidly between street culture, architecture, community organizing, and public policy, Yes challenges the systems that determine who gets to belong, build wealth, and shape the places they call home. Grounded in the belief that great design belongs to everyone, YCA seeks to redistribute creative power, opportunity, and agency toward systematically marginalized communities. Yes holds a Master of Architecture and a Master of City Planning from UC Berkeley and previously served as chair of Berkeley's Zoning Adjustments Board. YCA's work and Yes's academic contributions have received numerous honors from the AIA, APA, ASLA, and UC Berkeley.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Paul Salvaire | Environmental Diplomacy: Where do we Stand? Challenges and sources of hope
events.description: After a summer of extreme heat in Europe— and one of the hottest ever recorded globally — where does international climate action stand? Paul Salvaire, an expert in the domain, will take stock of what has been achieved in environmental diplomacy, discuss current challenges, and highlight the solutions that continue to emerge. And perhaps, he will offer us a glimmer of hope. Paul Salvaire has been Deputy Consul General of France in San Francisco since September 1, 2023. A career diplomat, Paul Salvaire joined the Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs of France in 2011. He held various positions in Paris and in the French diplomatic network. Before arriving in San Francisco, Paul was deputy assistant director of environment and climate at the ministry in Paris (2020-2023). In this capacity, he represented France in international negotiations on climate and biodiversity. From 2017 to 2020, Paul Salvaire was counsellor for global issues at the French Embassy in New Delhi. He was in particular responsible for strengthening Franco-Indian cooperation in the field of energy and climate. Paul is a graduate of the Paris Institute of Political Studies (Sciences Po) and Paris-Sorbonne University. events.title: Rachel Rutishauser: Targeting virus-specific CD8+ T cells to cure HIV
events.description: Antigen-specific CD8+ T cells are a key component of antiviral defense. Due to chronic antigen exposure, HIV-specific CD8+ T cells in the majority of people living with HIV are dysfunctional (poor effector function and proliferative capacity). However, they are highly functional and may mediate viral control in the rare individuals who control the infection spontaneously and are therefore an attractive target for immunotherapies seeking to achieve durable HIV remission in the absence of antiretroviral therapy. We will discuss T cell-intrinsic regulatory programs that promote HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function and dysfunction and new approaches being tested in pre-clinical and clinical settings to enhance HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function.This seminar is partially sponsored by NIHDivision(s): Division of Immunology and Molecular Medicine

events.title: Visions of Hope: Pathways to Shared Society in Israel Helen Diller Institute
events.description: Shared Society Series, Session II Rana Fahoum, leading voice on shared society in Israel, will join Masua Sagiv (Senior Fellow, Helen Diller Institute; Senior Faculty, Shalom Hartman Institute) to discuss the current state of Jewish-Arab relations in Israel, viable models of coexistence, and pathways to healing and rebuilding shared society. Rana Fahoum, Vice President and Director of the Center for Shared Society at the Shalom Hartman Institute, draws her insights and experiences from serving in many different leadership roles over the years – CEO of the International YMCA in Jerusalem, senior supervisor at the Ministry of Education, founder of a secondary school for girls in East Jerusalem, lecturer of English and linguistics at Hebrew University, and board member of several leading social and cultural institutions, both in the arts and in education. The events of the last three years have had a unique impact on Jewish and Arab-Palestinian communities across Israel, and have posed significant challenges for intergroup relations. Rana Fahoum and Masua Sagiv will discuss these challenges and Fahoum's vision for pathways forward at this precarious juncture.Rana Fahoum, Vice President and Director of the Center for Shared Society, Shalom Hartman InstituteMasua Sagiv, Senior Fellow, Helen Diller Institute for Jewish Law and Israel Studies, UC Berkeley; Senior Faculty, Shalom Hartman Institute Register: https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_zj3kSi3VSe-3Tb8rUTt1nQ (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_zj3kSi3VSe-3Tb8rUTt1nQ)

events.title: Recovery from Democratic Backsliding: Lessons From—and For—Europe, with Prof. Tom Ginsburg (Chicago)
events.organizer: Miller Institute for Global Challenges and the Law
events.description: Institute for European Studies Director’s Theme Lecture Series for 2026-2027: Democracy in Peril This year’s election in Hungary ending 16 years of Viktor Orban’s rule raises important questions about the tactics of recovery from backsliding in Europe and around the world. Questions of sequencing, institutional redesign, and the balance between looking backward and forward have come to the fore, echoing the democratic transitions of 35 years ago. Are the answers different? Drawing on the experience of several countries, this lecture argues that today’s transitions raise distinct challenges and require different tools those of the prior generation. Shoring up the core institutions and practices of constitutional democracy is the immediate challenge. Tom Ginsburg is the Leo Spitz Distinguished Service Professor of International Law at the University of Chicago, where he serves as Faculty Director for the Forum on Free Inquiry and Expression, as well as the Malyi Center for the Study of Institutional and Legal Integrity. He holds B.A., J.D. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of California at Berkeley, and currently co-directs the Comparative Constitutions Project, an NSF-funded data set cataloging the world’s constitutions since 1789, that runs the award-winning Constitute website. The second edition of his book with Aziz Huq, How to Save a Constitutional Democracy has just been published, and he is the author of numerous other volumes on comparative constitutional studies and international law. He currently serves a senior advisor on Constitution Building to International IDEA and is also on the faculty of the American Bar Foundation. events.title: OITM Seminar - David Simchi-Levi
events.description: David Simchi-Levi (https://cee.mit.edu/people_individual/david-simchi-levi/) David Simchi-Levi is the William Barton Rogers Professor in Energy, and Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Engineering Systems at MIT. He also serves as the head of the MIT Data Science Lab. (https://dsl.mit.edu/) He is considered one of the premier thought leaders in supply chain management and business analytics. His Ph.D. students have accepted faculty positions in leading academic institutes including U. of California Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon U., Columbia U., Cornell U., Duke U., Georgia Tech, Harvard U., U. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, U. of Michigan, Purdue U. and Virginia Tech. Professor Simchi-Levi is the current Editor-in-Chief of Management Science, one of the two flagship journals of INFORMS. He served as the Editor-in-Chief for Operations Research (2006-2012), the other flagship journal of INFORMS and for Naval Research Logistics (2003-2005). In 2023, he was elected a member of the National Academy of Engineering. In 2020, he was awarded the prestigious INFORMS Impact Prize for playing a leading role in developing and disseminating a new highly impactful paradigm for the identification and mitigation of risks in global supply chains. He is an INFORMS Fellow and MSOM Distinguished Fellow and the recipient of the 2020 INFORMS Koopman Award given to an outstanding publication in military operations research; Ford Motor Company 2015 Engineering Excellence Award; 2014 INFORMS Daniel H. Wagner Prize for Excellence in Operations Research Practice; 2014 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Practice Award; and 2009 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Prize. He was the founder of LogicTools which provided software solutions and professional services for supply chain optimization. LogicTools became part of IBM in 2009. In 2012 he co-founded OPS Rules, an operations analytics consulting company. The company became part of Accenture in 2016. In 2014, he co-founded Opalytics, a cloud analytics platform company focusing on operations and supply chain decisions. The company became part of the Accenture Applied Intelligence in 2018.

events.title: Jorde Symposium 2026: ‘After the Fall: Recovering Constitutional Democracy’
events.description: Please join the UC Berkeley Law community for the annual Jorde Symposium, featuring Tom Ginsburg, Prof. of International Law at the University of Chicago, who will speak on “After the Fall: Recovering Constitutional Democracy”. Lecturer Tom Ginsburg is the Leo Spitz Distinguished Service Professor of International Law at the University of Chicago, where he serves as Faculty Director for the Forum on Free Inquiry and Expression, as well as the Malyi Center for the Study of Institutional and Legal Integrity. He holds B.A., J.D. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of California at Berkeley, and currently co-directs the Comparative Constitutions Project, an NSF-funded data set cataloging the world’s constitutions since 1789, that runs the award-winning Constitute website. He is the author of several award-winning books including How to Save a Constitutional Democracy (with Aziz Huq), just released in a second edition. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: John Eiler, Robert P. Sharp Professor of Geology and Geochemistry, CaltechExploring the organic chemistry of the early solar system using molecular isotopic structureOrganic chemistry is ubiquitous across extraterrestrial environments and dominates the processing and delivery of carbon and nitrogen to rocky planetary bodies. Extraterrestrial settings and materials also present the most clearly revealed and diverse collection of constraints on the ways in which 'prebiotic' chemistry takes its first steps towards life. Some of the most detailed and nuanced constraints on this subject come from the laboratory study of the thousands of organic compounds sampled by carbonaceous meteorites and returned samples of asteroids. However, detailed understanding of these materials has been challenging because they may be intimate mixtures of the products of chemistry operating across many settings and processes. I will explore the origin and evolution of early solar system organic materials through application of molecular isotopic structure — the study of the distributions of naturally occurring rare isotopes (D, 13C, 15N, etc.) at scales of individual atomic positions and considering the very rare versions of molecules that contain two or more rare isotopes. These studies were enabled by more than two decades of inventions in mass spectrometry, studies of the chemical physics of previously unexamined isotopic forms of molecules, and applications to meteorites, returned samples, ancient earth materials and their laboratory analogues. The results reveal the long, complex journey of carbon and other volatile materials from synthesis in the interstellar medium, through the early history of the protoplanetary disk and into the 'prebiotic cauldron' of solar system bodies.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.EVENT POSTER _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. _____________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) Support us by donating online HERE (https://give.berkeley.edu/fund/FU0742000)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Andrew Hogan // The New Rules of Design
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Andrew Hogan, Head of Insights at Figma. Drawing on years of research at Figma and his time as an analyst at Forrester, Andrew studies how design is changing in an era where AI, new tools, and new roles are reshaping how digital products get made. His work focuses on the real behavior inside teams: who is actually doing design, how decisions get made, and what separates the organizations that ship consistently great experiences from everyone else. ​In his talk, The New Rules of Design, Andrew will present empirical findings on the changing role of designers and the increasing participation of "designers by another name" across product, engineering, marketing, and other functions. He will examine how AI-generated interfaces and accelerated prototyping are reshaping design practice, and identify domains where distinctly human judgment, interpretation, and taste remain central. Moving from popular discourse to research-backed insights, he will articulate emerging principles for contemporary design work, including cross-disciplinary collaboration, pathways for junior practitioners in a senior-leaning labor market, and strategies for sustaining a distinctive design language in a world where interface creation is widely accessible. events.title: [AALJ x SALSA x APALSA x Miller Institute] Diwali Ram ke Naam Film Screening + Discussion
events.description: Join us for a screening of Anand Patwardhan’s Ram ke Naam scheduled for Tues. 11/10, 6-8pm followed by a discussion moderated by AALJ Associate Editor Aman Madan. We will also be providing dinner. The documentary examines the Hindu nationalist campaign to build a Ram temple at the site of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya. Given the association of Diwali with Rama’s return to Ayodhya, we thought the occasion would provide an opportunity to examine how religious narratives shape political movements and legal claims. The discussion would ask what happens when a political movement co-opts a religious tradition, and how that shapes the interpretation and enforcement of constitutional protections for religious freedom and equality. While grounded in India, these questions have global relevance as movements elsewhere — including in the United States — invoke religion to justify state power and define whose rights the law should protect. We will reach out prior to the screening for some optional readings to provide further context for our discussion. Please RSVP by Sun. 11/8 12pm (put reminder on your calendar) so we can make the food order in advance.

events.title: Performance: Breath in this World
events.description: Join us at the Arts Research Center for Breath in this World, a solo performance of spoken word, sung voice, and body by poet, artist, and performer Aine Nakamura. About the work: The moon holds no light of its own. It receives the sun's light while the earth's shadow reshapes it. Two years ago, Nakamura began to consider the moon's shape as a membrane between stories, between inside and out. Since then, its swaying line and rings of light have led her toward questions of soul, wounds, and the human eye. In this work she follows light and darkness, line and shape through voice and breath. Premiered in March 2026 at Indexical in Santa Cruz, Breath in this World has traveled to the UCSD Music Spring Festival, ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theatre near Beijing, UrBANBUILD in Kyoto, and Chicago. It continues to evolve through each performance and the time shared with audiences, who help shape what it means to see. About the artist:Aine Nakamura, is a performer of voice and body, poet, and artist. She focuses on the potentialities of an injured voice and the listening and sensing bodies. She often writes words and considers shapes as if her throat is a membrane and each body part is a shape, phenomenon among worldly phenomena, in relations. Through her practice, while aiming to be a vessel, she understands about herself and pursues meanings of lines, seeing and connecting. She is a PhD candidate at UC Berkeley and is based in the Bay Area/East Bay, presenting works locally and internationally. Her recent works include solo performance "Breath in this World" premiered at Indexical in SC, which continues to evolve at ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theater near Beijing, UrBANGUILD in Kyoto, Chicago, and will be presented at Arts Research Center; month-long site-specific exhibition and performance project "hands on tape," presented at The Lab in SF; solo performance "Under an Unnamed Flower" during an invitation to the 50th International Theatre Festival at the Venice Biennale; solo multiple performance project "Circle hasu We plant seeds in the spring of mountains" presented at Theatertreffen at Berliner Festspiele after its premiere at the Gallatin Galleries in NY. She also engages in listening and walking in relation to long-term soul work, which resulted in her performance at The Listening Biennial Singapore. In exploring the presence of wounds and repair, she seeks the concepts of fragile kindness and love to access pathways to vulnerability. She is also a committed collaborator and improviser, through which she develops her approach to attunement, spaces and listening.

events.title: Film Screening: Samurai Rebellion
events.description: Rebellion is the fitting original title of this relentless social portrait of those who demand subservience and those who have had enough. A magisterial Toshiro Mifune slow burns his way through the role of dutiful samurai Sasahara, whose attempts to be a "good servant" are about to end. "You retreat, and retreat," says his friend Asano (Tatsuya Nakadai), "until finally you attack." Rare for the genre, the film's plot is set in motion by a woman, one whose willful stand against injustice inspires the men to act. Effective or not, it is the act of rebellion, Masaki Kobayashi implies, that matters.

events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg. Through Cal Performances' Golden Bear Circle program, UC Berkeley students are eligible to purchase a limited number of $10 tickets for this evening's performances. Information about this and more student events and discounts is available at calperformances.org/ucb-students.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Zoe Samudzi | Autotheorizing German Genocide Denial: A Dresden Museum Case Study
events.description: Following decades worth of efforts to broaden the historiographic and political boundaries of national genocide memory, German institutions have been pushed to contend with the country's history of colonial genocide, namely the attempted annihilation of Ovaherero and Nama people in the former colony of South West Africa (present-day Namibia). This lecture traces the contours of conflict that emerged from an invitation by the Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen Dresden (the Dresden State Art Collections) to produce an exhibition engaging the ethnopolitical threads of genocide denialism undergirding the relationship between East Germany and the South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) in relation to the history (and present afterlife) of the genocide. The institution's objection to a central claim that Germany had not fully recognized the Nama and Ovaherero genocide — one that reiterated existent tensions between the state's regime of memory as enforced by cultural institutions — compels consideration of how anti-black disciplining by a state institution might lead one to embrace withdrawal as an ethical imperative. Dr. Zoé Samudzi is a Provost's Fellow to Faculty scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies and an affiliated faculty in the Department of the History of Art. Her work contends with genocide memory and registers of denialism; political mythologies of the postcolonial African nation-state and the relationship between ethnicity and the national question; visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing; human remains and the state and community politics around repatriation and restitution; and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. She is a writer and critic, as well as an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine; and she is 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom."If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: A collections-based approach to bryophyte diversity and disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa
events.description: How do we explain patterns of biodiversity when our knowledge of species and their distributions is incomplete? Despite their diversity and ecological importance, bryophytes remain poorly documented across much of the tropics, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of where species occur and why. Historical herbarium collections offer opportunities to reveal overlooked diversity, refine our knowledge of species distributions, and investigate the ecological and evolutionary processes shaping regional floras. Realizing this potential requires attention to both the specimens themselves and the histories of collecting and access that shape our knowledge.In this seminar, I will talk about three connected themes in my ongoing collections-based research on bryophytes in Madagascar, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Neotropics. The first focuses on how revisiting historical collections can reveal previously unreported species occurrences and inform our understanding of species richness and endemism. The second focuses on the "silent herbaria" of sub-Saharan Africa: how the history of botanical exploration, the visibility of local collections, and their representation in digital resources such as GBIF influence our understanding of bryophyte diversity. This raises a fundamental challenge for ecological inference: distinguishing biological patterns from gaps in collecting and access to knowledge. The third addresses bryophyte species with disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa. Integrating herbarium specimens, genomic data, and spatial modelling provides a framework for testing hypotheses about long-distance dispersal, historical isolation, and intercontinental gene flow, and for examining how niche evolution shapes colonization and diversification across continents.

events.title: The Revolutionary Center: The Lost Genius of Liberalism
events.description: Wooldridge will speak on November 12, 12:30 - 2 pm in 223 Philosophy Hall as he reflects on the cultural history of liberalism - one of our most widely used yet misunderstood terms. He reveals why the world urgently needs a more liberal mindset. Liberalism was once a revolutionary social idea built on individualism, tolerance, and skepticism of power, rather than big or small government. It has lost its way due to technocratic complacency, elite self-indulgence, and internal splintering. Now it must reclaim its bold, critical roots to survive global authoritarianism and populismSpeaker Bio Adrian Wooldridge is an author and political columnist, currently working for Bloomberg Opinion. Wooldridge received a Doctorate of Philosophy from Oxford University as a Fellow of All Souls College. Wooldridge was also a Harkness Fellow at our very own UC Berkeley! Prior to taking on his role as a writer for Bloomberg, he spent 32 years working for The Economist, where he fulfilled numerous columnist roles. Wooldridge served as its Washington Bureau Chief, covering Washington D.C and the American government, and later as its Lexington Columnist, which covered American politics and culture. Wooldridge eventually became The Economist's Schumpeter Columnist where he offered commentary and analysis on entrepreneurial and business trends. Wooldridge was awarded the Gerald Loeb Award in 2017 as a result of his work as the Schumpeter Columnist. In 2021 Wooldridge was appointed The Economist's Bagehot Columnist, covering British culture and politics, before going on to work for Bloomberg Opinion in 2022. While working as a columnist, Wooldridge published numerous books! In 2018, Wooldridge co-wrote Capitalism in America: A History with former Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan. Wooldridge wrote The Aristocracy of Talent: How Meritocracy Made the Modern World in 2021, which went on to become The Times Book of the Year. In 2026, he published The Revolutionary Center: The Lost Genius of Liberalism, a book highlighting liberalism's strength as an ideology capable of adaptation, change, and reform, and what it may need to become in order to ensure that it can surpass the challenges posed to it by the world's autocracies and upstart populist movements.

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies - Shaun Ossei-Owusu
events.description: Law on Trial: An Unlikely Insider Reckons with Our Legal System The law promises justice. Too often, it delivers inequality. This contradiction raises a basic question: Why does a legal system that claims to stand for fairness and equality fail to uphold these ideals over and over? In Law on Trial (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324091264), legal scholar and Bronx native Shaun Ossei-Owusu draws on more than a decade of observation and reflection—first as a scholar of racial inequality, then as a law student, practicing lawyer, and now as an Ivy League law professor—to provide an unvarnished account of the legal system. He reveals that the promise of justice is too often a convenient fiction invoked by lawyers, recited by textbooks, and betrayed in practice.Shaun Ossei-Owusu is an interdisciplinary legal scholar with expertise in legal history, criminal law and procedure, civil rights, and the legal profession. He has held fellowships and visiting professorships at Harvard, Princeton, Columbia, the University of Chicago, and the University of Southern California. His work sits at the intersection of law, history, and sociology and focuses on how governments meet their legal obligations to provide protections and benefits to poor people and racial minorities. He also works on stratification in legal education and the legal profession. His first book project, Law on Trial (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324091264): An Unlikely Insider Reckons with Our Legal System, (https://www.amazon.com/Law-Trial-Unlikely-Insider-Reckons/dp/1324091266) was published by W.W. Norton in 2026. His second book project, Steps Toward Equality: A Multiracial History of Legal Organizing, will be published by Princeton University Press in 2027. He received his PhD from the Department of African American Studies at UC Berkeley and his JD from Berkeley Law. He previously practiced litigation and healthcare enforcement law at Sidley Austin LLP in Washington, D.C., and worked as a Loaned Associate focusing on public benefits appeals with the Barbara McDowell Appellate Advocacy Project at the Legal Aid Society of the District of Columbia. He is a proud Bronx-born native.

events.title: All Education is Political: Students on Agency, Power and the Myth of the Neutral Classroom
events.location: 554 Social Sciences Building (the Barbara Christian Conference Room)
events.description: What do students today consider to be the "appropriate" time, place, and manner for political engagement in the classroom? Although many educators employ "political neutrality" as a default practice, such approaches feel outdated. Further, scholars, educators, and students alike would argue that a truly politically neutral classroom has never existed. From school segregation to ongoing debates over how race and history are taught, education in the U.S. has always been shaped by political choices about whose stories are told and whose are left out. This session asks, How can students' political education be constituted, supported, and valued? Are students expecting it? Where has political engagement in the classroom been successful and why? When students' political engagement is shut down, how have students successfully organized to reclaim their political agency? To explore these questions, the event will engage participants collaboratively. In addition to a student panel, attendees will work in collaborative discussion circles, thinking alongside students on this topic of political education, praxis, and organizing.

events.title: Ashon Crawley: Open Rehearsal 1
events.description: Open Rehearsals open a door onto work still in the middle of itself. The Arts Research Center's Open Rehearsals invite artist-scholars to bring unfinished work, an animating question, process material, or a place they're stuck—not to present it, but to think with it, out loud. This is a space for contemplation that understands itself as rehearsal. It welcomes thinking undertaken with materials, or as practice. It makes room for work that, in its improvisational open-endedness, knows itself to be incomplete, unfolding over time and across practitioners and institutions. About the Artist:Ashon Crawley is a multidisciplinary artist working in the visual and the sonic, and a Professor of Religious Studies and African American and African Studies at the University of Virginia. Crawley has been an interdisciplinary arts fellow at Yaddo and MacDowell, a New City Arts Initiative Fellow, and a LIT (Learning It Together) Artist Fellow, and his work has been featured on the National Mall in Washington DC, Bridge Projects, and the California African American Museum. He is author of Blackpentecostal Breath: The Aesthetics of Possibility (Fordham University Press), an investigation of aesthetics and performance as modes of collective, social imagination; and The Lonely Letters (Duke University Press), an epistolary exploration of the interrelation of blackness, mysticism, quantum mechanics and love. His third book, From Infinite World:The Sound of the Hammond Organ and the Tragedy of AIDS in the Black Church (WW Norton Dec 2026), addresses the impact of the AIDS crisis for black social life. Entering the conversation by considering musicians, singers and choir directors that labored for black churches, "From Infinite World" explores the ways gender, sex, sexuality remain unthought and untheorized but are no less real practices of the living and the dead. All his writing and his approach to art practices is about what he calls otherwise possibility.

events.title: Lecture | Biography of a Revolution: Rethinking Egypt's 2011 through Feminist Genealogy
events.description: Abstract: Why does a revolution need a biography? In Biography of a Revolution: The Feminist Roots of Human Rights in Egypt (2025), Lucia Sorbera argued against a still-persistent framing of the 2011 Egyptian and Arab revolutions as a sudden rupture. Drawing on a collective biography of the Egyptian women's movement across a century of nationalist, Marxist, labor, student, and democratic movements, she showed that 2011 was the culmination of decades of slow, relational, often unrecorded feminist labor — not its origin. In this talk, Sorbera returns to that argument more than a decade after the 2013 coup foreclosed the political openings the revolution seemed to promise, to ask what is at stake in continuing to recover this genealogy today: not only a historical correction, but a methodological one. She reflects on how testimony, intimacy, and relationality as historical evidence — informed by decolonial and indigenous feminist epistemologies — model a way of writing revolutionary history that resists both event-based narratives and Western-centric periodisations of Middle Eastern political history. Sorbera closes by turning from the book to the field: what new research agendas does this genealogical approach open for scholars of Egypt and the wider region, and how might we study movements that persist, transform, and go underground rather than culminate and end? Bio: Dr. Lucia Sorbera is Associate Professor in Arab, Islamic and Middle East Studies at the University of Sydney, where she serves as Chair of the Discipline of Arabic Language and Cultures. Her research focuses on the colonial and postcolonial history of Southwest Asia and North Africa, with particular attention to women, gender, and sexuality. She is the author of Biography of a Revolution: The Feminist Roots of Human Rights in Egypt (UC Press, 2025), along with numerous other books and essays on women's and gender history in the region. She co-leads the Research Cluster on Cooperation and Conflict at the University of Sydney's Vere Gordon Childe Centre, and co-edits the "Third Space" section of the Journal of Middle East Women's Studies.

events.title: The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon
events.description: The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon Thursday, November 12, 4:00 - 5:30 pm Dwinelle Hall Room 3335REGISTER (https://forms.gle/HUaNJxa4CNMmpXBH8) "In the fall of 1938, a young, frail American explorer set off down a river in the western Amazon in search of curare, a poison he thought might save his life. Richard Gill had learned that local tribes used curare-laced blow darts to kill animals, but it was also potentially a cure for many ailments, including his own. He also thought he could make a fortune by connecting the knowledge of two worlds. Obsessed with curare, he raced to make deals with Indigenous poison masters in the Amazon and pharmaceutical companies back home, even as his Russian-born rival Boris Krukoff sought to do the same. In The Flying Death, the historian Matt O'Hara asks who and what we are willing to sacrifice in the name of discovery and profit. O'Hara brings to life Gill's epic quest, a stranger-than-fiction true story that moves from unexplored territory in the Amazon to rogue medical trials and cutthroat corporate boardrooms in the United States. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare–industrial complex, as the plant became a key element in shock therapy, transformed surgery in the United States and across the globe, and eventually led to a Nobel Prize. The Flying Death offers a thrilling ride across Indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, unearthing a story of discovery that poses searching questions about the price of progress, who pays it, and who gets credit."

events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

events.description: Bangladesh is at a turning point. The economy is under strain, hard-won gains for women are being tested, and global aid is shrinking. What should the country's agenda be for the years ahead, what role can institutions like BRAC play, and how can Bangladeshis abroad help shape it? Join Asif Saleh (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/), Executive Director of BRAC and a 2026 TIME100 Philanthropy honoree, and Tamara Hasan Abed (https://www.bracinternational.org/about-us/people/tamara-hasan-abed/), Managing Director of BRAC Enterprises and Chair of the BRAC University Board of Trustees, for a candid conversation about Bangladesh's future.Asif (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/) will make the case for getting the basics right: jobs and livelihoods, women's safety and economic participation, and partnering with government and markets to change systems at scale. Tamara (https://www.bracinternational.org/about-us/people/tamara-hasan-abed/) will speak to how social enterprises like Aarong connect tens of thousands of artisans, most of them women, to markets, and how BRAC University is preparing the next generation of policy and technology leaders. Together, they will explore how the Bangladeshi diaspora, with its talent, capital, and networks, can connect with this agenda in ways that go beyond remittances and donations. The conversation will be moderated by Jessica Olney (https://iis.berkeley.edu/people/jessica-olney), Executive Director of the Institute of International Studies. Welcome remarks by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. Please note that this is an in person event and will NOT be live streamed. ————–DATE: Thu, November 12, 2026 TIME: 5-6 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —��——– ABOUT THE SPEAKERSAsif Saleh (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/) is the executive director of BRAC. He brings with him a diverse multi-sectoral experience in senior leadership roles in private, public, and non-government sectors, with a proven track record of effectively managing interfaces of development programming, operational and financial sustainability, and building effective partnerships, both within and outside BRAC. As part of the Government's Digital Bangladesh initiative, he led the policy effort to expand affordable broadband connectivity across Bangladesh and devised the Government's m-governance strategy. He spent 12 years in Goldman Sachs in different fin-tech roles in New York and London ending his term there as an Executive Director. He has also worked in Glaxo Wellcome, IBM and Nortel. Mr. Saleh is a non-resident fellow at the Center for Global Development in Washington, D.C. He is also an active member in a range of international networks and alliances advocating inclusive achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. He is a member of the Millions Learning International Advisory Group, Brookings Institute, a member of the advisory group of South Africa-based Innovation Edge, an institution promoting early childhood development. She currently serves on the boards of IPDC Finance, BRAC EPL Investments, BRAC EPL Stock Brokerage and edotco Bangladesh. events.description: Sponsor(s):The Redwood Center (https://redwood.berkeley.edu/), Simons Institute (https://simons.berkeley.edu/homepage) Today's AI systems are powerful, but they work on principles very different from those of the human brain. They typically learn from large, static datasets, operate as black boxes, and need retraining for each new task. The brain, by contrast, learns continuously through active interaction with the world, builds structured models of what it senses, and generalizes across many kinds of tasks with remarkable efficiency. In this talk, Jeff Hawkins explains how the brain's sensorimotor principles allow it to understand the world, and why reverse-engineering the neocortex may provide a blueprint for a new kind of artificial intelligence. The Thousand Brains Project is an open-source effort to turn these principles into a practical framework for researchers and developers. Reception at 5:30pm, talk at 6pm. Please register (https://redwood.berkeley.edu/intelligence/) in advance if you plan to attend. events.description: Would-be tough guys Franz (Sami Frey) and Arthur (Claude Brasseur) have little better to do than drive around Paris and act out scenes from B movies. But when they team up with Franz's English-class crush, wide-eyed Odile (Anna Karina), to plot a burglary, they stumble into the gap between playacting and reality. The atmosphere arises not only from the actors' interplay—their dance in a café and their sprint through the Louvre are among the most memorable and joyous moments in Godard's cinema—but also from Raoul Coutard's exquisitely bleak cinematography and Michel Legrand's jaunty, melancholy score.

events.title: Understanding catalytic reactivity at dynamic solid liquid interfaces
events.description: Catalytic properties have traditionally been linked to the concentration and nature of active sites. At gas-solid interfaces, characterizing these sites has largely sufficed to explain catalytic action, even though reacting molecules may modify them. At solidliquid interfaces, however, the dense and mobile environment changes the elementary steps themselves, as it influences the adsorption of reactants, intermediates, transition states and products, as well as the chemical and electronic state of the catalyst. The lecture will explore how activity and selectivity can be tailored by engineering the local chemical environment of active sites. In highly ionic media, for example, transition states in carbenium-ion chemistry for alkane conversions are strongly stabilized, lowering true activation energies by more than 100 kJ mol⁻¹ and enabling demanding reactions such as carbon–carbon bond cleavage near ambient temperature. Beyond acid–base catalysis, the local concentration of hydronium ions at the catalyst surface alters hydrogenation mechanisms on supported metals by shifting the rate-determining step, and applying an external electric potential can increase hydrogenation rates by nearly an order of magnitude. Together, these examples show that the catalytic microenvironment is a design parameter in its own right, as important as the active site, and one that opens routes to reactions that are otherwise hard to achieve.

events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368). If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: The Economies of Niágara: José María Heredia and US Spanish-Language Print Culture
events.location: Spanish & Portuguese Library, 5125 Dwinelle, Level E
events.description: I am a scholar of American literature and culture broadly conceived across the Americas, with specialties in the nineteenth century, print culture, and archival studies. Most of my rearch is on writers who cross the Americas and conceptualize new ways to publish and circulate their writing, often with the goal of enacting social and political transformation. My research is in dialogue with migration studies, Latin American Studies, Latinx studies, and US literary history. I am currently writing a book titled, Clandestine Spectacle: Torture Culture and the Language of Despotism, which considers the history of torture writing to shed light on post-9/11 cultures of US torture. My most recent published book is Letters from Filadelfia: Early Latino Literature and the Trans-American Elite, which won the best book in Early American Literature in 2022. I have edited special issues for the journals Leviathan and Early American Literature, and I am a general editor of The Broadview Anthology of American Literature.
