events.title: Composition Colloquium: Andrea Agostini
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Andrea Agostini was born on 21 May 1975 in Bologna, Italy. He studied at the Conservatorio Giovanni Battista Martini, where he received a degree in composition in 2000 (studying under Alessandro Solbiati, Giovanni Verrando, and Paolo Aralla), in electronic music in 2001 (studying with Lelio Camilleri), and piano in 2004. Between 1999 and 2006, he also took masterclasses with Ivan Fedele, Brian Ferneyhough, Michael Jarrell, and François Paris. In 2008-2010, he completed his studies with the Cursus (IRCAM's composition and computer music course). He was an IRCAM scholar-in-residence from 2011 to 2013. Andrea Agostini composes instrumental and electroacoustic music, for which he has won numerous prizes and awards, including the Zucchelli Prize in 1999 and in 2000, and the Magone Award in 2001. In 2002, he was a finalist for the Prix international Noroit-Léonce Petitot. In 2003, he won the Concurso Internacional de Composição Electroacústica Música Viva. In 2005 he received third prize for composition in the Seoul International Music Competition and an honorable mention at the Gaudeamus Festival Composers Awards. In 2007 he was a finalist in the Franco Evangelisti International Composition, sponsored by Nuovo Consonanza, and received a Commande d'état (a commission from the French Ministry of Culture) for Musica per il chiostro di Royaumont. His music is performed in festivals across the world, including Festival Musica in Strasbourg, MiTo and Sincronie in Milan, REC in Emilia-Romagna, the IMEB Festival in Bourges, Festival MIA in Annecy, and Northern Spark in Minneapolis. His curiosity for different musical languages led him to explore rock and improvisation, and to study non-Western musical practices. He plays bass with the rock band Frida X, for which he is also an arranger, progammer, and sound engineer. He also composes music for theater, cinema, and radio, and live electronics and motion capture for Project C, a group specialized in sound design for theater performances. He also designs sound environments for visual art installations. With Daniele Ghisi, he created a digital platform for computer-aided composition titled "bach: automated composer's helper". In 2017, during his research residency at IRCAM, he developed a programming language for the Max environment, creating a set of tools based on the bach library. As a musician, Andrea Agostini has collaborated with ensembles such as Icarus and the Orchestre national de la RAI in Turin, for concerts and recordings of works by Fausto Romitelli, Giovanni Verrando, and Oscar Bianchi. In addition, he has given masterclasses and workshops in the conservatories of Bologna, Genoa, and Strasbourg, and in several universities in the United States (Harvard, San Diego, and Stanford). He is currently professor of computer music (algorithmic and computer-aided composition) at the Conservatory of Turin. NOTE: Andrea is in residence at CNMAT for the Fall semester

events.title: Film Screening: Waikiki Brothers
events.description: Yim Soon-rye's cult classic captures a secret history of 1990s South Korea—when economic malaise was the norm and K-Pop was still a faraway dream—as told through its cover bands, sad power ballads, and faded resort towns. Staggering from one depressing gig to another offseason hotel, the now middle-aged misfits of the Waikiki Brothers band can feel their youth disappearing and their misfortunes mounting with every passing beat. Yim's own rhythm of quiet, static long takes brings a sense of admiration and respect to this tale of dreams stubbornly clung to in a society that could care less. Future superstars Hwang Jung-min and Ryoo Seung-bum have lead roles.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Josh Figueroa, Professor, UC San DiegoTitle: The Carbonyl-Isocyanide Relationship and BeyondRecent results concerning the synthesis and reactivity of low-coordinate transition-metal complexes featuring sterically encumbering m-terphenyl isocyanide ligands are presented. Given the isolobal relationship between organoisocyanides and carbon monoxide, these complexes serve as mimics of the unsaturated binary metal carbonyls. The latter have traditionally been studied in either the gas phase or by matrix-isolation techniques and, consequently, their condensed-phase reactivity patterns are largely unknown. Specifically addressed will be synthetic studies that have delivered homoleptic and heteroleptic isocyanide complexes that mimic several unsaturated binary carbonyls for the middle and late transition metals. An emphasis is placed on the generation of anionic isocyanide complexes and their use as metal-based nucleophiles. The constrained steric environment enabled by m-terphenyl isocyanides has allowed for the isolation of unique organometallic complexes when these anionic isocyanide complexes are treated with main group electrophiles. Such systems support the stabilization of the simple 10e– diatomic molecule boron monofluoride (BF) as a terminal ligand, as well as diphosphorus (P2) as side-on bound ligand to a mononuclear metal center. The reactivity patterns of these complexes are detailed, with purpose of establishing the electronic structure features of the bound diatomic ligands. Also discussed is the synthesis of other, diatomic main-group species within the protective environment of the m-terphenyl isocyanide framework, as well as the use of m-terphenyl isocyanides as agents for the construction of new materials. The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Ioanida Costache (Stanford)
events.description: "Unsilencing the Archive: Enunciation, Song, and Romani History" Dr. Ioanida Costache, Stanford University Abstract: This talk explores the silence of the archive and its attendant epistemic regimes in relation to Romani people, who have served as an "Ontological Other" in the European imaginary (Wynter 1987). I posit that archival silence registers the racialization that undergirds systems of knowledge production and ask: How might sound "augment" a Romani subjectivity conditioned by abjection? At stake is music's capacity to function as an affective archive and alternative site of historical enunciation. Bio: Ioanida Costache is Assistant Professor of Ethnomusicology and, by courtesy, of Anthropology at Stanford University. She is also a faculty affiliate of the Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity. Her work explores the legacies of Romani historical trauma and feminist critiques of the present inscribed in Romani music, sound, and art. Her writing has been published in EuropeNow, Revista ARTA, Critical Romani Studies, and European History Quarterly and is forthcoming in Ethnomusicology. Her research has been supported by two Fulbright grants and the Council for European Studies. She has held visiting and postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Pennsylvania, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and the USC Shoah Foundation. A reception will follow.

events.title: Film Screening: The Inheritance
events.description: "For his follow-up to The Human Condition, Masaki Kobayashi turned to an intimate, character-driven story. As superficially different as the family-scandal melodrama The Inheritance may be from that nine-and-a-half-hour epic, it shares its moral sensibility. Shot mostly in interiors, the film charts the quiet chaos that erupts after a dying businessman (So Yamamura) announces that the lion's share of his fortune is to be divided among his illegitimate children, with only a small portion going to his much younger spouse (Misako Watanabe). . . . This is Kobayashi's first drama set in an exclusively bourgeois milieu, and its visual condemnation of materialism is especially pronounced" (Michael Koresky).

events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg. Prior to the Fri, Nov 13 performance William Kentridge will participate in conversation with Debarati Sanyal (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/debarati-sanyal), director of UC Berkeley's Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry. From 6-7pm the two will explore the creative and historical context of the work, as well as its relationship to Cal Performances' 2026–27 Illuminations theme, "Innocence & Experience." This talk is free to all ticket holders to the performance that evening.

events.title: Across Eurasia with the Sogdians: Trade, Religion, and Cultural Exchange
events.location: Society for Asian Art, Asian Art Museum
events.description: The Sogdians were an Iranian-speaking people from the great Central Asian cities of Samarkand and Bukhara. Between the fourth and eighth centuries CE, they became the most influential merchants of the Silk Roads, establishing trading communities that stretched from Central Asia to China and beyond. More than traders, they served as cultural brokers, carrying not only goods but also artistic traditions, technologies, and religious ideas across Eurasia. Through their far- reaching networks, they helped shape the spread of Buddhism, Manichaeism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism, leaving a lasting imprint on the art, architecture, and urban life of the Silk Roads. events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: Film Screening: Just Like Weather
events.description: Mixing fact and fiction, "Just Like Weather centers on a young couple. The wife is the breadwinner, with a job in real estate; the husband dreams of saving the marriage by emigrating to join his mother in the United States. Between interviews and re-enacted scenes from their everyday lives, Allen Fong entangles the couple in fictional episodes: an abortion, a shady used-car dealer, a randy veterinarian. On top of that, he folds the film in on itself by taking them to America to confront their indecisions. Worries about Hong Kong's future after 1997 lie beneath the surface, but the surface is engrossing enough" (Tony Rayns).

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: OpenAI's proof of isomorphism of free group factors, and further developments
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Dima Shlyakhtenko, UCLAWe will present a version of OpenAI's proof of free group factor isomorphism. A strengthening of the proof also shows that the reduced C*-algebras of free groups have strong reduced free products absorption properties. Moreover, C*-algebras generated by n=2, 3,… or countably many semicircular elements are all isomorphic, and the same is true for reduced free products of copies of the Jiang-Su algebra. A common ingredient is a certain automorphism approximation property; a relative version of that property appeared in our recent work on the identification of von Neumann algebras of Fuchsian groups.

events.title: Pavement Management Systems and Preservation Strategies
events.description: Description Pavement networks are often the most valuable asset that an agency owns. This asset is not only expensive to replace, but it is an essential component to the traveling public's safety. Agencies are looking for more cost-effective ways to perform engineering, maintenance, management, and rehabilitation of roadways more than ever before to stretch funding allocations. A pavement management system is an essential tool to assist in cost-effective roadway maintenance planning. This is the primary overview course on pavement management systems and preservation strategies in the training certificate program offered by the City and County Pavement Improvement Center (CCPIC) in partnership with TechTransfer. Topics IncludePavement management principles Street inventory development Pavement condition surveys (pavement distress) Pavement condition indices Quality management Types of PMS software Types of maintenance treatments Performance prediction models Funding scenarios Developing a work plan using appropriate prioritization techniques Data to use in communicating with elected officials What You Will Learn This class will cover the fundamentals of pavement management systems (PMS). The student will learn the types of distresses included in a typical PMS, how pavements are surveyed for condition, and how condition and classification is used within a PMS. In addition, the inner workings of a PMS are described, covering prediction models and the use of varying funding scenarios and prioritization techniques to maximize your pavement network condition. The important topic of communicating with elected officials to sell your program will be covered. And preservation and maintenance techniques, commonly used by local agencies will be presented. Who Should Attend This course is designed for engineers or maintenance superintendents responsible for:Collecting data and updating a pavement management system Determining the types of repairs for streets Preparing cost-effective multi-year work plans e.g. resurfacing, seal programs, etc. Planning how much funding is required for the future Making presentations on funding street repairs to elected officials Managing or maintenance of PMS software Requirements Students should bring a calculator and pencil for in-class problems

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Structured Generative Models for Offline Model-Based Optimization
events.description: How can machine learning move beyond predicting properties and generating familiar objects to designing better ones? This talk studies offline model-based optimization, where a fixed dataset is used to search for high-performing designs without additional objective evaluations. A central challenge is that optimization can exploit errors in learned models rather than discover genuinely better solutions. Drawing inspiration from offline reinforcement learning, I explore how structural decomposition enables the recombination of familiar components into novel designs. I introduce functional graphical models as a theoretical framework for this idea, followed by Cliqueformer, a structured generative model for optimization, and CliqueFlowmer, which extends these principles to crystalline materials discovery. Together, these contributions demonstrate how exploiting the compositional structure of complex objects can enable more effective optimization and scientific discovery.

events.title: Optimal transportation under McKean–Vlasov dynamics (Camilo Hernández, University of Southern California)
events.description: Title: Optimal transportation under McKean–Vlasov dynamicsAbstract: We study a broad class of stochastic transport problems under controlled McKean–Vlasov dynamics, allowing control of both drift and volatility, with weak terminal constraints. In contrast to the classical Schrödinger problem, the reference dynamics depend on the evolving law of the process, leading to nonlinear optimization problems on path space, while the terminal constraint is formulated through weak optimal transport, permitting a flexible treatment of distributional targets. This framework encompasses several problems of current interest, including the mean field Schrödinger problem, martingale optimal transport, and Schr��dinger–Bass bridges. We establish three main results. First, we prove the existence of optimal controls under general coercivity, continuity, and convexity assumptions. Second, we derive a convex dual representation that extends weak Kantorovich duality and stochastic optimal transport duality to controlled McKean–Vlasov dynamics. Finally, for the mean field Schrödinger problem, we prove convergence, at the level of value functions, of the associated finite-particle Schrödinger bridge problems to the mean field limit, thereby identifying the nonlinear problem as the exact infinite-particle limit of finite-particle Schrödinger bridges. As a byproduct, we establish the existence of an optimal mean field Schrödinger potential, providing a variational foundation for duality in nonlinear stochastic transport. This is joint work with Ludovic Tangpi.Bio: Camilo Hernández is an Assistant Professor in the Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at the University of Southern California. Before joining USC, he was a Presidential Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering at Princeton University (2022–2024) and a Chapman Fellow in Mathematics at Imperial College London (2021). He received his Ph.D. from the Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research at Columbia University in 2021, where he was a Cheung–Kong Innovation Fellow, and holds an M.S. and B.S. in Mathematics and a B.S. in Economics from Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá, Colombia. His research centers on the theory and applications of continuous-time stochastic control, with interests in Schrödinger problems, Stackelberg games, contract theory, and time inconsistency. He also serves on the Advisory Board of the USC-Capital One Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF).

events.title: Rahul Parson | Kathā-Kalkattā: Hindi Literature in a Bengali City
events.description: A talk by Rahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson), Assistant Professor of Hindi Literature and Culture, at UC Berkeley, that recovers Calcutta as a major center of Hindi literary production from the 1950s to the 1990s, showing how its multilingual archives complicate conventional linguistic geographies of Indian literature and illuminate questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition.Sukanya Banerjee (https://english.berkeley.edu/people/sukanya-banerjee), Associate Professor of English will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, November 16, 2026 (NOTE NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT Calcutta, Kolkata, Kalkattā: three names for one city, and the last one belongs to the Hindi and Urdu speakers who make up more than a third of its population. The conventional geography of Indian literature follows the linguistic boundaries drawn by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 — literary habitations of Bengali for Bengal, Hindi for north India, Tamil for Tamil Nadu — a map that effaces Hindi writing produced outside the Hindi belt. Calcutta has been a Hindi literary city for over two centuries, since Bengal gave Hindi its first printed newspaper. This talk takes up the decades from the 1950s to the 1990s, when writers, editors, and theatre-makers set out to define what a Calcutta Hindi literature might be. They compiled their own archives, collections, and critical practices: R̥shi Jaiminī Kauśika's Kalakattā ke Hindī kathākāra (1952), Sharad Deora's two-volume Mahānagar (1969), the annual Kalkattā (1985–98), the journal Aṇimā, named for the yogic power of becoming infinitesimally small, and Shyamanand Jalan's theatre group Anamika. What emerged was a literature shaped by contact and separation at once — from Bengali locally, and from the movements of the Hindi belt. Reading the city as a literary confluence rather than a single tradition changes our account of both Hindi literature and Calcutta. The map was drawn over the multilingual city; the paper trail shows what it covered. The archive poses questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition in Calcutta and similar global port cities. ABOUT THE SPEAKERRahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson) received an MA and PhD in the Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, with a specialization in Modern Hindi literature. Before returning to the Berkeley in 2021, he served as an Assistant Professor of Hindi and Urdu at the University of Colorado, Boulder (2016-2020) and a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter (Postdoctoral Researcher) at Max-Weber-Kolleg, Universität Erfurt, Germany (2014-2016). Rahul Parson's area of specialization is Hindi literature and literary history, with a particular emphasis on Hindi movements in Bengal. His book project, Confluences at the End of the Ganges: Modernity, Migration and Hindi Literature in Kolkata, fills in the Bengal portion of the map of Hindi studies. The monograph reveals the dynamism and syncretism of the hitherto overlooked world of Hindi literature in Bengal and the affective archives and narratives of migrants. It inaugurates research on the literatures of displaced and migrant peoples in South Asia by using cultural texts to explore the articulations of life-worlds of women and migrants. Additionally, he researches early-modern Jain poetry and philosophy, particularly the Jain adhyātma (spiritual or mystical) poetry. Dr. Parson participated as a core member of a research group based at the Max-Weber-Kolleg. In this capacity, he worked as a co-editor of a four-volume series entitled: Religious Individualisations: Historical Dimensions and Comparative Perspectives (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2020). events.title: The 2026 Emilio Segrè Lecture Featuring 2026 Nobel Laureate Francis Halzen: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South Pole
events.description: In person at Chevron Auditorium, International House (limited seating)orLivestreamed (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share). ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South PoleLivestreamed lecture with 2026 Nobel laureate Francis Halzen (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share) — The IceCube project melted 86 holes 2.5 kilometers deep in the Antarctic ice to construct an enormous astronomical observatory, discovering a flux of neutrinos from deep space with energies more than a million times those of neutrinos produced at accelerator laboratories. Francis Halzen, a visiting lecturer and winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, will discuss the telescope, discovery, and launch of multiparticle astronomy. Monday, November 16, 5:30 p.m., in-person at the International House or livestreamed. Learn more, or link to the livestream. (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share) Francis Halzen Born in Belgium, Halzen received his Master's and PhD degrees from the KU-Leuven, Belgium, and has been on the physics faculty at UW–Madison since 1972. He is the 2026 Nobel Laureate in Physics. In 2021, Halzen was named a Vilas Research Professor, one of the university's most prestigious honors. He has been a fellow of the American Physical Society since 1994 and a member of the US National Academy since 2024, and is the recipient of numerous awards, including the 2014 Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award, the 2015 Balzan Prize, a 2018 Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, the 2019 IUPAP Yodh Prize, the 2021 Bruno Rossi Prize, the 2021 Homi Bhabha Award, and honorary doctorates at several universities. Halzen is the Principal Investigator of IceCube, a cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope buried in the Antarctic ice at the South Pole. IceCube's first observations of high-energy cosmic neutrinos garnered the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award. In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the direction of a blazar called TXS 0506+056. This was the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since they were discovered over one hundred years ago. Also a skilled science communicator, Halzen travels widely, giving about 20 or more invited talks per year at conferences, workshops, and colloquia. He also gives regular public talks to local and national groups and interviews for television and radio. Halzen is the co-author of Quarks and Leptons, a classic textbook on modern particle physics that continues to be used extensively throughout college campuses today. He has a large number of publications to his credit and has written or edited several other books. His essay "Antarctic Dreams," about the early days of AMANDA, IceCube's precursor, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000.

events.title: Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel | Making sustainable Europe: The growth of sustainability in EU policymaking, 1992-2026
events.description: Join Ph. D. Candidate Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel in conversation with Professor Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann for a presentation of new horizons in historical research. Sustainability has become one of the defining political aspirations of our time. Few political actors have embraced it more strongly than the European Union, which has repeatedly cast itself as a global frontrunner of the sustainability transition. Yet today, even as the European Commission insists that Europe must 'stay the course', it is simultaneously weakening parts of the regulatory framework intended to make that transition materialise. How can Europe stay the course while seemingly changing it? This is one of the puzzles that this lecture takes as an entry point into the political economy of sustainability. Rather than treating sustainability as a self-evidently good or politically neutral ideal, it examines how the concept has been constructed, mobilised, and institutionalised in EU policymaking since the early 1990s. Drawing on public and archival documents as well as interviews, it traces how sustainability became a central normative horizon of European integration and how its meaning has changed alongside transformations in European and global political economy.Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel is a PhD candidate at Aarhus University, and a former visiting researcher at the European University Institute. Holding his MA in International Political economy from King's College London, his research examines the political economy of sustainability in the EU through a focus on discourse, conceptual change, and modes of governance. Before his PhD, he worked on sustainable finance policy and EU-coordination at the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority under the Danish Ministry of Business. Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann is Chancellor's Professor of History in the Department of History at UC Berkeley. He is an historian of German, European and International History from the late 18thcentury to the present. He is the author, editor or co-editor of 15 books including Geschichte der Menschenrechte (under contract from Princeton University Press).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Founders and Their Heterogeneous Firms"
events.description: Abstract: Firm creation is at the heart of macroeconomic growth, but entrepreneurial outcomes are highly unequal. In this paper, we study the determinants of which entrants become large firms with macroeconomic importance. Using employer-employee-shareholder linked Canadian administrative data based on tax records, we find that workers with higher employment earnings are more likely both to enter entrepreneurship and to found larger firms with greater growth potential. We incorporate this link between founders' labor-market and entrepreneurial capacities into a quantitative model of endogenous occupational choice. In the presence of ex-ante heterogeneity, small business tax deductions induce negative selection by drawing lower-potential entrepreneurs into entry, largely oﬀsetting their positive eﬀects in alleviating financial frictions and generating a quantity-quality trade-oﬀ in the design of entrepreneurial policies.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: David Limmer, Professor, UC BerkeleyTitle: On the Stability and Function of Chemical Reaction NetworksThe remarkable complexity of living systems emerges from networks of chemical reactions that operate persistently far from equilibrium. These networks sustain stable states despite incessant fluctuations, reorganize in response to changing environments, and process information with extraordinary fidelity. Yet the physical principles that govern their stability and constrain their function remain poorly understood. Unlike equilibrium systems, where free energy provides a unifying organizing principle, nonequilibrium chemical networks lack a comparably general framework. Developing such a framework is a central challenge for modern statistical mechanics. In this talk, I will discuss advances in nonequilibrium theory connecting fluctuations, dissipation, stability, and function. First, I will describe a theory for the stability of reaction–diffusion systems based on the statistical mechanics of rare trajectories. Using instanton approximations and fluctuations around the most probable transition paths, we uncover how nonequilibrium driving and path entropy determine the relative stability of competing states. Second, I will consider biochemical signaling networks and introduce a general dissipation–error bound connecting the energetic cost of driving to the accuracy of responses to time-dependent signals. Together, these results reveal organizing principles that transcend specific molecular mechanisms, with broad implications for chemistry, materials science, and biology.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Aditya Balasubramanian | Crossings Interrupted or Invisibilized? Rethinking Migration Across the Bay of Bengal
events.description: A talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a), Senior Lecturer in History at the Australian National University, drawing on a rare archive of family letters and remittances to examine the understudied history of Indian middle-class migration to Southeast Asia and the ways the Depression shaped mobility, economic insecurity, social isolation, and transimperial connections to home. Event moderated by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Nov 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–ABSTRACT: Studies of migration across the Bay of Bengal focus largely on the movement of millions of Tamil labourers between the second half of the 19th century and the 1930s to serve the demands of British imperial capital accumulation during the first era of globalization. While connected histories of South and Southeast Asia and memory point to "a large middling group of Indians, clerks in government and private offices, doctors, drivers, lower management in the oilwells and teak sawmills," shopkeepers, and traders (Bayly and Harper, 2005), they fail to say very much about this class of people because of their invisibility to the colonial archive. This paper begins to illuminate what has been hidden thus far. It draws chiefly on the author's collection of 500 pages of remittances and correspondences exchanged between his maternal grandfather P.K. "Java" Raman (1909-97) who migrated to work as a typist in Batavia (today's Jakarta) in the Dutch East Indies and his family members in the Malabar region of British India, between 1930 and 1934. The paper suggests the Depression as a period of migration rather than its eclipse; explores structures of feeling around economic insecurity and isolation of the thin stratum of Indian professionals in Southeast Asia; and sketches an earlier history of remittance between Indians overseas and in the homeland, across empires. Looking beyond the letters, it discusses possible sources and themes for microhistories of crossing the Bay of Bengal.ABOUT THE SPEAKER:Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a) is a Senior Lecturer at ANU's School of History, in the College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS). Aditya's first book, Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2023), is a history of economic ideas and politics (UK/US link (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691205243/toward-a-free-economy) South Asia link (https://www.amazon.in/Toward-Free-Economy-Swatantra-Opposition/dp/0691256578)). It was shortlisted for the 2022 Elder Prize in the Social Sciences of the American Institute of Indian Studies and the 2024 W.K. Hancock Prize for best first monograph of the Australian Historical Association, and longlisted for the 2024 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Prize of the New India Foundation. A suite of peer-reviewed articles published over the last several years have interrogated various aspects of Indian political economy between the 1940s and the 1970s. Topics range from India's role in the international economic order, famine in Travancore during World War II, Hindu nationalist economic thought and policy, and anticorruption. He is currently working on two projects. The first is an environmental and economic history of roadbuilding and transport in India. Initial thoughts appeared in this post (https://histecon.fas.harvard.edu/climate-loss/roads/index.html) for the Harvard Center for History and Economics' "Visualizing Climate and Loss" blog in October 2023. During 2025-2028, he is the recipient of an Australian Research Council Discovery Early Career Research Award (DECRA) for this project. The second is a synthetic history of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984, the world's largest industrial disaster. This project is especially concerned with failures of relief and rehabilitation, chronic illnesses, and ongoing environmental pollution. He has just completed an article on forest management in India and is working on an article that sketches a revisionist history of migration between South and Southeast Asia. At ANU, Aditya teaches or has taught historical methods, environmental history, the history of political economy, and South Asian history. His teaching has been recognized with nominations for College and University-wide prizes. He is the Deputy Director of ANU's Center for Environmental History (https://history.cass.anu.edu.au/centres/ceh) and founded the ANU Capitalism Studies Network (http://csn.anu.edu.au/) with Will Bateman (Law) and Melinda Cooper (Sociology). He is completing a second term as Board Member of the South Asia Research Institute (2020-2021, 2024-6). From 2018 to 2024, he created and coordinated the Archives of Economic Life in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.histecon.magd.cam.ac.uk/archives-asia/index.html) website (you can learn more about it in this (https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/doing-online-south-southeast-asian-history/) Toynbee Prize Blog interview). events.title: Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā - Not a moonless night: Śamathadeva's Upāyikā, the oral life of Mūlasarvāstivāda scripture, and early Buddhist philology
events.description: An exposition of the Abhidharma without the Āgamas, however flawless, "does not capture the heart, just like a moonless night." So runs the colophon of Śamathadeva's Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā (Upāyikā for short), a monumental Sanskrit commentary now extant only in Tibetan translation. The Upāyikā is a commentary of an unusual kind. Rather than explaining Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya through standard exegetical procedures, it traces its scriptural citations back to their authoritative canonical settings in the Āgamas, often reproducing extensive passages, some of which do not otherwise survive in the received corpora. The same colophon states that these canonical materials were recalled from memory. Taking this seriously, the lecture will treat the Upāyikā both as a companion reader to the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya and as a witness to the oral textual life of the contemporaneous Mūlasarvāstivāda lineages of recitation in India. It will examine how the scriptures available to Śamathadeva were organized and transmitted, and will try to locate the otherwise unknown figure of Śamathadeva in time and space. Close philological engagement with this text will show what the practice of early Buddhist philology has to say about what counts as a text and as text-historical evidence.Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is a Visiting Associate Research Professor in the Department of Buddhist Sudies at Dharma Drum Institute of Liberal Arts (Taiwan), Director of the Āgama Research Group, and currently the Numata Visiting Professor for Buddhist Studies at the University of California at Berkeley. link (https://bhikkhunidhammadinna.com/)

events.title: Dawn Danby & David McConville // Planetary Repair, Shared Futures
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Dawn Danby and David McConville, co-founders of Spherical, an integrative research and design studio working to regenerate the health and integrity of Earth's living systems. Through design, research, and technology, Spherical explores how human systems are embedded within larger ecological, cultural, and planetary webs of relation, and how new forms of infrastructure might support reciprocal relationships with the living Earth. ​In this talk, Dawn and David will examine how climate action is often made politically viable through the language of infrastructure, and why that framing is both necessary and incomplete. Rather than treating infrastructure as a purely technical system, they will argue for a broader understanding that includes the nested scales, living relations, and more-than-human worlds that sustain life. Drawing on their work across ecological design, planetary systems, and media arts, they will explore how climate solutions demand new ways of seeing, mapping, and designing in relation to the Earth. Attendees will be invited to rethink infrastructure not simply as built form, but as a living scaffold for reciprocal care, repair, and transformation. ​This talk is open to the public and is for designers, researchers, students, and anyone interested in climate, systems thinking, and the role of design in shaping more livable futures. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: BPM 207 Leading Change
events.description: Access to registration is disabled two days prior to the event. This 6-hour workshop is part of the BPM Part 3: Grow Your Team series and is an elective option for the UC Systemwide People Management Certificate. In this highly interactive workshop, each participant's experience is drawn upon for the learning. Ideally, to contribute to and enhance understanding, participants will come with current and/or previous people management experience. The content provides the knowledge and skills necessary to successfully lead a team through a change initiative. By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to: *Identify the organizational approach to change related to their particular change initiative *Write a case for change, a vision for the future, and create a change plan *Create a team-specific communication plan *Explain the leader's role in change management and the skills required to successfully lead a change initiative *Explore resistance to change, and learn ways to address it productively *Identify ways to inspire commitment and help implement change *Locate resources to guide and support change management efforts

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Ignacio Navarrete
events.description: In Sneaking into Print (Toronto, 2026), Ignacio Navarrete (Spanish & Portuguese) explores the impact of early printing on narrative literature in Spain. He reveals how new technology enabled older texts and translations to circulate alongside newly written works, giving rise to a distinct narrative culture. Through an in-depth study of various narrative subgenres including hagiography, the epic, and sentimental fiction, Sneaking into Print integrates historical bibliography, material book features, and literary analysis. By examining texts as physical artifacts and narrative constructs, the book sheds light on their broader implications for narrative theory, offering fresh perspectives on the intersections of literature, materiality, and the early print marketplace. Navarrete is joined by Nicholas Paige (French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Tianyue Zhou (CTML GSR)
events.description: This week's seminar brings another thought-provoking discussion! Join us on October 28th to hear from CTML GSR Tianyue Zhou (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/tianyue-zhou) presenting his talk on "A CV-TMLE Global Test Approach to Improve Power in Rare Disease Clinical Studies with Multiple-Component Endpoints." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.Abstract: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.Bio: Tianyue Zhou is currently a PhD student in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley, working with Mark van der Laan and Maya Petersen. His research interests primarily lie in the intersection of causal inference and machine learning, with a focus on real-world evidence generation and improving efficiency in randomized trials.

events.title: The Canadian Transition from Whaling to Whale Watching
events.description: Despite the International Whaling Commission's establishment of a moratorium on commercial whaling in the 1980s, some countries and indigenous communities continue to take part in the practice commercially, for research, or subsistence. Whaling is a centuries-long practice whose data baseline is often set without deep historical consideration, and whale watching has taken the legacy of these human-cetacean relations, rebranded it, and brought it into public view through the lens of conservation and sustainability. One recommendation the IWC makes to shift cultural perceptions and economic viability of what it deems "putting the cetacean population to use" is to transition whaling into a whale watching industry. This highlights the inherent reliance on capitalistic drivers to incentivize international compliance. This study explores the historical trajectory of whaling to whale watching, and investigates arguments regarding their compatibility and continuity within Canadian contexts. It also seeks to elucidate how international nongovernmental organizations have mobilized whale watching as a new purveyor of conservation education, the realistic ability of community-based transitions to an industry highly reliant on tourism, and the ecological implications of whale watching as a capital driven industry. By honing in on Canadian participation in both the whaling and whale watching industries, this study will frame a global issue through commercial and indigenous Canadian and First Nations perspectives. By assessing centuries-long global whaling industries and investigating the fairly new IWC whale watching transition agenda, this historical analysis transcends maritime boundaries to interrogate the realities of imposing strict top-down regulations and expectations on communities whose ability to implement them may be limited or nonexistent.About the SpeakerSophia Chapple is a PhD candidate at Trinity College Dublin. She is one of four PhD students on the Life in the Currents Project, which seeks to better understand the interplay between marine extraction, ecosystem dynamics, and global climate change by combining methodologies and expertise from computer engineering, zoology, physics, and history. She is particularly interested in the human experience of the Early Modern climatic cooling phenomenon known as the Little Ice Age, and questions whether coastal communities turned to the sea to alleviate terrestrial subsistence pressures, and in what capacity they were able to do so. Her PhD thesis focuses on community resilience and the experiences of marginalized people in Early Modern Scotland, but her background in Political Science and work as a Research Assistant with 4OCEANS has allowed her to expand her scope beyond her typical temporal and spatial boundaries in order to trace specific historical narratives through to present day.

events.title: International Court of Justice: Judicial Fellowship Panel
events.description: ICJ Judicial Fellowship Panel Wednesday, November 18 · 1:00 PM · Berkeley Law, Room 141 Each year, the International Court of Justice selects fifteen Judicial Fellows from hundreds of candidates nominated by law schools around the world to clerk at the Peace Palace in The Hague for ten months. Berkeley Law nominates up to four candidates each year and provides a significant fellowship stipend for any Berkeley nominee the Court selects. Join BJIL and ILS, with support from the Miller Institute, for a conversation with four recent Judicial Fellows: Félix Aguettant (Berkeley Law LL.M. ’23), Allyson Ping, Lara Manbeck, and Marina Wilbraham. They will talk about the application process, their time at the Court, and where the fellowship has taken them since. PANELISTS Félix Aguettant is a lawyer in the Legal Service of the European Commission, in the EU External Relations and International Law team, based in Brussels. He is also a PhD candidate in public international law at the Sorbonne. He was a 2024-25 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Abraham and H.E. President Iwasawa. He is an alumnus of Berkeley Law’s executive LLM program and was nominated to the fellowship by Berkeley Law in 2024. He is currently the head coach of Berkeley Law’s 2026-27 Jessup team. Félix is bilingual in English and French and is a member of the California Bar. To date, Felix is the only Berkeley Law alum to have ever been a judicial fellow! Allyson Ping is a litigation associate at Debevoise & Plimpton, New York. From 2024-2025, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. President Iwasawa Yuji. Allyson received a J.D. from Columbia Law School in 2024, where she was a member of the Jessup Moot Court team and was co-Executive Editor of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law. Lara Manbeck is an Associate at Covington & Burling in Washington, D.C. From 2025 to 2026, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. Judge Nolte and later as an Associate Legal Officer at the Court. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law, an MPhil from the University of Cambridge, and a B.A. from New York University. Prior to law school, she worked in the Office of the Director-General of the International Development Law Organization. Marina Wilbraham is currently a Law Clerk at White and Case LLP, in the firm’s LA office, where her practice focuses on international technology disputes. She was a 2025-2026 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Sarah H. Cleveland. Previously, she was an Associate at Debevoise & Plimpton LLP for two years in New York, in the Litigation Department, where she worked on a mix of international arbitration, public international law, and commercial litigation matters. Marina is a 2023 Yale Law School graduate. BERKELEY LAW’S JUDICIAL FELLOWSHIP APPLICATIONS Applications for the 2027–28 judicial fellowship, run by the CDO, will open in December 2026 and close in January 2027. Details about the 2026-27 application for Berkeley Law’s nomination process here. You can find details about the fellowship on the ICJ Judicial Fellowship website. JD and LL.M. students in the classes of 2025, 2026 and 2027 are eligible to apply, provided they meet other eligibility criteria of the Court. LUNCH Lunch will be provided if you RSVP here.

events.title: First Encounters with AI: Writers on Writing
events.description: Part of a series on the social dimensions of AI organized by CSTMS, this event is a book launch for First Encounters with AI: Writers on Writing, a forthcoming book edited by Nina Beguš (CSTMS). The panel includes your colleague Hannes Bajohr (German), Alex Saum-Pascual (Spanish and Portuguese), and Nicholas Nardini, an LA-based screenwriter who has worked on some major series for Netflix. Nina Beguš will be moderating.First Encounters with AI gathers some of today's most original literary minds to explore one of the central artistic and cultural questions of our era: What happens to writing when language is no longer used only by humans? As large language models enter the public imagination and everyday creative practice, writers across genres—novelists, poets, screenwriters, essayists, translators, scholars, technologists, language artists—are grappling with profound shifts in how stories are conceived, crafted, and shared. This volume brings together seventeen acclaimed contributors from around the world to reflect on their early, intimate encounters with generative text at a moment when artificial intelligence feels at once thrilling, unsettling, and unavoidable. Their essays portray AI not as a monolith, but as a dynamic field of possibility and tension between creativity and computation, where longstanding human questions about intention, desire, authorship, labor, and value gain new urgency. Ranging from deeply personal meditations to critical provocations, from philosophical investigations to playful experiments, these writers reveal how writing tools shape writing itself—and what is at stake when those tools begin to imitate us. Curated and introduced by editor Nina Beguš, First Encounters with AI offers readers an essential guide to navigating this new literary landscape. Together, these essays map the terrain of our first contact zone with AI, offering clarity, insight, and imaginative depth at a moment of radical change.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Fractional eigenvalue escape rates on quantum graphs, and a Hermitian preparation theorem
events.description: Speaker: Gregory Berkolaiko, Texas A&M UniversityTake a quantum graph with a core whose edges have length of order s, attach a few infinite leads, and let s go to 0. Some negative eigenvalues will run off to -infinity, and an a priori bound says they cannot go faster than \(s^{-1}\). Simple examples show that this bound is sharp. Surprisingly, an eigenvalue can also escape at the rate \(s^{-2/3}\). Nothing in the problem (the Laplacian, the vertex conditions, the edge lengths) contains a cube root. So which other strange rates are possible?The answer turns out to be: none. For any graph and any fixed self-adjoint vertex conditions there are exactly two escape rates, \(s^{-1}\) and \(s^{-2/3}\). The number of eigenvalues of each kind, and their leading coefficients, can be read off explicitly from the vertex conditions.The proof turns the problem into the study of the zero set of an analytic function of two variables, and that brings tools from algebraic geometry into play. The Newton–Puiseux theorem tells us that solution branches follow fractional powers; the difficult part is to show that only two powers are possible. The key tool is a Hermitian matrix version of the Weierstrass preparation theorem, recently proved by Nils Dencker. It leads to an "implicit Rellich theorem": the solutions of a certain class of Hermitian determinantal equations in two variables behave like the eigenvalues of a one-parameter Hermitian family; in particular, they are analytic, as in Rellich's classical theorem. I will explain this result, which may be useful elsewhere, and show how it produces the two rates.Joint work with Denis Borisov, Marshall King and Julien Royer.

events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The US nuclear weapons complex is undergoing its biggest transformation since the end of the Cold War. Increasingly sophisticated experimental, computational, and manufacturing techniques that emerged to support a strategy of science-based stockpile stewardship are now being applied as tools for vertical proliferation as emphasis shifts from ‘stewardship’ to production. events.title: Book Talk. California Dreams: The Making and the Remaking of the University of California
events.organizer: Center for Studies in Higher Education
events.description: Join us for a talk by Miriam Pawel (Pulitzer Prize winner) on her new book California Dreams: The Making and the Remaking of the University of California (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/california-dreams-9781639732739/&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1791997065344272&usg=AOvVaw1px12Uw7pdUP8N5QRGPvQT) Distinguished by its founding mission as an engine of upward mobility, the University of California-a constitutionally independent public trust-is a great American experiment that has persevered through fraught battles over access, funding, and leadership. The University has been at the nexus of nearly every public policy debate and social movement since the Civil War, from women's rights to student protests, from academic freedom to affirmative action, shaping policies that reverberate throughout the United States.California Dreams narrates UC's rise and resilience through the lens of those whose lives it has transformed-in particular, five pioneering graduates whose diverse paths underscore why the University remains, in the words of Berkeley graduate Joan Didion, "California's best idea of itself." At a time of staggering inequality and uncertainty, as higher education faces unprecedented threats, that role has never been more crucial. Drawing on extensive research in ten archives and dozens of interviews, California Dreams weaves together the linked history of the school and state in all its drama, significance, and humanity; the result is a magisterial narrative of both a remarkable public institution of higher education, and also California itself.Registration (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSewZcRai7S4v5_mpzJboBxEucrS75zzh6_CRVyj12JwyiitPw/viewform?usp=dialog) requested

events.title: Descriptive Set Theory Working Seminar: Ergodic theorems for amenable groups
events.description: Speaker: MohammedSaid Alhalimi, UC BerkeleyThe goal of this talk is to introduce amenability of groups and its consequences for the existence of convergent averaging sequences. I will define tempered Følner sequences and Tempelman's condition and explain their relation to averaging problems using the ideas in Ornstein-Weiss (1983). Following Hochman (2006), I will show that finite abelian rank is a sufficient condition for the existence of Tempelman Følner sequence for countable abelian groups. Finally, I will explain the proof of Lindenstrauss (2001) of a pointwise ergodic theorem for amenable groups along tempered Følner sequences.

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Provable Privacy and Security for Autonomous Agents — Are We There Yet?
events.description: In this talk, we take the position that agent security must be approached as a systems problem: the AI model powering the agent must be treated as an untrusted component, and security invariants must be enforced at the system level. Through this lens, efforts to increase model robustness (the dominant viewpoint in the ML community) are insufficient on their own. Instead, we must complement existing efforts with techniques from the systems security domain. We will cover some example solutions that follow this viewpoint, and discuss their pros and cons. We will also identify the challenges that stand in the way of implementing these principles in agents. Somesh Jha received his B.Tech from Indian Institute of Technology, New Delhi in Electrical Engineering. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Carnegie Mellon University under the supervision of Prof. Edmund Clarke (a Turing award winner). Currently, Somesh Jha is the Lubar Professor in the Computer Sciences Department at the University of Wisconsin (Madison). His work focuses on analysis of security protocols, survivability analysis, intrusion detection, formal methods for security, and analyzing malicious code. Recently, he has focused on trustworthy ML. Somesh Jha has published several articles in highly referenced conferences and prominent journals. He has won numerous best-paper and distinguished-paper awards. Prof. Jha received the CAV award for his work on CEGAR and also has received the IIT-Delhi Distinguished Alumni award. Prof. Jha is a fellow of the ACM, IEEE, and AAAS.

events.title: Seminar 291, Department Seminar joint with Labor and Public Finance: Xavier Jaravel (LSE) - Distributional Consumer Price Indices
events.description: Abstract: This paper develops a new public database to estimate inflation heterogeneity across socio-demographic groups in the United States in real time. These distributional CPIs (D-CPIs) are fully consistent with the methodology of the official CPI and are available from 2002 to the present day by household income, age, race and other characteristics. Using this database, I establish three results showing that D-CPIs have important implications for the measurement of long-run trends in inequality and poverty, as well as of real wage dynamics during crises. First, "real" inequality across household income quintiles increased about 45% faster with D- CPIs between 2002 and 2019, compared to the official CPI. While the pre-tax income gap between the top and bottom household income quintiles increased by 15.7 % during this period according to the official CPI, it increased by 22.6 % with D-CPIs. Similarly large adjustments apply to consumption inequality and inequality in pre-tax and post-tax national incomes. Second, today 2.3 million people are below the "real" poverty line using D-CPIs but above the poverty threshold using the official CPI. Third, during the inflation burst following the Covid-19 pandemic, inflation was higher for the middle class, compared to low-income and high-income households. This pattern is driven by gas and vehicles and implies that the compression of "real" wages was about 28% faster with D-CPIs than with the official CPI. Similar patterns of inflation heterogeneity hold in extensions allowing for geographic heterogeneity in inflation, non-homothetic price indices, and expanding the analysis back to 1983. See full paper here (https://www.xavierjaravel.com/_files/ugd/bacd2d_40a5d2231f0847e1a2e20f6ca4031c7d.pdf).

events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description: Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.Lecture 1 of 2

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: CCB Seminar: Charles Whittaker, Assistant Professor, Infectious Diseases & Vaccinology, School of Public Health
events.description: Title: Modelling the next generation of medical countermeasures for pandemic preparedness and controlAbstract: Medical countermeasure (MCM) development has largely been reactive: vaccines and therapeutics are developed against known, circulating pathogens, or only after a novel pathogen has been identified and sequenced. This poses a problem for pandemic preparedness - even on accelerated timelines, reactive development of vaccines or antivirals against a newly emerged novel pathogen may take many months, and leave a substantial gap between detection (of the novel pathogen) and availability (of the MCMs). It is in this window that much of an pandemic's health burden, and the need for costly non-pharmaceutical interventions, accrues. Broad-spectrum MCMs that are active across an entire viral family or genus rather than a single pathogen, offer a way to close that gap. Because they don't depend on knowing the exact threat in advance, they can be manufactured and stockpiled ahead of time, and deployed immediately following novel pathogen detection. In this talk I'll present two case studies exploring what that early availability could achieve. The first examines a broadly protective sarbecovirus vaccine, considering its use for outbreak containment and for protecting high-risk groups during a hypothetical future SARS-X pandemic [1]. The second examines the potential impact of a pan-filoviral oral antiviral used as post-exposure prophylaxis during ebolavirus outbreaks; a use-case motivated by our ongoing work responding to the Bundibugyo epidemic in DRC [2]. In both cases, the work will explore how we can most effectively use these emerging tools to support pandemic preparedness and response efforts; as well as the factors influencing their public health impact and overall value. [1] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-63399-x (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-63399-x) [2] https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00437-8/fulltext (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00437-8/fulltext)Bio: Dr. Charles Whittaker is an Assistant Professor of Infectious Diseases and Vaccinology at Berkeley Public Health, where he directs the Pandemic and Epidemic Threat Analytics Lab (PETAL). His research focuses on the dynamics, detectability and control of pathogens with pandemic potential, and uses state-of-the-art analytical approaches spanning viral phylodynamics, epidemiological modelling and machine learning to uncover new insights into how pathogens spread through populations and to enhance preparedness and response strategies for public health emergencies. Central to this work is a focus on equity, addressing how the inequitable distribution of resources hinders effective outbreak response, and developing solutions to ensure everyone is protected from pandemic threats. Current research topics include projects on novel pathogen surveillance, the drivers of zoonotic spillover, and next-generation medical countermeasures such as broad-spectrum vaccines.
