events.title: Katherine Nagel: Understanding the logic of the fly navigation system
events.description: All animals need to navigate to find food and resources in their environment. My lab has been using odor-guided navigation to uncover the organization and logic of the fly navigation system. I will present recent and ongoing work aiming to describe how the fan-shaped body, a part of the fly navigation system thought to specify allocentric goal directions, organizes multi-sensory input and computes goals based on ongoing experience. One of our guiding interests is understanding what is similar and different across the navigation systems of different species. I hope this question inspires some interesting discussions!

events.title: Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution
events.organizer: Institute for the Study of Societal Issues
events.location: Berkeley Way West (Second Floor Lobby), 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley CA
events.description: The event will feature Nicholas L. Baham III, Jocyl Sacramento, and Carlos Salomon—editors of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge, 2026)��in conversation with Cati V. de los Rios. The book presents key theories, concepts, practices, and movements in Ethnic Studies, illuminating the complex processes of race-making and power in the U.S.Nicholas L. Baham III is a Professor of Ethnic Studies at California State University East Bay and teaches courses in Black Studies and Genders & Sexualities in Communities of Color. Dr. Baham is a graduate of the College at the University of Chicago, earned his Master's degree in Anthropology at Stanford University, and received his Ph.D. in Anthropology at Indiana University, Bloomington. In addition to serving as co-editor and co-writer of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution, Dr. Baham is also the author of The Coltrane Church: Apostles of Sound, Agents of Social Justice, co-writer for The Podcaster's Dilemma: Decolonizing Podcasters in the Era of Surveillance Capitalism, and co-writer of When is Wakanda: Afrofuturism and Dark Speculative Futurity. He has published articles and book chapters on Jazz, James Baldwin, Afrofuturism, and Critical Media Literacy. In 2015, he published his first mystery novel, The People's Detective: A Sonny Trueheart Mystery, a fictional account of missing and trafficked young women of color in Oakland, California. He is currently serving as Interim Associate Dean for the College of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences. For more information, go to nicholasbaham.com (http://nicholasbaham.com/)Jocyl Sacramento (she/her/siya) is an Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at Cal State East Bay. She specializes in Asian American Studies, K-12 Ethnic Studies, critical pedagogies, comparative racialization, and Pinayism. Dr. Sacramento completed her MA and Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley School of Education, where she was a Graduate Fellow at the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues. She received her BA in Ethnic Studies and Sociology from the University of California, Riverside and earned her MA in Asian American Studies from San Francisco State University, where she taught Filipinx American Studies with Pin@y Educational Partnerships. Her praxis-oriented work emerged from her participation in youth-led action research and her service with various youth programs and schools. Dr. Sacramento currently serves as Co-Principal Investigator for Cal State East Bay's AANHPI Student Achievement Program. You can find Dr. Sacramento's published work in Amerasia Journal, AAPI Nexus, Journal of Asian American Studies, The Urban Review, Equity & Excellence in Education, Peabody Journal of Education, Review of Educational Research, and Journal of Educational Psychology. She is co-editor of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge). Carlos Manuel Salomon is a Chicano author, educator and activist with indigenous roots in the Arizona and California borderlands region and Professor of Ethnic Studies, California State University, East Bay. His research interests include borderlands ancestry, collective and cultural memory, Chicano/a folklore, migration, and oral history. He received his Ph.D. from the University of New Mexico in Borderlands and Latin American History. He is the author of "Pio Pico: The Last Governor of Mexican California (https://www.oupress.com/books/9782065/pio-pico)" (Oklahoma 2010), which covers the astonishing life of the nineteenth-century Afro-Mexican politician Pío de Jesús Pico. Dr. Salomon is the Editor of the "Routledge History of Latin American Culture (https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-History-of-Latin-American-Culture/Salomon/p/book/9780367217839)" (Routledge, 2018). The volume gathers authors from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay, Mexico, the United States and other nations to reveal the enduring impact of resistance on Latin American and US Chicano/Latina cultural production. He is co-editor of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge, 2026), which brings together over 50 of the top Ethnic Studies researchers in the country to guide students and instructors toward new avenues of praxis-centered, community-driven learning. Moderator:Cati V. de los Ríos is an Associate Professor of Language, Literacy, and Culture at UC Berkeley's School of Education and a former Spanish, ELD, and Ethnic Studies high school teacher. Her ethnographic, community-based, and participatory research is situated at the axes of literacy studies, educational anthropology, civic and political learning, and ethnic studies, with an emphasis on studying the linguistic-semiotic repertoires that Latina/o/x youth and families deploy and develop across educational settings. Her writing has been published in Aztlán: A Journal of Chicano Studies;Applied Linguistics; TESOL Quarterly; Language Learning; Harvard Educational Review; Reading Research Quarterly; Journal of Literacy Research; Research in the Teaching of English; Anthropology & Education Quarterly; Written Communication; and Learning, Media and Technology.

events.title: Life and Death in the New El Salvador
events.location: CLACS Conference Room (2334 Bowditch St, Berkeley, CA 94720)
events.description: El Salvador's twenty-first century is defined by a social dialectic where life and death remain in entangled relation and in which popular lifeways exist in a fragile state between function and disrepair. Seemingly, society vacillates between authoritarian safety and gang insecurity. Today, the Central American nation finds itself also in a critical moment of political and organizational enclosure due to the violence wrought by Nayib Bukele alongside the exhaustion of the traditional Salvadoran left. Situated within the longer histories of civil war, postwar violence, neoliberal restructuring, migration, political disillusionment, and the erosion of democratic institutions, the talk argues that Bukelismo cannot be understood solely as a product of propaganda or charismatic populism. Rather, it has drawn force from widespread exhaustion with insecurity, corruption, exclusion, unending hurt, and the unfulfilled promises of the postwar order. Against this backdrop, I identify a source of nonviolent counterpower emerging to confront rising authoritarianism that, often virally, appears to us as carcerality, punitivism, and militarized order. Theorizing from within Bukele's regime, I locate practical activities that are taking place inside El Salvador's contemporary death-world that are, curiously, focusing on an important cultural figure, Monsignor Óscar Romero, whose "living corpus" is being reworked to imagine new horizons, overturn progressive slowdown and reconnect political efforts with the cultural and spiritual lives of ordinary Salvadorans.Speaker bio:Jorge Cuéllar is an interdisciplinary scholar who focuses on the politics and daily life of modern Central America. Cuéllar's first book, a grounded study of El Salvador's turbulent postwar to "post-postwar" transition is entitled, Everyday Life and Everyday Death in El Salvador, forthcoming with Duke University Press. In addition to publications in scholarly journals and volumes, his writing appears in El Faro, NACLA, The Los Angeles Review of Books, New Left Review, and The Abusable Past. Cuéllar is appointed Assistant Professor of Central American Studies in the Department of Latin American, Latino & Caribbean Studies at Dartmouth College and is a Co-Executive Editor of the North American Congress on Latin America (NACLA)Co-sponsors: Associate Professor of Comparative Literature, Spanish & Portuguese, and New Media and Craigslist chair Tom McEnaney; Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies; Department of History; Central American Studies Working Group, Townsend Center for the Humanities

events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description: A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema.Maya Sidhu (https://french.berkeley.edu/people/maya-sidhu), Lecturer in the Department of French and a scholar of film and media studies, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia—industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.EVENT POSTER _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. _____________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) Support us by donating online HERE (https://give.berkeley.edu/fund/FU0742000)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Lecture | Camera Palestina: War, Spectacle and the Flaneur
events.description: The Center for Middle Eastern Studies, the UC Berkeley Department of History, the Palestinian and Arab Studies Program, and the History of Art Department welcome Professor Salim Tamari for a lecture titled:Camera Palestina: War, Spectacle and the Flaneur This talk will examine how the notion of spectacle and the spectacular in photography was influenced by the situationist text of Guy Labord's Society of Spectacles—which describes how capitalist modernity has degraded social life by replacing all experienced phenomena into its representation. WWI images from Palestine deal with the spectacle of war and its degradation against theatrical images from shadow theatre (Karagoz) in Palestine collected by the musician Wasif Jawhariyyeh.Wasif's diary has been described by the Guardian newspaper as one of the top ten witness accounts of the twentieth century. The British Historian Montefiore selected it as one of the best five historical narratives of all time.Bio Salim Tamari is a Senior Research Associate at the Institute for Palestine Studies and Professor Emeritus of Sociology at Birzeit University. He is the outgoing editor of The Jerusalem Quarterly and holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Manchester. His research focuses on Palestinian social history, urban transformation, and the Ottoman era in Palestine. His books include The Great War and the Remaking of Palestine (2017), The Storyteller of Jerusalem: The Life and Times of Wasif Jawhariyyeh (2015), and Camera Palestina: Patronage and Photography (2022). He received the Palestine Prize for Achievements in the Social Sciences and Humanities in 2018 and the Middle East Monitor Prize for Lifetime Achievement in Social History that same year.

events.title: Film Screening: La Chinoise
events.description: In an apartment defaced with political graffiti, Jean-Luc Godard's "petit Maoists" debate the principles of the Cultural Revolution, their shortwave tuned to Radio Peking. This Parisian cell, consisting of five young people—Veronique, a student; Guillaume, an actor; Henri, a chemical engineer; Kirilov, an artist; and Yvonne, a country girl—deliberates on the need for action while gorged on the predigested language of revolution. In an almost slapstick assemblage of skits that joins Pop and agitprop, La Chinoise charts the progress of these radicals as they veer from playing at revolution to making it. Godard advances his self-possessed film forward with a lucidity of means that refuses distraction.

events.title: Qalandariyya as Method: Tracing Baba Rahim Mashrab in Contemporary Central Asian Culture
events.description: The figure of Baba Rahim Mashrab, the 17th century poet and itinerant dervish is an important icon amongst Uzbeks and Uyghurs. Born in Namangan, Mashrab travelled across the region of Central Asia, to Kashgar, Khotan, Bukhara, and Balkh, leaving behind a rich repertoire of ecstatic ghazal poetry, and a collection of extraordinary tales of his exploits and encounters, in the Divan-i Mashrab. This paper traces Mashrab's journeys and his legacy in contemporary musical performance. It reflects on the diverse ways in which his poetry is realised musically in different contexts and locales, and the diverse ways in which his poetic texts and his life stories are listened to and interpreted. Taking the qalandar as our starting point allows a richer kind of mobile and connected cultural history to emerge. The footsteps of Baba Rahim Mashrab traverse multiple boundaries and binaries : secular-religious, national-local, classical-folk, traditional-popular. The multiple interpretations of his repertoire in different locales cast light on patterns of oral tradition, twentieth century processes of national culture making, and the legacy and practice of Sufism in Central Asia. Professor Rachel Harris's research is centered on China and Central Asia, with a particular focus on the Uyghurs. She has conducted ethnographic fieldwork in Xinjiang, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan over a period of twenty years. Her work focuses on maqam traditions, intangible cultural heritage, music and Islam, soundscapes, and state projects of territorialization. She applies her research through performance and transmission projects, including concerts, workshops, and recording projects. With twenty years of experience in teaching and doctoral supervision in the field of ethnomusicology, she welcomes inquiries from prospective PhD students. Her most recent book is Soundscapes of Uyghur Islam (IUP 2020), and her most recent edited volume is Ethnographies of Islam in China (U Hawaii 2020). She has previously co-edited the journal Ethnomusicology Forum and served as series editor for the Routledge SOAS Studies in Music series.

events.title: Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right
events.description: For four years, Jair Bolsonaro led Brazil and the popular, far-right movement that bore his name. His rise, defeat, and the chaos he left in his wake reflect patterns that are playing out in several countries, from the US to Argentina to India. In Anatomy of Disintegration(Haymarket Books, 2026), Rodrigo Nunes uses Brazil as a point of departure to make sense of why the far right is on the rise all over the world, where its appeal comes from, and explain the dystopian horizon it is moving toward. Through sharp, original analyses of the social composition of its supporters, the material and affective conditions that underpin it, and the mainstream's inability to respond to it, Rodrigo Nunes argues that the contemporary far right is better understood not as an effort to block but as an attempt to harness and accelerate forces of social disintegration set in motion by capital and intensified by the crisis of neoliberalism. Rodrigo Nunes is an associate professor in philosophy at PUC-Rio, Brazil, and a visiting fellow at the University of Essex, UK. He is the author of Neither Vertical nor Horizontal: A Theory of Political Organisation and Organisation of the Organisationless: Collective Action After Networks. His articles have appeared in Boston Review, Les Temps Modernes, Radical Philosophy, Jacobin, and The Guardian. He lives between London and Rio de Janeiro.

events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description: Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.Lecture 2 of 2

events.title: Film Screening: Harakiri
events.description: Masaki Kobayashi harnesses the breathtaking beauty of black-and-white, widescreen cinematography to create an abstract epic. Starring Tatsuya Nakadai, the film depicts one man's desperate attempt to crack the blind, absolute authority that characterizes the feudal age and, Kobayashi suggests, our own. In an Edo-period mansion, the camera inches down hallways and finds rooms within rooms to explicate a complex flashback narration. In the bloody climax, the black-robed figures who were caught and dissected by a stationary camera throughout the film come into their own as an inexorable prophecy, like Toru Takemitsu's haunting music and the words that emerge almost rhythmically from the dialogue: harakiri . . . (seppuku).

events.title: Film Screening: Samurai Rebellion
events.description: Rebellion is the fitting original title of this relentless social portrait of those who demand subservience and those who have had enough. A magisterial Toshiro Mifune slow burns his way through the role of dutiful samurai Sasahara, whose attempts to be a "good servant" are about to end. "You retreat, and retreat," says his friend Asano (Tatsuya Nakadai), "until finally you attack." Rare for the genre, the film's plot is set in motion by a woman, one whose willful stand against injustice inspires the men to act. Effective or not, it is the act of rebellion, Masaki Kobayashi implies, that matters.

events.title: Film Screening: Raging Bull
events.description: Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro make the biography of boxer Jake LaMotta into a visceral meditation on existential suffering. Eschewing the romance associated with the sport, Raging Bull shows the struggle of an athlete whose willful determination to succeed on his own terms takes its toll on all those around him—friends and adversaries in equal measure—before he is undermined by self-loathing. Every punch is framed, lit, and cut for maximum impact, with black-and-white cinematography inspired by James Wong Howe. "A fusion of Hollywood genre with personal vision . . . closer to poetry than pulp. Its sculptural weight can only be appreciated on the big screen" (Amy Taubin, Village Voice).

events.description: Saturday, November 21, 7:30pmJazzJason Moran and the Harlem HellfightersJames Reese Europe and the Absence of RuinProgram:The Absence of Ruin is jazz pianist and composer Jason Moran's multidisciplinary meditation on the life and legacy of James Reese Europe, the underrecognized Black American composer and bandleader who landed in France with the Harlem Hellfighters on New Year's Day 1918. The celebrated all-Black unit helped break the stalemate on the Western Front during the First World War, while composer Europe's finely honed military music ensemble popularized the new spirit of jazz in a war-torn France fascinated with Black culture. Moran's layered work explores the idea of memory in Black culture, augmenting his long-standing Bandwagon bandmates––bassist Tarus Mateen and drummer Nasheet Waits––with a seven-piece horn section and visuals by Oscar-nominated cinematographer Bradford Young. events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Javanese Gamelan
events.description: A cornerstone of the department's season, student performers join Gamelan Sari Raras and take the stage under the lead of longtime ensemble director Midiyanto. This intricate ensemble art form—which famously inspired the impressionist harmonies of 19th-century Western composers—continues to bridge the divide of global music. events.title: Film Screening: Rouge
events.description: Rouge is a sensuous and melancholy film about a beautiful ghost searching for her lost lover in modern Hong Kong. Fleur (Anita Mui) and "Twelfth Master" (Leslie Cheung) committed suicide fifty years ago, intending to spend eternity together in Hell rather than be separated by his disapproving parents. But when "Twelfth Master" fails to join her in the afterlife, Fleur returns to Earth to find him. She befriends a journalist couple. Fascinated by her archaic clothes, language, and otherworldly manner, they agree to help. Slipping back and forth in time, "Rouge is something like the Platonic ideal of a cinematic ghost story" (Dennis Lim, Criterion Collection).

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Real Infinitesimal Freeness of Wigner Matrices
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Samuel Gurrola Viramontes, CIMAT GuanajatoIn this talk, within the framework of real infinitesimal free probability introduced by Cebron and Mingo, we will discuss the calculation of the real infinitesimal free cumulants of independent complex Wigner matrices. Our approach relies on establishing a combinatorial relation between annular non-crossing partitions and families of directed graphs. As a consequence, we show that independent complex Wigner matrices are asymptotically real infinitesimally free. In particular, under mild conditions, a complex Wigner matrix is asymptotically infinitesimally free from its transpose. This is based on joint work with James A. Mingo (arXiv:2609.24023).

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis"
events.description: Please join us on Tuesday, November 24th from 4:00–5:30pm for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis by Matthew Shutzer, Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. Professor Shutzer will be joined in conversation by Youjin Chung, Associate Professor in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy & Management and the Energy & Resources Group at UC Berkeley, and Daniel Aldana Cohen, Assistant Professor of Sociology at UC Berkeley. The talk will be moderated by Michael Watts, Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Departments of South & Southeast Asia Studies and Geography, and the Energy and Resources Group.About the Book India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. In the book, Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.PanelistsMatthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching are concerned with the place of the environment in global history, with a particular focus on fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. He has also worked on topics that connect global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. He is currently at work on a second book project on climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945.Youjin B. Chung (https://youjinbchung.net/about) studies the relationship between gender and inequality, rural development, and socio-environmental change in East Africa, with a focus on Tanzania. The overarching question that drives her research program is: how and why do development policies and processes that aim to improve sustainability and equity outcomes often reinforce existing power structures and marginalize the groups they intend to serve? Over the years, she has channeled this central animating concern into three specific research projects. Using Tanzania as an analytic case, these projects investigate some of the most contentious issues in global development and environmental politics: large-scale farmland investments, sustainable livestock intensification, and the critical minerals rush. She is the author of Sweet Deal, Bitter Landscape: Gender Politics and Liminality in Tanzania's New Enclosures (Cornell University Press, 2024). At Berkeley, she convenes the Critical Ruralities Lab, a research workshop and collaborative mentoring space that promotes empirically grounded and justice-oriented scholarship on development and socio-environmental change in the global countryside.Daniel Aldana Cohen (https://aldanacohen.com/) is Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he is Director of the Socio-Spatial Climate Collaborative, or (SC)2 (https://sc2.berkeley.edu/), and serves as a faculty affiliate in the graduate program on Political Economy. He is also Founding Co-Director of the Climate and Community Institute, a progressive climate and economy think tank. He has been a CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar (2021-24) and Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey (2018-19). He is the co-author of A Planet to Win: Why We Need a Green New Deal (Verso 2019). Cohen works on the intersections of the climate emergency, housing, political economy, social movements, and inequalities of race and class in the United States and Brazil. As Director of (SC)2, he is leading qualitative and quantitative research projects on Whole Community Climate Mapping, green political economy, and eco-apartheid. He was also co-founder and co-PI of the Superstorm Research Lab (https://superstormresearchlab.org/), in New York City.Michael Watts (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-emeritus-michael-watts) is Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. He served as the Director of the Institute of International Studies at Berkeley from 1994 to 2004 and was Director of Social Science Matrix at Berkeley in 2019–20. He was most recently a Non-resident Long-term Fellow at the Swedish Collegium for Advanced Study (SCAS). Watts is a member of the British Academy, was a Guggenheim Fellow in 2003, and was awarded the Victoria Medal by the Royal Geographical Society in 2004, and the Berlin Prize by the American Academy in Berlin in 2016. He was awarded the Ester Boserup Prize in 2024. Watts' writing has addressed a number of development issues especially famine and food security, political violence and the agrarian question in Africa, South Asia and Vietnam, natural resources and especially the energy and mineral sectors, and the political economy of development and governance, more generally. Watts has worked for UNDP, OECD and other development organizations, including the Ford, Rockefeller and MacArthur Foundations. He has published over fifteen books and three hundred articles and has worked extensively with the renowned photographer Ed Kashi. Watts has written extensively on the oil industry, extractive economies and international commodity trading firms.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Film Screening: Modern Times
events.description: It starts with an overhead shot of sheep and cuts to the throngs coming out of a subway station. Was Charlie Chaplin a Surrealist, or just a realist? His version of modern times looks forward in equal measure to Jacques Tati and 1984. This "silent" is full of modern sounds, heard over loudspeakers and big corporate television screens (not to mention the Tramp's outburst of French-inspired gibberish). Charlie, the ever-elegant Tramp, is an industrial swashbuckler with an oilcan for a sword, but he's begun taking on the characteristics of factory machines, obsessively twisting buttons no matter where they are.

events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. events.title: Film Screening: Center Stage
events.description: After a string of memorable performances as strong-willed, beautiful, and virtuous women, the actress Ruan Lingyu committed suicide in 1935, at the age of twenty-four. Stanley Kwan's innovative film goes far beyond the traditional biopic to offer up several strata of "reality," "reenactment," and "cinema." Detailed re-creations of scenes from the actress's too-short life combine with documentary interviews of her contemporaries, actual footage from her existing silent films, and even discussions between star Maggie Cheung, Kwan, and other cast members. Like a Russian doll, Center Stage reveals a Modernist take on the ways in which cinema and culture create an actress, a legend, and a woman.

events.location: BAMPFA — Berkeley Art Museum & Pacific Film Archive
events.description: Luchino Visconti is in an unusually comic mode for this satire on urban life and movieland ambition. The incomparable Anna Magnani plays a mother trying to launch her young daughter in show business.

events.title: Film Screening: Bellissima
events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Film Screening: White Nights
events.description: This adaptation of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's tale about displaced, disconnected people drifting along crossing, doubling paths was shot in moody black-and-white on a soundstage simulacrum of Livorno, Italy. With it Luchino Visconti veered away from verisimilitude and toward an emphatically subjective style—from neorealism to neoromanticism. As a quiet man who accidentally befriends a troubled, lonely young woman (Maria Schell) and finds himself playing understudy for the absent object of her affections (Jean Marais), Marcello Mastroianni mingles subtly passionate yearnings with a characteristic note of annoyance. His character is both distrustful of and seduced by the romantic dreams that preoccupy the woman he loves.

events.title: Film Screening: GoodFellas
events.description: Working with trusted accomplices, including editor Thelma Schoonmaker, cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, actors Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci, and brilliant first-time collaborators Ray Liotta and Lorraine Bracco, Martin Scorsese combines varied cinematic styles, camera techniques, and a precisely executed collage of popular music, adapting Nicholas Pileggi's chronicle of real-life Mafia associate Henry Hill. events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: The hyperinvariant subspace problem
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Hari Bercovici, Indiana University at BloomingtonAmong the results announced by Open AI, there is a solution of the hyperinvariant subspace problem: there is an operator T on a Hilbert space that is not a scalar multiple of the identity, does have nontrivial invariant subspaces, but none of these subspaces is invariant under every operator in the commutant of T. In particular, the commutant (T)' is a nonselfadjoint transitive algebra. The construction uses weighted shifts with few invariant subspaces, and a modicum of ergodic theory: a transformation known as an odometer. The resulting operator T is quasinilpotent. I will argue that the example is correct. Moreover, the example can be modified so that it yields a contraction with essential spectrum equal to the closed unit disk. Such contractions are known to have a large variety of invariant subspaces, and one could ask whether the techniques used to produce these subspaces can be improved to yield a hyperinvariant subspace.

events.title: Adaptive Traffic Control Systems
events.description: Description This newly updated online course offers a summary of fundamental principles, operational requirements and expected benefits of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. The first session presents various traffic control systems and general characteristics, market state, and evaluations of the ATCS along with other solutions like traffic responsive and Artificial Intelligent (AI) based signal timing. The second session focuses on SCATS (one of the oldest and widely deployed systems in the entire world) and other ATCSs from the US market. The third session presents SynchroGreen and InSync, recent ATCSs which recently gained a lot of popularity among the US customers. Finally, the fourth session addresses SCOOT and ACS Lite, two systems with similarities in algorithms but various detection and communication requirements. Each session is divided into three major parts: the first offers a summary of fundamental principles of a selected adaptive technology, the second covers summary of operational and institutional requirements to run adaptive control, and the third presents operational benefits from available case studies. Topics IncludeFundamental principles of ATCS operations Adjustment of signal timings and operational flexibility Traffic responsive and AI based signal timing Detection requirements Communication requirements Software and hardware requirements Reported operational modes Institutional preparation for deployment of an ATCS Reported operational benefits What You Will Learn Students will obtain a significant amount of technical information to understand fundamental principles of operations, deployment requirements, and reported operational benefits (highlighted through exemplary case studies) of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. This information will help students to become familiar with these relatively new signal control technologies and develop a realistic set of expectations regarding their deployments and operational benefits. Who Should Attend This course is intended for traffic engineers, planners, technicians, and decision makers in municipal, county, and state agencies interested in the operations, requirements and benefits of Adaptive Traffic Control System technologies, particularly those with the responsibility for the planning, design, implementation, operation, and maintenance of traffic signal control systems for urban areas.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.description: CRG Forum Series + Book Talk*Every Man’s Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism withJulia Bowes, Lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, and author of Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026) and discussantLydia Mathews, PhD Candidate, Department of History, UC Berkeley Dr. JuliaBowes is a lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, where her research focuses on the relationship between gender, the family, and conservatism in the United States. Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. She has held fellowships from the Jefferson Scholars Foundation, the Institute of Citizens and Scholars (formerly the Woodrow Wilson Institute), and, prior to joining the University of Melbourne, was an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong. She is now researching a project on the gendered politics of alternative health movements, including anti-vaccination, anti-fluoridation, and home birth movements, in the twentieth-century United States.Event hosted by the Center for Race and Gender (https://crg.berkeley.edu/), and co-sponsored by the Berkeley Center for Right-Wing Studies (https://issi.berkeley.edu/crws) and the Department of History (https://history.berkeley.edu/home). *Lunch provided on a first-come, first-served basis. **If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: OpenADMET (Bay Area Open Science Group)
events.description: OpenADMET - Raising the bar on ADMET prediction with open sciencevZoom information registrationDrug discovery programs frequently stall due to the Avoid-ome, which comprises the complex off-target interactions and ADMET liabilities that traditional heuristic methods struggle to address. To solve this, OpenADMET combines high-resolution structural biology, directed data generation, and machine learning into a systematic framework for predicting and mitigating these liabilities. Central to this mission is generating targeted datasets to host large-scale blind benchmarks that test community predictive models on real-world drug design problems. By uniting hundreds of academic and industry teams through these challenges, webinars, and conferences, the initiative fosters widespread collaboration to establish transparent, data-driven standards across the field.Pat Walters is Chief Scientist at OpenADMET, an open-science initiative that integrates high-throughput experimentation, structural biology, and machine learning to advance ADMET prediction. Alongside his work at OpenADMET, he serves as an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Bioengineering & Therapeutic Sciences at UCSF. Pat brings over thirty years of industry leadership to his roles, having previously held senior positions at Relay Therapeutics and Vertex Pharmaceuticals. A dedicated educator and communicator, he is the author of the widely read blog "Practical Cheminformatics," where he shares technical insights on computational drug discovery.Bay Area Open Science GroupThe Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. events.title: Aaron Nyerges, "Counter-Mapping Modernism: Literature, Oil, and the Cartographic Imagination"
events.description: Aaron Nyerges' recent book American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination (Cambridge UP, 2025) is a new reading of American modernism that examines the cartographic literature of the United States and places it in context of the state's overseas expansion. Dr Nyerges stretches the map of US literature across an imperial archipelago of territories and outlines a method of comparative reading that brings canonical American authors into dialogue with under-represented writers from across the contested dominions of US empire. He argues that literary artists from across US dominion responded to space-dominating technologies of empire and retooled them to imagine counter-cartographies, designs that challenged the official geographies of the United States. This talk explores the cartographic imagination of modernist literature as it relates to the territorial expansions of the United States in the early decades of the twentieth century. We begin with Langston Hughes's construction and destruction of cartographic material, his tearing apart of his world atlas, and his vision of a nation made errant by oceanic flux. From there we will assemble – and collaboratively analyse – a group of poems that make visible the divergent investments modernists made in the production of "counter-maps," forms of geographic knowledge that challenge the maps made by governments and corporations. In particular, we will attend to the oil maps deposited in Ezra Pound's Cantos, by which he critiques the resource expropriation of former Ottoman territories by Anglo-American cartels. At that very locus, the Iraqi modernist poet Nazik al-Malā'ikah envisions a different kind of energy poetics, where the dividing line between oil's extractive and consumptive spheres is decidedly smudged. Her mapping of an abysmal geography provides anti-colonial counterpoint to the expanding highway infrastructure of the United States, as well as the thermodynamic aesthetics that exhilarate the lyrics of Pound and William Carlos Williams.Aaron Nyerges (https://www.ussc.edu.au/aaron-nyerges) is a Senior Lecturer in American Studies at the United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney. His book, American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

events.title: Book Talk: An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa
events.description: Book Talk:An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa (Cambridge University Press, 2026) In what measure could education be an agent of African freedom? Combining histories of race, economics, and education, Elisa Prosperetti examines this question in two West African contexts, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, from the 1890s to the 1980s. She argues that a Black Atlantic perspective changes how we see decolonization and development in West Africa, by revealing schooling's essential role in aspirations of African emancipation. Rejecting colonial exploitation of the African body, proponents of anticolonial development instead claimed the mind as the site of economic productivity for African people. An Anticolonial Development shows how, in the middle of the twentieth century, Africans proposed an original understanding of development that fused antiracism to economic theory, and human dignity to material productivity. Elisa Prosperetti is an Assistant Professor of History at the National Institute of Education/Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She is a historian of modern African and global history, specializing in histories of race, development, education, and decolonization, with a geographic focus on West Africa and the Black Atlantic world. She received her PhD in History from Princeton University in 2020, and currently serves on the Editorial Review Board of the African Studies Review and as a podcast host for the African Studies channel of the New Books Network.

Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ���———–DATE: Tue, Dec 1, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKIn Coming of Age in Macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand), anthropologist and filmmaker Harjant Gill examines how Punjabi men in India, disillusioned by promises of power and control, contend with patriarchy: by submitting to it, attempting to transgress it, migrating to escape it, or coming undone by it. Gill takes readers deep inside men's worlds to show how boys come of age and how masculinity is produced through pervasive violence, while also being underwritten by intimacy, fraternal love, and homosocial bonds. Based on four years of fieldwork conducted over a decade and hundreds of interviews, Gill explores how boys learn to become men against the backdrop of patriarchal constraints, political violence, shifting agrarian economies, and steady outward migration. He shows the extent to which violence is a function and a reflection of powerlessness. By tracing the making of masculinity in a society where sexuality is sanctioned almost exclusively through heteronormative frameworks of marriage and family, this book documents how patriarchy forecloses agency and autonomy. Ultimately, Coming of Age in Macholand offers a powerful indictment of patriarchy as a system that not only oppresses women and queer people, but also constricts men's intimate, sexual, and emotional lives. ABOUT THE AUTHORHarjant Gill (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html) is a professor of anthropology and an award-winning documentary filmmaker whose work bridges ethnography, visual storytelling, and public scholarship. His research and creative practice explore masculinity, migration, media, religion, and popular culture in South Asia and its diasporas, with a particular focus on Punjab and Sikh communities. Through film and writing, he examines how intimate lives are shaped by patriarchy, nationalism, violence, and transnational mobility. Gill is the director of the internationally recognized documentary films Roots of Love, Mardistan/Macholand, and Sent Away Boys. His work has been broadcast on the BBC, PBS, and Doordarshan and screened widely at universities, film festivals, and public forums around the world. His scholarship appears in leading journals including American Anthropologist, Ethnography, and Visual Anthropology Review. His forthcoming book, Coming of Age in Macholand (University of Chicago Press), offers a deeply personal ethnographic exploration of patriarchy, masculinity, violence, and migration in Indian Punjab. Gill has received fellowships and awards from the American Institute of Indian Studies, Fulbright-Nehru, Point Foundation, Wenner-Gren, Whiting, and Woodrow Wilson foundations. events.title: Claudine Chalmers | French Eyes on the Gold Rush – Artists and Chroniclers witness early California's astonishing transformation
events.description: Long before the frenzy of the 1849 Gold Rush, French explorers such as the Comte de La Pérouse visited and charted the coast of California. They were followed by French diplomats in Monterey, notably Jacques-Antoine Moerenhout, whose official reports documented the early discovery of gold and the extraordinary changes it set in motion. Beginning in 1849, the Gold Rush brought a new wave of French emigrants to California, drawn by the dream of El Dorado. These fortune seekers—who came to be known as "Argonauts," after the adventurers of Greek mythology—did more than search for gold. A remarkable number of them observed, wrote, sketched, and recorded what they saw, aware that they were witnessing an extraordinary moment in history. Through travel accounts, letters, journals, and drawings, these French-speaking witnesses captured the unruly excitement of San Francisco, the hardships and disappointments of life in the mining camps, and the cultural encounters—and collisions—of a new cosmopolitan society taking shape almost overnight. Their distinctive perspective, shaped by European traditions, a critical eye, and a certain Romantic sensibility, complements the accounts of French diplomats and earlier explorers. Together, these voices offer a vivid and surprisingly rich record of what California felt and looked like as it transformed almost overnight into one of the most dynamic places in the West. Born in Cannes, Claudine Chalmers, Ph.D., is a historian, author, and independent researcher. Her passion for art, history, and the American West led her to dedicate several decades to tracing the lives of the French men and women who left for California in the 19th century. Her work include Chronicling the West for Harper's, and Splendide Californie!Drawing on archives in France and the United States, she seeks to breathe new life into figures whom history has gradually forgotten—artists, explorers, pioneers, and adventurers whose stories reveal a French presence in the American West far richer than is commonly imagined. events.title: Dissertation Talk: Enforcing Least Privilege in the Cloud
events.description: Cloud developers increasingly hand their infrastructure and data to third-party services, such as orchestrators that launch and manage jobs, chains of services that process data on their behalf, and data lakes that store it. To do their work, these services typically receive broad access to everything a developer owns. Attackers have exploited that over-privilege in incidents ranging from the ShadowRay cluster takeovers to the Capital One breach, hijacking compute, stealing credentials, and exfiltrating data at massive scale. The principle of least privilege offers a clear fix, but today's cloud permission models cannot express it for these settings. My dissertation shows how combining proxy-based system design with cryptographic protocols makes least privilege practical without changing cloud providers or the services themselves. In this talk, I will focus on Skydentity, which enforces least privilege on third-party workload orchestrators by separating a service's ability to manage resources from its ability to access them. I will show that Skydentity reduces exposure to real-world attacks, including ShadowRay, SCARLETEEL, and cryptomining campaigns on EC2, at modest cost. I will also briefly discuss how these ideas extend to chains of services.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Vivian Irish | Thorny questions: citrus development and disease
events.description: Thorns are plant defensive structures that arise from axillary shoot apical meristems that proliferate for a time and then terminally differentiate into a sharp hard tip. Like other meristems, thorn meristems contain stem cells but, in the case of thorns, these stem cells undergo a programmed cessation of proliferative activity. Using citrus as a model system to examine this unusual form of stem cell regulation, we have characterized a transcriptional gene network necessary for thorn development. Not only has this work illuminated some of the molecular mechanisms controlling plant stem cell activity, but the methods we have developed have allowed us to tackle some of the challenges facing citrus agriculture today.
