events.title: Restless Ground: Lilah Nethanel on Writing Israel
events.description: Helen Diller Institute Literary Series, Session II*Co-sponsored by the Center for Jewish Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature, UC Berkeley What can a sleepless man reveal about the history of a country, and what forgotten paths might Hebrew literature have taken? Israeli novelist and literary scholar Lilah Nethanel approaches some of Hebrew literature's most familiar and contested subjects—home, land, desire, language, and belonging—from startlingly unexpected angles. In The Tired Ones, one man's longing for sleep opens onto Israel's fraught histories of land and ownership, while Works and Days compresses fifteen years of marriage, desire, and betrayal into two hours of an ordinary summer evening. Her newly published study, The Last European-Hebrew Writer, returns to David Frishman to recover two possibilities for modern Hebrew culture that once coexisted: a European-Hebrew literature centered in Warsaw and a Hebrew-Arabic literature emerging in Ottoman Jerusalem. In conversation with Yael Segalovitz, Nethanel will explore how intimate lives and forgotten literary alternatives can unsettle the familiar stories Israel tells about itself.Lilah Nethanel, Literary scholar and Israeli novelist; Senior Lecturer, Department of Literature, Bar-Ilan UniversityYael Segalovitz, Joan Bieder Visiting Professor of Jewish and Hebrew Literature, Helen Diller Institute, UC Berkeley; Comparative Literature Department, UC Berkeley; Assistant Professor, Ben-Gurion University of the NegevRegister: https://HDILitSeries2.rsvpify.com (https://hdilitseries2.rsvpify.com)

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

events.title: Dave Pagliarini: Mining mitochondria—proteins, pathways, and pathogenesis
events.description: Despite their iconic status in cell biology, mitochondria remain surprisingly mysterious. These organelles harbor hundreds of uncharacterized "orphan" proteins and are linked to a vast array of physiological processes, often through unclear means. Many well-known mitochondrial activities rely on enzymes, chaperones, and transporters yet to be identified. Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies hundreds of rare diseases, yet nearly half lack molecular diagnoses and there remains but two FDA-approved drugs to treat them. My talk will cover how we aim to clarify this remarkable opacity by blending new systematic methods with rigorous mechanistic biochemistry and chemical biology to discover new protein activities, link them to new biology and unresolved diseases, and manipulate them through customized small molecule interventions.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1

events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: From dispersal to divergence: exploring the many faces of allopatric speciation
events.description: Freshwater fishes of eastern North America, particularly darters, are an exceptional system for studying the mechanisms and outcomes of allopatric speciation, given their high regional diversity and strong habitat specificity. Allopatric speciation is predicted to leave sister species in separate but adjacent river systems; yet a time-calibrated phylogeny of nearly all 290 darter species, combined with genomic species delimitation, reveals far more varied outcomes. Some sister lineages achieve secondary sympatry rapidly, while others persist in deep allopatry, never overlapping even with distant relatives, raising questions about why lineages differ in their transition rates from isolation to co-occurrence. At finer scales, case studies of recently delimited species complexes identify multiple drivers of allopatric speciation, including dispersal into newly available habitat and ecological divergence along resource axes like diet and substrate, extending well beyond classic vicariance models. This work establishes a research program linking speciation mechanisms to their long-term geographic and ecological consequences, contrasted with dynamics of island and lake adaptive radiations.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Pilar Cossio, Senior Research Scientist, Flatiron Institute
events.description: Title: Inferring Biomolecular Ensembles from Cryo-EM Images with Physical and Generative Priors. Abstract: Biomolecules are dynamic, and understanding their function requires characterizing not just individual structures but entire conformational ensembles and their populations. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) captures noisy snapshots of individual molecules, providing direct experimental access to these ensembles, yet extracting them remains challenging. In this talk, I will present a unified framework for ensemble inference in which prior knowledge, either from molecular dynamics (MD) force fields or pretrained diffusion models, is integrated by cryo-EM data. With MD, we bias simulations using a likelihood computed directly from particle images, jointly inferring structures and population weights without a pre-sampled ensemble. With diffusion models, we guide generation toward experimental data, including by optimizing the model's conditioning to shift the prior itself. Applied to proteins and RNAs, these approaches recover multiple conformational states and their populations from synthetic and experimental data, opening the way to ensemble-level quantitative structural biology of flexible biomolecules.Bio:Pilar Cossio has worked at the Flatiron Institute, Center for Computational Mathematics, since 2021 as the Research Scientist and Project Leader for Biomolecular and Biophysical Inference (BBI). Previously, Cossio was Max Planck Tandem Group Leader associated with the University of Antioquia (Colombia) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics (Germany). She also has held postdoctoral positions at the National Institute of Health (NIH, USA) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics. Cossio focuses on the development of mathematical and computational methods to characterize proteins' structures and dynamics from cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule spectroscopy and biomolecular simulations. Cossio holds a Ph.D. in Physics and Chemistry of Biological Systems from the International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA) in Italy and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Antioquia.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, December 3, 2026 (NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Myungji Yang (University of Hawai'i, Mānoa) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

Established in 1991 by June Jordan and rooted in her work in the departments of African American Studies and Gender and Women's Studies at UC Berkeley, Poetry for the People (P4P) taught students to speak their truth through poetry. Drawing students from a range of backgrounds and areas of study, June Jordan's P4P engaged in rigorous study of a diversity of poetic traditions, organized public poetry readings and open mics, published anthologies of student work, and brought P4P to community partners around the Bay Area. Today, with the clarity and political commitment of June's vision more necessary than ever, "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" asks, how do we teach P4P now? "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" is a convening intended for UC Berkeley faculty, students, and staff; P4P program alumni; P4P instructors; community partners; and anyone committed to the future of P4P at UC Berkeley and beyond. The day-long program will include workshops about the history and legacy of P4P, how P4P is being taught today, and new models of P4P for the modern university. Together, we will envision how to bring P4P to the next generation of student poets. All members of the public are invited to an evening conversation at 6:00 pm to celebrate the forthcoming publication of June Jordan's Poetry for the People (Expanded Edition): A Revolutionary Blueprint from Haymarket Books. events.title: BLC Talk | Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change | Deb Reisinger
events.description: Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change Deb Reisinger Dean of Undergraduate Education; Trinity College, Duke University In "Creating the Conditions", Reisinger examines how content-based language programs can expand the role and reach of language study within a contemporary liberal arts education. Drawing on established approaches in Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum (CLAC), community-based language learning (CBLL), and Languages for Specific Purposes (LSP), she considers how language courses and programs can connect linguistic development with disciplinary knowledge, critical inquiry, experiential learning, and transferable skills. Examples from undergraduate curricula illustrate the distinct possibilities of these models. CLAC integrates languages and intercultural perspectives across disciplines; CBLL creates reciprocal relationships between classroom learning and community engagement, and LSP connects language learning to professional fields and practices. Together, these approaches make visible the intellectual and practical value of language study across academic, professional, and civic contexts. This presentation also considers what allows such programs to take root and thrive. Curricular innovation depends on more than compelling individual courses. It requires faculty leadership, meaningful institutional partnerships, coherent pathways for students, and structures that support collaboration across departments, programs, and schools. It also requires clear narratives that help students, faculty colleagues, and university leaders understand how language learning advances broader institutional commitments. By bringing curricular models into conversation with questions of advocacy, leadership, and institutional design, Reisinger invites participants to consider the conditions that support language study at their own institution. Ultimately, she asks how content-based programs can help build connections, create new points of entry, and position linguistic and intercultural learning as essential dimensions of a liberal arts education. Bio: Deb Reisinger is Dean of Undergraduate Education at Duke University. A professor of French Studies and affiliate faculty in Global Health and Markets & Management, Deb directs Duke's Language Outreach Initiatives(link is external), including Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum and the Shared Online Consortium for LCTLs. Deb's work explores the connections between language learning and the disciplines. She is lead author of Affaires globales: S'engager dans le monde professionnel en francais, niveau avancé and co-author of Community-based Language Learning, a methodology of critical service-learning in world languages. In 2022, she was named Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Palmes Académiques by the French Republic.

The concept of self-similarity and its use as an agent of form and sound production will be presented, along with the Recursive Granular Synthesis software. Globally recognized since winning the 2002 First Prize and Audience Prize of the Geneva International Music Competition. She is a champion of existing repertoire and a prominent voice in the collaborative creation of new works. Huang has premiered over two hundred works in her three decades as a performer and producer. The Globe and Mail critic Robert Everett-Green describes Huang's playing as "engrossing to hear and to watch" and her choice of repertoire as capable of "renovating our habits of listening." Her past highlights include performances with the St. Lawrence String Quartet, L'Orchestre de la Suisse Romande, Taipei Symphony Orchestra and San Diego Symphony Orchestra. She has appeared in international festivals and venues including the Victoria Hall in Geneva, Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra's Green Umbrella Series, LACMA Concert Series, Holland Festival, Agora Festival in Paris, Banff Arts Festival, 7éme Biennale d'Art Contemporaine de Lyon, Vancouver New Music Festival, CBC Radio, La Jolla Summerfest, Scotia Festival, Montreal New Music Festival, Cervantino Festival in Mexico, and the National Concert Hall and Theater in Taipei. Born in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, Aiyun holds a DMA degree from UC San Diego. Between 2006 and 2017, she led the percussion program at McGill University and held the position of William Dawson Scholar. She currently holds the position of Professor of Music at the Faculty of Music, University of Toronto where she heads the percussion area and directs the University of Toronto Percussion Ensemble as well as the Technology and Performance Integration Research (TaPIR) Lab. She was named Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2024.CONCERT: 8pm Wu Hall

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Stefan Minasian, Staff Chemist, LBNLThe Counterintuitive Relationship between Orbital Energy, Orbital Overlap,and Covalency in f-Element Molecules Why are some metal–ligand bonds more covalent than others? Typically, chemists invoke two factors: how well the metal and ligand orbitals overlap in space, and how closely their energies match. Yet these contributions have been surprisingly difficult to separate, by either experiment or theory. This lecture will describe how ligand K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), combined with high-level spectral simulations, can measure both. Comparisons of isostructural fluoride and chloride complexes of transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf), lanthanides (Ce), and actinides (U, Np, Pu) show that the two factors often work against each other. Greater orbital overlap does not necessarily produce a more covalent bond, and the balance between overlap and energy matching depends on the metal and on the symmetry of the interaction. These results also provide experimental benchmarks against which computational descriptions of bonding can be tested. The second part of the lecture will extend this approach to organometallic lanthanide complexes, probed using carbon K-edge XAS. In molecules such as cerocene, Ce(C8H8)2, and Cp′3Eu, the ground state cannot be described by a single electronic configuration. In these systems, the 4f orbital mixing observed by X-ray spectroscopy also appears as partial charge transfer from the ligands to the metal. Relating these two descriptions shows how 4f electrons can participate in bonding while remaining largely localized, and how 4f covalency can shape physical properties such as magnetic susceptibility. This leads to broader questions about how covalency and multiconfigurational ground states are connected across the f-block.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.description: Berkeley World Language Project - 2026-2027 LEARN | CONNECT | INSPIREJoin us for a year of learning in community! Practical Strategies & Real Classroom Impact Engaging Workshops: Practical ideas you can use right away Supportive Community: Collaborate with educators who inspire Student Success: Build world language skills that last Office Hours: Collaborate between workshop sessions! Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! This strand is for all language teachers who want to take their instruction to the next level, whether beginning or experienced. You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. You will build a complete Lesson over time while learning and practicing strategies to implement immediately. Prerequisite: an open mind, curiosity, and a desire to grow. Strand B: Creating Authentic Themed Units for Today's Learners Develop meaningful, real-life themed Units for modern language learners. Build a thematic unit grounded in authentic materials that reflect real language and culture. You will learn how to design a unit that aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), AP themes and CA World Languages Standards while integrating global competence, social justice, and social-emotional learning. Using backward design, you'll craft essential questions, Can-Do statements, and assessments that support meaningful communication across all modes—creating immersive, relevant learning experiences that connect students to the real world and help them grow as confident, culturally aware language users. events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection

events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: David Jekel, University of OttawaOpen AI recently generated the first examples with $-\infty \chi \chi ^*$. I will contextualize and give a detailed proof of similar example, and more explicitly show the separation between free Fisher information and the large-n limit of classical Fisher information. The upper bound on free Fisher information comes from a cumulant-bound for Fisher information that draws on higher-order conjugate variable/Stein kernel techniques from classical and free settings. The lower bound on classical Fisher information comes from volume bounds on the space of matrices admitting a noticeable block structure with respect to some projections reminiscent of the volume arguments in Voiculescu's paper on absence of Cartan algebras and many subsequent works. I will derive the upper bound using a sup-formula and showing the relationship with my study of model theory and Wasserstein distance in the context of random matrices.

events.title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust Optimization (Ruiwei Jiang, University of Michigan)
events.description: Talk title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust OptimizationAbstract: Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) finds a wide range of applications including, for example, electric power systems, supply chains, and transportation. Unfortunately, ARO models are NP-hard in general, and practical applications of ARO often resort to decision rules for tractability but sacrifice accuracy. In this talk, we propose a novel algorithmic framework for solving ARO with performance guarantees in both tractability and accuracy. The framework introduces soft separation, a probabilistic mechanism for identifying worst-case uncertainty realizations. As opposed to solving an exact separation problem iteratively, which is intractable in general, soft separation carries adversarial information forward, co-evolves with the optimization iterates, and recovers exact separation at terminal iterates with high probability. When the first-stage (here-and-now) decisions are continuous, we design a first-order method that uses soft separation to produce adaptive gradient estimates. Accordingly, we prove polynomial convergence to a surrogate that approximates the true optimum to any prescribed accuracy. When the first-stage decisions are mixed-integer, we embed soft separation in a branch-and-cut framework to generate valid cuts for the robust objective and obtain a high-probability final optimality certificate. Numerical experiments show strong performance against state-of-the-art methods, especially under scenario-based uncertainty.Bio: Ruiwei Jiang is an Associate Professor of Industrial and Operations Engineering at the University of Michigan. His research and teaching interests lie in stochastic and integer optimization, with applications in power systems and healthcare operations. Recognitions of his work include an NSF CAREER Award, two INFORMS Junior Faculty Interest Group paper awards (1st place and honorable mention), an INFORMS Computing Society prize (honorable mention), and an IISE Operations Research Division Teaching Award.

events.title: An attempt towards the Autistic Image feat. Perwana Nazif
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media lecture with Perwana Nazif Visiting Faculty, California Institute of the Arts, and Artistic Director, Los Angeles Review of Books - Monday, December 7, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfCVu9yc8DDE25JwxXsk8JBXMFwmawFEoFCQw71XrKximqkdQ/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MGxuYnJuZWpqNGd2ZGo1MGppNXRzMmVyM2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - It's here that the two attempts—allowing autistic children to exist and camering— have a trait in common: to evade intention, which requires a strange rigour that can't be intentional. "Miscreating" (1979) Just as tracing is not drawing, camering is not filming. "Miscreating" (1979) An attempt lays itself bare—and you can certainly hear all the connotations of that word. It does not present itself as a request. Le Croire et le Craindre (1978) In 1968, French educator and writer Fernand Deligny began the "Cévennes network," also known as the attempt. The Cévennes attempt was an informal, non-clinical collective of autistic children and (non-autistic) "close presences," who together enabled autistic existence. The Cévennes experiment attempted to work within a non-verbal and non-institutional framework, to respond to what Deligny marked as the autistic children's needs to experience life in the absence of language and neurotypical relation. The network both followed and radically departed from Deligny's prior para-clinical and social work with neurodivergent, psychotic, "troubled" or "delinquent," children, many of whom would have otherwise been incarcerated or permanently institutionalized. Here, in the attempt, they experimented with collective aesthetic and/or media practices outside of language: purposeless objects and common actions, non-representational cartography, tracing (unlike drawing), and camering (unlike filming). So, what or how is the collective attempt—when its conditions of emergence are indeterminacy, precarity, non-relation, and detours from if not a total outside to language and the subject? To hazard a presentation of the (Cévennes) attempt is to present it through what Deligny calls the autistic image—that which means nothing, says nothing, or does anything. This talk, then, will explore the apparatus of the autistic image, its point of seeing, and what it enables to come into the world. About Perwana Nazif Perwana Nazif teaches at the California Institute of the Arts and serves as the artistic director of the Los Angeles Review of Books. She recently edited Everybody Wants to Be a Fascist: Institutional Psychotherapy as a Resistance Movement (semiotext(e), 2025) and is a contributing editor at Parapraxis Magazine. She recently curated François Pain, Psychiatry is what Psychiatrists do at JOAN, Los Angeles and is currently working on an exhibition at CAC Brétigny in France. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.

We'll examine whether feeding content into AI tools qualifies as fair use under copyright law, and how overarching contracts such as library e-resource agreements or a website's terms of use may restrict, shape, or even override your fair use rights. We'll explore whether those clickthrough or browsewrap terms of use are enforceable, and why you may need to pay closer attention to them than you think.The second part of the session will cover how using AI in your writing can affect your copyright and authorship, what current publisher and journal policies require you to disclose, and how AI training on scholarly work intersects with your rights as an author.You'll leave with a working understanding of where the law currently stands, what remains unsettled, and how to make informed choices about using these tools in your own work.If you require an accommodation to fully participate in this event, please contact schol-comm@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7 days before the event.

events.title: Multimodal Transportation Impact Analysis: California Best Practices
events.description: Description The multi-modal Transportation Impact Study (TIS) is one of the most effective tools for assessing the impacts of new land development (or redevelopment) and establishing a nexus with project mitigations, including impact fees. Recent legislation as well as public sentiment have made it imperative that transportation professionals better understand how to prepare and review these studies. Although current California environmental regulations (CEQA) require specific methods for use in analyzing transportation impacts, focusing on vehicle-miles traveled, this class will consider a broader variety of transportation impacts. A good TIS can consider a much wider range of impacts than CEQA and therefore can better reflect local community values. The class will consider such topics as site access and off-site improvements to satisfactorily accommodate project traffic, including traffic signals. It also considers how impact fees can be applied consistent with California law to recover costs associated with the new development. It also considers non-VMT impacts, such as multi-modal impacts, delay to buses, providing the right amount of parking, internal circulation, and improving the pedestrian/ bicycle environment. This 8-hour course (in 4 two-hour modules) provides the basics and practical applications of analysis procedures for determining impacts using various performance metrics on all modes (pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and auto). It emphasizes the best practices that are being employed in California and other areas. This course focuses on urban/suburban streets (non-freeways), internal circulation planning, and providing just the right amount of parking. Applications of analyses include improving transportation impact studies, environmental impact reports (EIRs) and project mitigation, new development design standards, and the CEQA review process. Attendees will also become familiar with:Labor-saving shortcuts for data collection (because some multimodal level of service methodologies can be very "data hungry") How 'induced travel demand' is defined, and when it does (or does not) create a significant environmental impact under the law Cross-modal impacts (when capacity or physical characteristics of one mode are changed and thereby affect another mode using the street) How to assess "fair share" impact fees to pay for project mitigations How parking can be used as an effective demand-management measure Available resources (web and paper) that provide further guidance This class has been updated to reflect many changes in California law between 2020 and 2024. Updates to important references-such as the 2023 Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, and ITE Recommended Practice on TIA-will also be considered. This course is a combination of instructor presentations with interactive engagements to apply the techniques in the real-world, with case studies and applications of the material. The material complements TE-43 (Multimodal Transportation Operations: Evaluation Methods & Performance Measures) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE430000), and TE-60 (VMT Metrics Policy Applications and Technical Analysis for SB 743 Compliance) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE600000), although each can be taken as a stand-alone class. Topics IncludeLevel-of-Service (LOS) concept– what it means and why do it, pros and cons of different methods cross-modal impacts how to calculate VMT from a proposed project gathering field information & data collection shortcuts software available to assist in analysis California statutory requirements (especially CEQA and SB 743) relationship to the latest Caltrans' guidance applications to Context Sensitive Design assessing safety impacts of projects relationship to Sustainable Transportation Indicators incorporation as part of project mitigation typical schedule and budgetary requirements increasing transit as a share of regional VMT applying analytical and simulation tools to multi-modal impact analysis What You Will Learn Students will learn how to prepare– and review– a comprehensive multi-modal transportation impact study. This includes studies prepared both to support CEQA documentation as well as stand-alone studies. Topics include basic level-of-service (LOS) concepts for all modes, and how to apply them to conduct performance and level-of-service analysis for various types of urban streets with various levels of accommodation for different modes; determine the impacts of system improvements using vehicle miles traveled (VMT); and analyze operational impacts of possible changes in the allocation of street cross-section to various modes. Who Should Attend Planners, engineers, technicians, and others at all levels of experience, who prepare or review transportation impacts from land developments will benefit from this class. A minimal level of mathematics is required (basic algebra). Requirements Participants will need a basic calculator for several in-class problem sets. A complete PDF set of Course Notes will be provided by the instructors.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Tuning In Together: Using Music to Navigate Caregiving
events.description: This workshop explores the healing potential of music for both caregivers and their loved ones. Drawing from neuroscience, psychology, and lived clinical experience, psychologist and musician Barbara Minton will discuss how music affects the brain, supports emotional regulation, reduces stress, enhances connection, and can create moments of presence and meaning even in the midst of caregiving demands. She will be joined by her colleague, Peppino D'Agostino, a virtuosic guitarist, who will perform live music from their collaborative work in which they create compositions designed to support nervous system regulation and emotional well-being. Participants will leave with practical insights and simple music-based tools to support resilience, connection, and well-being in everyday life. Presenter: Dr. Barbara Minton, Phd Dr. Minton earned her BA in Psychology, summa cum laude, from the University of Denver, followed by PhDs in Psychology with an emphasis in developmental and child clinical practice. Demonstrating her deep commitment to brain science, she is Board Certified in Neurofeedback and holds the distinction of Diplomate in Quantitative Electroencephalogram (QEEG). Her diverse career includes private clinical practice in Boise, Idaho, serving as Mental Health Education Coordinator for the State of Alaska's Department of Health and Social Services, and as Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Alaska Southeast. These roles have allowed her to cultivate expertise not just in psychological assessment and neurofeedback, but also in the deeply human areas of giftedness and hypnotherapy. Peppino D'Agostino A native of Italy, D'Agostino has made his considerable international mark as a musical artist on the guitar since he arrived in America 40 years ago. In 2017 Guitar Player listed him as one of the 50 transcendent guitar superheroes of all times. The CD "Every Step of The Way" was awarded by Acoustic Guitar's People's Choice Awards with a Bronze medal for Best Acoustic Album of All Time. His signature Seagull acoustic guitar has been voted among the ten best signature guitars by Guitar Player magazine. Peppino gives guitar workshops, master classes and seminars worldwide. To date Peppino has recorded 19 CD's, performed in over thirty five countries at international festivals and concert halls. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection (copy)
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. As a boy chorister, Sternath toured the world with the esteemed Vienna Boys Choir; since then, he has gone on to perform with leading European orchestras, making his debut with the Vienna Philharmonic during the 2025–26 season. His Cal Performances debut recital program features the second suite from Liszt's Années de pèlerinage, which includes Liszt's famous Petrarch Sonnets and his Dante Sonata; a beguiling selection of Schubert songs arranged by Liszt; and Schubert's epic, restless Wanderer Fantasy.

events.title: Lecture | The Invention of the Fertile Crescent: Historical Lessons from American Orientalism
events.description: Abstract: During five decades that spanned the turn of the twentieth century (about 1870 to 1920), a tradition of oriental scholarship took firm root in the United States. American orientalists conducted rigorous research into the history and languages of the ancient Near East. These scholars were early defenders of a modern liberal education in the United States. They invented the idea of "Western civilization" and argued that the origins of the West lay in the ancient Orient. They coined the concept of the "fertile crescent" to suggest that the lands of the Near East gently nurtured humanity in its early days, "cradling" civilization in the nascent stage. This lecture will examine American orientalism's quest to find historical, rather than biblical, origin stories for humanity. In the orientalist scheme, the civilizations of the East were the first to develop monotheistic religion and thus to foster humankind's capacity for empathy. Empathy, in turn, played an essential role in the functioning of democratic society in the modern West.Bio: Serena Shah is a PhD candidate in U.S. History at Stanford University. She works on the history of ideas and the production of knowledge in major American cultural institutions, especially universities and museums. Her dissertation examines the uses of American oriental scholarship for liberal education in the fin-de-siècle United States. Serena also broadly studies Americans' ideas about antiquity in the nineteenth century; she is in the process of publishing a research article on Greek and Roman slave-naming practices in the antebellum era. She received her A.B. (summa cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa) from Harvard University in 2021 and her M.A. in History from Stanford in 2023.

events.title: Lunch Poems: Bianca Stone
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Bianca Stone. Bianca Stone is the author of four collections of poetry. Her three most recent, all from Tin House Books, are The Near and Distant World (2026); What Is Otherwise Infinite (2022), winner of the 2022 Vermont Book Award; and The Möbius Strip Club of Grief (2018). Her work has appeared widely in such magazines as The New Yorker, The Atlantic, and Poetry. She is a visiting lecturer in poetry at Dartmouth College and teaches classes on poetry and poetic study at the Ruth Stone House in Goshen, Vermont, where she hosts the Ode & Psyche Podcast. Stone is currently serving as the poet laureate of Vermont (2024-28). The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. For more information or to be added to the Lunch Poems mailing list, please email poems-library@berkeley.edu (mailto:poems-library@berkeley.edu) or follow @PoemsLunch on Instagram (http://instagram.com/poemslunch) and X (https://twitter.com/PoemsLunch).

events.title: TDPS presents "Berkeley Dance Project: What Moves Between Us"
events.description: Choreography by SanSan Kwan (Two Doors) and Lisa Wymore (Cycle) Zellerbach Playhouse Showtimes: Thursday, February 18th at 8pm Friday, February 19th at 8pm Saturday, February 20th at 2pm Saturday, February 20th at 8pm Sunday, February 21st at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) This collaboration offers two dance works that sit inside the friction of seeing and not seeing, doing and not doing. Together they unsettle passivity. They treat perception not as something fixed or solitary, but as something shared and in motion. The audience is invited not only to watch, but to notice and to sense where attention settles, and where it drifts. In this space, seeing, listening, and feeling become forms of participation. Two Doors is inspired by an incident in New York City in 2021 in which doormen closed their doors just afer seeing an attack on an Asian woman outside their lobby. Through a choreographic study of the aftermath of violence, Two Doors explores the viscerality of anti-Asian racism and the sovereignty that we wrest for ourselves in response. Dancers experiment with closings and openings, weight sharing and weight bearing, playing with the kinetics of in/visibility, and Asian American model minoritization. Two Doors depicts a journey toward self-possession via relational vulnerability. Cycle, inspired by Professor Georgina Kleege's book More Than Meets the Eye, is built with language and sound as equal partners with the dance. Audio description does not trail behind the movement - it generates it. The result is a reorientation of how we watch dance, and an insistence that dance can be heard, felt, and imagined beyond the primacy of sight. events.title: 2027 Sheng Yen Conference
events.description: The scholastic traditions associated with Sarvāstivāda and the Abhidharma corpus more broadly were transmitted to China beginning in the fourth and fifth centuries and became a significant focus of translation activity under the direction of Xuanzang in the seventh century. Yet modern scholarship often assumes that Chinese Buddhist scholiasts had little sustained interest in, or use for, Abhidharma. According to this view, Abhidharma was dismissed as "Hīnayāna" and overshadowed by the rise of indigenous Chinese Buddhist traditions such as Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan. There is, however, ample evidence that Abhidharma continued to be studied and valued by Chinese exegetes irrespective of their doctrinal or school affiliation, and that it retained an important place in monastic curricula from the medieval period down to the present day. This conference seeks to reconsider the reception and enduring influence of Abhidharma in Chinese Buddhism.Titles, Abstracts, and Bios (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/66-titles-abstracts-and-biospdf).Friday 2:30-5:30 pmAbhidharma Learning in China Chair: Alexander von Rospatt Eric Greene (Yale University): "Abhidharma Methodology in the First Era of Chinese Buddhist Scholasticism." Hou Xiaoming (Ghent University): "A Curriculum in Diagram: Dunhuang Path Charts and the Teaching of Abhidharma." Patrick Magoffin (Postdoctoral Fellow, UC Berkeley): "Interpreting and Teaching the Lengyan jing: A Conduit for Abhidharmic Learning and Textual Practices in the Song (960–1279)."Saturday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Exegesis I Chair: Jacob Dalton Lu Huang (UC Berkeley): "Views of Pre-Xuanzang Abhidharma Masters as Preserved in the Jushe lun ji." Howard Mu (UC Berkeley): "Shentai's Interpretative Approach: Some General Features of the Jushe lunshu 俱舍論疏." Jackson Cole Macor (UC Berkeley): "Jizang's Critique of Abhidharma in the Sanlun xuanyi." Lin Qian (Qing Dao University): "Analysis of Mind in Zongjinglu: The Adoption of Abhidharma Methods in Chan Buddhism."Sunday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Abhidharma Philosophy Chair: Robert Sharf Ernest Brewster (Austrian Academy of Sciences): "On the Nature and Existence of Cessation: Sinitic Analysis of Indic Intra-Abhidharma Debates." events.title: Talk and Film Screening: Disavowal as Belonging
events.description: This talk expands on Gelare Khoshgozaran's ongoing explorations of exile as a generative space to form a resonant collectivity—one that embodies alienation, embraces the impossibility of return, and makes a home through the continuous negotiation of borders. Three short films by the artist invite viewers to rethink cinema as a space to find our kin and comrades in exile spatially defined through the politics of belonging and disavowal.Gelare Khoshgozaran is an undisciplinary artist and filmmaker whose work engages with legacies of imperial violence manifested in war, militarization, and borders. They use film and video to form narratives that seek to redefine existing constructions of 'home' as a means of conceptualizing other forms of belonging. Born and raised in a city of four seasons, they are an assistant professor of art at UCLA School of Art and Architecture.

events.title: Genentech Lecture
events.description: Huw Davies, Asa Griggs Candler Professor, Harvard UniversitySite-selective and enantioselective C–H functionalization controlled by induced fitting and secondary noncovalent interactions A major challenge in organic synthesis is the selective functionalization of C–H bonds. As most organic compounds contain multiple C–H bonds with similar properties, distinguishing between them requires precise control. For some time, we have been using high symmetry chiral dirhodium catalysts to control C-H functionalization with donor acceptor carbenes. In this presentation we will highlight the design of our most recent high symmetry dirhodium catalysts (C4 symmetric and D4 symmetric) and illustrate the subtle site-selectivity exhibited by these catalysts. We will show how they can adopt many of the characteristics atypically associated with enzymes, leading to unprecedented site-selectivity of nonactivated C–H bonds. The catalysts adopt a bowl-shape on formation and the flexible microenvironment within the bowl causes an induced fitting to occur as the reagent and the substrate approach the catalyst. Recent synthetic application of this methodology to the synthesis of various chiral scaffolds will be described.

The revered 185-year-old orchestra and star conductor have enjoyed a close partnership over many years, a relationship finely honed through numerous tours and recordings. For these performances the focus is Mahler, a particularly important figure in the Philharmonic's history whose Ninth Symphony received its posthumous premiere by the orchestra in 1912. The composer's music is a perfect match for the towering institution, which will be joined by a selection of internationally acclaimed guest artists throughout the Berkeley residency. The first performance features Mahler's poignant final completed symphony, one of the most profound and emotionally complex works in the orchestral repertoire. The second night features both Mahler's Fourth Symphony, with Christiane Karg as soprano soloist, and Prokofiev's Concerto in C major, with superstar pianist Yuja Wang joining at the keyboard. In the final program, Mahler's Resurrection symphony takes the listener on a journey through earthly trials to ultimate transcendence, and features vocalists Christiane Karg and Elīna Garanča, and the San Francisco Symphony Chorus.
