events.location: David Brower Center, 2150 Allston Way, Berkeley, CA 94704
events.description: In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Event Schedule: 5:00 PM - Event Begins 6:30 PM - Cocktail Hour Begins (Hearty Refreshments Provided) 6:45 PM - Book Signing Begins 7:30 PM - Event Ends NOTE: A small number of books will be available for purchase at the event for participation in the book signing. You may also bring copies of the book you purchased separately. The Center for Korean Studies at UC Berkeley is honored to announce the 2026 winner of the UC Berkeley Hong Yung Lee Book Award in Korean Studies: Triangle Republics: Cross-Border Literary Transits between the Cold War Koreas and Japan (https://cup.columbia.edu/book/triangle-republics/9780231219846/) (Columbia University Press, 2025) by Professor I. Jonathan Kief (https://asianstudies.unc.edu/faculty/kief-i-jonathan/) (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill).Triangle Republics is a groundbreaking contribution to literary studies of Korea and beyond, one that turns the production and circulation of texts into the occasion for rethinking the impact of the Cold War on the Korean peninsula and its diaspora. Upending the conventional view of the Korean division as one of separation and antagonism between two diametrically opposed and mutually exclusive cultural spheres, the book reveals how North and South Korean literature surreptitiously formed and transformed each other through the Korean diaspora in Japan. Following the circuit of Korean texts via Japan from 1945 until the 1980s, Kief uncovers the creative ways that writers, critics, and intellectuals crossed the boundaries of nation, language, ideology, and genre to challenge Cold War entrenchments. This required tracking not only Korean language texts, but also Japanese language ones, often published in obscure journals, painstakingly gathered from multiple archives through rigorous research employing cross-disciplinary tools and methods. The result is a work that changes not only what we know about Cold War Korean literature, but also how we might write cultural and intellectual history when the nation-state is no longer assumed to be its natural container. Established in 2022 to honor Berkeley Political Science Professor and longtime CKS Chair Hong Yung Lee (1939-2017), each year this award and its $10,000 prize recognizes a groundbreaking, English-language academic monograph that advances Korean Studies by combining scholarly merit, research prowess, and methodological innovation. The award recognizes Professor Lee's enduring influence on Korean Studies, but also commitment to situating the field in a broad intellectual landscape. Learn more about the Hong Yung Lee Book Award here: https://ieas.berkeley.edu/cks/hylbookaward (https://ieas.berkeley.edu/cks/hylbookaward) Triangle Republics is available for purchase in paperback, hard copy, and as an e-book. You can order copies of the book in all formats here:https://cup.columbia.edu/book/triangle-republics/9780231219846/ (https://cup.columbia.edu/book/triangle-republics/9780231219846/) Awardee Bio: I. Jonathan Kief is Associate Professor of Korean Studies at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he also serves as Associate Chair and Director of Graduate Studies in the Department of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies. He is a scholar of modern Korean literature and culture whose research explores the movement of words, sounds, and ideas across the spatial, ideological, and media boundaries of the Cold War era. His first book, Triangle Republics: Cross-Border Literary Transits between the Cold War Koreas and Japan (Columbia UP, 2025), follows the multi-directional itineraries of literary exchange linking Cold War-era North Korea, South Korea, and Japan. His second book, tentatively titled "Interference/Interface: Broadcast Sound in the Divided Koreas," looks at how wired and wireless broadcasts crossed the Cold War Koreas, reshuffled media and genre boundaries, and transformed conceptions of labor, leisure, gender, and power.

events.title: Shiben Banerji | Object, Site, Antecedent, Exemplar: India in the Occult Imagination of the Globe
events.description: A talk by Shiben Banerji, (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) Associate Professor of Architecture and Urbanism, History of Art Department, at UC Berkeley, exploring how occult and modernist visions of global unity drew on colonial India to shape early twentieth-century debates on architecture, urban planning, and a shared global ethos.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley will serve as discussant.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ——–DATE: Thu, Mar 4, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————- ABSTRACT The wars, rebellions, revolutions, and slumps of the early twentieth century seemed destined to rip asunder the ties that bound colonizers and colonized subjects to one another. The upheaval represented an opportunity, and not just for nationalists who imagined new homelands or for socialists who dreamed of international brotherhood. For modernists in the orbit of various occultisms, the crisis of empire also represented an opportunity to reveal humanity's fundamental unity and common fate. In this talk, Shiben Banerji critiques representations of India in occult imaginings of a global future for metropolitan and colonized societies. Focusing on prints, drawings, buildings, and films, as well as on texts in Dutch, French, Italian, Spanish, German, English, Hindi, Gujarati, and Bengali, created between 1905 and 1945 across the Americas, Europe, South Asia, and Australia, the talk reconstructs the centrality of late colonial India and early post-independence India in early twentieth-century debates on the virtue of forming a global ethos in planned urban space. SPEAKER BIOShiben Banerji (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) is Associate Professor in the Dept of History of Art. He interested in the rhetorical and performative dimensions of architecture. His classroom teaching and historical scholarship are animated by three questions. First, how did architects in early modern Europe describe their interest in the nature of political oratory at the very moment that they began studying architectural forms that were not derived from Roman antiquity? Second, how did architects across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia mediate new conceptions of public association in the context of nineteenth-century colonialisms, and how did concomitant experiments in old and new media present architectural and urban space as objects of artistic depiction and literary invention? Third, how did twentieth-century theorists of alternatives to liberal modernity in the ex-colonial world conceptualize the work of architectural media in altering perception and consciousness? Shiben is the author of Lineages of the Global City(link is external) (University of Texas Press, 2025), which was supported by a Mellon fellowship in the urban humanities and a publication grant from the Graham Foundation. Explicating the conjunction of planning and occultism in the early twentieth century, the book examines the designation of planned urban space as a site for forming a global ethos—meaning both an outlook on oneself as inescapably linked to every creature and thing, as well as the obligation to choose and act with a regard for one's inexorable impact on others. A similar attention to forms of rhetorical action that sustain notions of belonging informs Shiben's coedited volume In the Shadows of Democracy(link is external) (Intermezzo, 2025). Shiben is currently writing Time on the Road to Civil Rights, which foregrounds the salience of planning in civil rights discourse to advance a genealogical critique of the synchronic emergence of rhetorical theory and planning theory in the mid-twentieth century. He has also begun editing an anthology of uses and meanings of "spirit" in twentieth-century aesthetic, economic, and political thought. A dedicated teacher, Shiben was named Faculty of the Year by his students at the School of Art of Institute of Chicago when he was an Assistant Professor. To encourage new lines of graduate research, Shiben regularly contributes to Oxford Bibliographies in Architecture, Planning, and Preservation. ______ The South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) at the University of California, Berkeley promotes research-based conversations and collaborations around the arts of South Asia + its diasporas from the ancient period to the now. To read more about the Initiative and help support its various fundraising goals, please click HERE (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) ______ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.description: by Sarah Ruhl Directed by Patrick Russell Durham Studio Theater Showtimes: Thursday, March 11th at 8pm Friday, March 12th at 8pm Saturday, March 13th at 2pm Saturday, March 13th at 8pm Sunday, March 14th at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) What if sadness were an exquisite force of beauty? For Tilly, a melancholic bank teller, her heaviness becomes something luminous—strangely alluring, powerfully magnetic—drawing others toward her with a disarming pull and, in the process, revealing their truest selves. The poetic farce of Melancholy Play invites us into a whimsical world where emotional truth is contagious, where identities slip free from the mundanity of everyday life and reform in response to longing, perception, and desire. Moving between sincerity and absurdity, Tilly's journey creates a space where vulnerability and humor coexist, and where transformation becomes both surprising and inevitable, unfolding in a world that is at once heightened and immediate. This surreal, magical story speaks to the simple truths of the human condition: the need for connection, and the profound value of feeling deeply. events.title: A Book of the Civic Silk Road: Translating Ming China for the Ottoman World
events.description: A Book of the Civic Silk Road: Translating Ming China for the Ottoman World The Book of China is the most detailed description of China's government and society written by any foreigner before the age of European maritime empires. 'Ali Akbar Khatayi, a Persian-speaking merchant from Central Eurasia, spent six years in China around 1503 before traveling west to Ottoman Istanbul where he completed his book in 1516. Khatayi description of the Ming state advances a theory of bureaucracy that anticipates that of Max Weber. His vivid descriptions of Ming society range in content from the lunar New Year to funerary customs to street toughs and legends of flying monks. Drawing on our new annotated English translation, we explore how knowledge of Ming China was transmitted across the Persianate and Ottoman intellectual worlds, while also examining his account alongside contemporary Chinese sources.Kaveh L. Hemmat is Associate Professor of History at Benedictine University. His research focuses on interaction between the Islamic world and East Asia with a focus on representations of East Asia in Islamicate political writing. He is also translator of the Kushnameh: The Persian Epic of Kush the Tusked, and co-editor and translator of the Book of China.Hyunhee Park is Professor of History at the City University of New York, John Jay College of Criminal Justice and the CUNY Graduate Center. She specializes in cross-cultural exchanges in premodern Eurasia, particularly between the Islamic world and East Asia, author of Mapping the Chinese and Islamic Worlds and Soju: A Global History, and co-editor of the Book of China.

events.title: The Later Spread Spreading Further: Study of A Tangut Tantric Anthology
events.description: The Later Spread Spreading Further: Study of A Tangut Tantric Anthology The past two decades have seen a steady growth in scholarship on the influences of Tibetan Buddhism in the Tangut State, also known as Xixia (Chin. 西夏) or Minyak (Tib. མི་ཉག་/མེ་ཉག་). During the period of its sovereignty between the 11th and the 13th century, this inner Asian state actively promoted various Tibetan Buddhist traditions, as attested by the abundant Tibetan Buddhist materials in multiple languages unearthed from important archaeological sites. While they enjoyed popularity and authority in the Tangut State, these traditions were themselves the products of a highly eclectic era in Tibet, the so-called "Later Spread of Buddhism" (Tib. bstan pa phyi dar), when Tibetan intellectuals were assimilating the newly imported Indic teachings. This talk focuses on a Tangut manuscript that presents an anthology of five tantric Buddhist texts. While the contents reflect a known tantric practice lineage from twelfth-century Tibet with some Tibetan textual counterparts already identified, this talk will examine some textual discrepancies between the Tangut and Tibetan versions. These discrepancies, along with the Tangut texts' anthologized format, lead to the conclusion that they might not be literal translations of the Tibetan counterparts. Instead, I propose that the anthology might have served the pragmatic purposes of local interests in the tantric rituals. Then too, the talk demonstrates how these Tibetan Buddhist materials from the Tangut State may be used to enrich our knowledge of the "Later Spread", a formative era in the history of Tibetan Buddhism.Xingjian Zhang is a PhD student in the Group in Buddhist Studies at UC Berkeley. He received a B.A. in World History and Foreign Languages (Archaeology track) from Peking University in 2022 and an M.A. in Religion and Philosophy in Asia from LMU Munich in 2025. He is primarily interested in the history and literature of Tibetan Buddhist traditions in the 11th–13th centuries, with a particular focus on their transmission into the Tangut State (Xixia).

events.description: From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture In recent decades, scholarship on the Portuguese legacy in artistic expressions in Asia has hesitated to move beyond the global taxonomy of Indo-Portuguese, especially because of the difficulties of choosing or assuming the obvious terms on a case-by-case basis. Nationalisms, in the context of the nation-state crisis and religious-ethnic conflicts, are key clues to explaining this hesitation. Goan Catholic architecture is omnipresent in the promotional material of that fast-developing Indian state, an indisputable emblem of its brand and identity. What has defined its distinctive expression, its architectural grammar and discourse? In this lecture, I will present my contribution: between the colonial and the Goan, folk played a decisive role. Walter Rossa (Caracas, 1962), Architect (Lisbon, 1985), MA in History of Art (Lisbon, 1991), PhD and aggregated in Architecture (Coimbra, 2001 and 2013). Professor in the Department of Architecture and researcher at the Centre for the History of Society and Culture of the University of Coimbra. He holds the UNESCO Chair in Intercultural Dialogue in Heritages of Portuguese Influence (2019) and teaches courses in cultural heritage, town and regional planning, urban design, history, and architecture. Beyond his past work as a practising architect and town planner, he dedicated his efforts last year to cooperation and the relationship among heritage, history, planning, and development. He seeks to establish links between his academic work and development cooperation activities. A significant set of his publications is available at https://coimbra.academia.edu/WalterRossa

events.title: Lecture: Aurélie Godet, "The Festive Work of Empire: Ritual and Colonial Power in French Louisiana"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: How did the French monarchy govern a distant and precarious colony such as Louisiana? This lecture by Aurélie Godet (Nantes) argues that ceremony and festivity constituted a "technology" of imperial power as much as military force, administrative regulation, and Catholic evangelization. Royal celebrations, religious processions, Te Deum services, and other officially sanctioned festivities were transferred from metropolitan France to Louisiana as part of an imperial cultural policy designed to reproduce the ceremonial idiom of the monarchy overseas. Yet these rituals were not simply transplanted: colonial governors adapted and sometimes instrumentalized them to cultivate the allegiance of local elites, while their capacity to generate collective joy helped naturalize social and political hierarchies. For the Indigenous and African populations who inhabited this imperial festive landscape, festivity could function as a form of "counter-technology." Indigenous ceremonial practices – including calumet rituals, gift-giving, feasting, music, and dance – did not merely facilitate French diplomacy but enabled Native communities to reshape and sometimes contest the ritual terms of imperial encounters. Likewise, enslaved Africans exploited the temporal and spatial openings created by the colonial religious calendar and the ambiguities of the 1724 slave code to organize feasts and "noces." Such gatherings helped preserve cultural practices, create alternative communities, and occasionally challenge colonial restrictions on mobility and interracial sociability. By examining festivity as both an instrument and a site of contestation, this talk proposes to broaden the concept of imperial technology beyond bureaucratic and material systems to include the management of collective affect.Aurélie Godet is Professor of North American History at Nantes Université, France, and a junior fellow of the Institut Universitaire de France (2023–2028). After a decade of research on the history and ascendency of conservative movements and ideas in the United States, she shifted her focus in 2015 to the history of festivity in the Americas, with particular attention to the circulation of festive practices in the Atlantic world from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century. She recently completed a manuscript entitled Empire of Joy? The Cultural Politics of Festivity in French Colonial Louisiana (1682-1769), and serves on the editorial board of the Journal of Festive Studies, the peer-reviewed online journal she cofounded in 2019.

events.title: Ayesha S. ​Mahmud | Infectious Diseases in an Era of Global Change: Examples from Bangladesh
events.description: A talk by Ayesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud), Associate Professor of Demography, UC Berkeley on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, April 13, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) —————- ABSTRACT The ecological landscape of our planet is increasingly being shaped by a combination of global demographic shifts, such as rapid urbanization and increased human connectivity, and climatic changes, such as increases in mean temperatures and a greater frequency of extreme weather events. These global changes have important consequences for the emergence, evolution, geographic spread, and burden of infectious diseases. This talk will present insights from recent work on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally. SPEAKER BIOAyesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud) is an Associate Professor of Demography at UC Berkeley. Her research broadly examines the interplay between population change, environmental factors, and infectious disease dynamics. Drawing on theory and methods from demography and disease ecology, her work explores questions such as why outbreaks occur at particular times of year, how and why the mortality burden of infectious diseases changes over time, how population mobility shapes the spatial dynamics of outbreaks, and how global environmental and demographic change may alter patterns of infectious disease burden in the future. She uses statistical methods and biologically mechanistic models to investigate these questions across a range of diseases and settings in Asia, Africa, and Central America, drawing on data from disease surveillance systems, hospital databases, climate models, human mobility data, and population surveys and censuses. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Mahmud was a Rockefeller Foundation Planetary Health Fellow at Harvard University. She received her PhD in Demography from Princeton University in 2017.Event Poster TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. _____________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Ning Zheng: Molecular Glues: From Mechanisms to Therapeutics
events.description: Molecular glue (MG) degraders represent an exciting new modality in drug discovery highlighted by their ability to degrade undruggable targets and their favorable pharmacological properties. Thus far, only a very small number of MG degraders have been serendipitously found, most of which act on CULLIN4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. The scarcity of these novel compounds limits our understanding of their activity requirement, E3 ligases preference, and functional versatility, thereby hindering the prospective discovery of new MG degraders. In this presentation, I will highlight our latest studies on the identification of new MG degrader compounds as well as human disease mutations acting as genetic glues that foster neo-substrate-E3 interactions. These findings point to potential rational strategy for rational discovery of target-centric MG degraders.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: (Thomas Carell) Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture: "The second dimension of the genetic code"
events.description: Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture - DNA stores genetic information in the sequence of the four canonical bases dA, dC, dG, and T and, in addition, carries epigenetic information encoded by the four modified cytidine bases: 5-methylcytidine (mdC), 5-hydroxymethylcytidine (hmdC), 5-formylcytidine (fdC), and 5-carboxycytidine (cadC), with 5-hydroxymethyluridine (hmdU) potentially playing a role as well. These additional nucleosides are generated by TET(1–3) enzymes, which catalyze the stepwise oxidation of mdC or T to all the others, with the help of oxygen and -ketoglutarate. This oxidation chemistry in the genome thus establishes a second, largely uncharted layer of information. While the sequence code is static, the writing and erasure of the epigenetic code creates a dynamic information layer that controls gene activity, e.g. the differentiation of cells or memory formation and erasure in the brain. In this lecture, I will cover the discovery of the new epigenetic bases that expand the genetic alphabet using quantitative mass spectrometry and I will discuss new insights into their symmetry and localization based on recent sequencing data. I will then describe how the TET-based chemistry is now being exploited to develop new epigenetic sequencing methods that enable earlier cancer detection, thereby improving the chances of successful treatment. If time permits, I will also discuss why the modified base pseudouridine in mRNA allows the molecule to evade the innate immune system.

events.title: Lecture: The Afterlives of Resource Sovereignty
events.description: According to a 1959 issue of the Middle East Economic Digest, nearly sixty percent of the global reserves in oil were held by five US-based companies (three of which were descendants of Standard Oil), another eighteen percent by two British firms (Shell and British Petroleum), and the remainder by the Soviet Union, Mexico and other, smaller, producers. Thirty years later, and after the tumultuous struggle for resource sovereignty, nationalisation of oil had enacted what historian Christopher Dietrich has called "the most concentrated peacetime transfer of wealth in history." In this talk, Dr Laleh Khalili will advance a provisional argument about how states, corporations, and capitalists that formerly benefited from their ownership of oil recuperated from such massive losses by their transformation of the mechanisms for pricing oil, exploring for and exploiting it, accounting for it, financing it, and transporting it. These new mechanisms were directly responsible for the dismantling of social democracy in the global North and the moment of decolonization in the global South.Laleh Khalili is a professor of Gulf Studies at the University of Exeter, and the author or editor of seven books including most recently Sinews of War and Trade: Shipping and Capitalism in the Arabian Peninsula (Verso 2020) and Extractive Capitalism: How Commodities and Cronyism Drive the Global Economy (Profile 2025).

events.title: Workshop: Work, War and Commerce
events.location: Center for Middle Eastern Studies, 340 Stephens Hall
events.description: In this workshop, we will read about the intertwined lives of war and commerce, and the people who work and whose work is defined by them. The workshop will engage with theoretical as well as empirical research works that engage with the work of trade, communication and transportation and the central role violence plays in their working and asks how do we research these intertwined subjects? About the Instructor:Laleh Khalili (https://experts.exeter.ac.uk/41005-laleh-khalili) is a professor of Gulf Studies at the University of Exeter, and the author or editor of seven books including most recently Sinews of War and Trade: Shipping and Capitalism in the Arabian Peninsula (Verso 2020) and Extractive Capitalism: How Commodities and Cronyism Drive the Global Economy (Profile 2025). On Thursday, April 29th, Dr. Khalili will be delivering lecture The Afterlives of Resource Sovereignty in Maude Fife Room on UC Berkeley's campus. Click here (https://iranianstudies.berkeley.edu/lecture-afterlives-resource-sovereignty) to learn more about the event.
